Uniform Title: *Prāṇatoṣiṇī*, Sarga-kāṇḍa Author: Rāmatoṣaṇa Compiler:
Rāmatoṣaṇa Bhaṭṭācārya Description: Compiled by Rāmatoṣaṇa Bhaṭṭācārya; originally published in Kolkata in Bengali script as part of the *Tantrasārādivividhatantrasaṃgraha*.
Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: December 11, 2007.
Publisher: Kalikātā.
Year of publication: Pre-1900.
Country of Publication: India || Śrīḥ ||
The *Prāṇatoṣiṇī* was composed by Śrī Rāmatoṣaṇa Bhaṭṭācārya,
having compiled it from the Tantric scriptures.
And it was published by the learned Kulapati, the bearer of the title *upādhyāya*, Śrī Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara Bhaṭṭācārya,
in the city of Calcutta.
Printed at the Calcutta Press:

1) In the dullness of the *Sarga-kāṇḍa*, the poem bestows the state of the ocean upon a drop of water that has quickly fallen; indeed, it even imparts the infinitesimal nature of a water-atom to the ocean itself.

O Jayatāre! By serving the lotus feet of you who are ever victorious, Brahmā, Upendra, Maheśvara, and the rest daily conquer their respective states— whether it be total subservience to one [of them], or being a mere speck of dust on a mountain, or possessing immovability amidst the dust, or having diverse desires at will— all with ease and in an instant through your grace.

Salutations to that Bhavānī, by worshipping whom Suratha attained the status of a Manu; may she herself— whose very nature is knowledge and meditative absorption— bestow upon us our desired fruits, she who performs the acts of creation and so forth.
In the lineage of Viśvāsa, there was one named Vimalamati-dayārāma-viśvāsa;
his son was Rāmahari, who was exceedingly self-controlled and pre-eminently virtuous.
Viśvāsa, devoted to the worship of the feet of Viśvanātha and the abode of universal trust, having resided for a long time in various ways in Vārāṇasī...
Having performed the true action, one attains liberation.

His son was the protector of the earth, Śrī Prāṇakṛṣṇa, who was most fortunate, venerable, and preeminent among various groups of scholars; his younger brother was the renowned Jaganmohana. Six sons were born to him, all of whom possessed pure intellects and were endowed with fortitude and profundity.
Their minds were solely intent upon supporting the poor, the helpless, the blind, their kinsmen, and the hosts of the twice-born.
There, Ānandamaya— ever the eldest, most excellent, and always compassionate, who dispels poverty— is absorbed in meditation upon the Great Goddess,
Maheśvarī’s queen. He is as skillful as Upendra, a devotee of the Blessed Lady, and a bee longing for the pair of lotus feet of the Lord of Bhavānī.
The younger brother is Śrī Rāmacandra;

he is a donor equal to Karṇa, like Arjuna in battle, and like Kṛtānta (Yama) toward his enemies. His younger brother is likewise Śrī Viśvanātha, a donor whose very nature is compassion for the distressed.
After that, the illustrious Śambhunātha appeared; after him came the beautiful [Sundara]; following him was his younger brother named Śrī Kāśīnātha; and then arose Candranātha, like the moon.
On the eastern bank of the celestial river (the Gaṅgā), there is the famous place called Khaḍḍahā, which is the eternal abode of the gods.

May that village, established by the great sages Nityānanda and others in a state of supreme purity, resembling the abode of Indra, and enriched by auspicious dwellings, gardens, and the temple of Bhīmā— situated two *yāmas* north of the city of Kalkātā (Calcutta), the capital of the land— be ever victorious.
In that city dwells the illustrious Śrī Prāṇakṛṣṇa, who has shaken off all personal desires; he is equal to Indra, the protector of a treasury filled with collections of most precious jewels,
and like the moon upon the earth, he is glorious, wise, and the crest-jewel of the lineage of Viśvāsa.
May he, who is like the sun itself in his majesty and who burns the grass of his enemies with his prowess, live long for the sake of his subjects.
Moreover:
Having examined various types of astrological treatises composed by many scholars,
he caused this compendium— which is an ocean for the practice of Prāṇakṛṣṇa— to be made. Then, having briefly observed those of diverse kinds, [he compiled it].
He diligently caused the ocean of the *Prāṇakṛṣṇīya* to be composed.
Having brought together various tantras from many different regions,
the wise subsequently composed various compendiums numbering fifty-six;
this is evident from the mention of the names of kings such as Jayasiṃha and others in those compendiums.

He considered the excellent fame of his work to be more imperishable than all other forms of renown; indeed, even for those who have long been dead, they continue to live well through the names preserved in books.
Thus, the accomplished author diligently sought out a wise person to cause the book to be composed.
He did not obtain it suddenly; therefore, he remained constantly absorbed in anxious thought.
Then, having made his mind a bee hovering around the lotus-feet of the illustrious Śiva, he constructed a monastery in the beautiful city of Kalkātā.
Śrī Prāṇakṛṣṇa Viśvāsa, the sun of the Viśvāsa lineage, commanded Śrī Gopīnātha Miśra— who had brought this work, the *Rāmatoṣaṇa*—
to compose a compendium of the best among the Tantric scriptures.
Having bowed down thousands of times to the six gurus who bestow all knowledge,
[I shall explain] the Muṇḍamālā, the Matsyasūkta Tantra,
the Mahiṣamardinī, the Māyā, the divisions of the Mātṛkā, and the excellent Mātṛkodaya.
The Mahānirvāṇatantra and likewise the Mālinīvijaya, the Mahānīla, the Mahākālasaṃhitā, the Merutantraka,
Bhairava, Bhairavī, and also this very Bhūtaḍāmara.
The Vīrabhadra, the Bījacintāmaṇi, and likewise the Ekajaṭī;
the Nirvāṇatantra, the Tripurāsāra, and the Kālīvilāsaka;
the Viśvasāra, the Varadā, and the Vāsudevarahasyaka.
The Vārāhī, the Vṛhadgautamīya, the Varṇoddhṛti, the tantra known as the Viśvasāra, the Viṣṇuyāmala,
the Vṛhannīla, the Vṛhadyoni, and the Rahasya approved by Viṣṇu.
And the Vāmakeśvaratantra is the knowledge of Brahman; beyond that there is nothing higher.
The Brahmajāmalamahaita, the Varṇavilāsa,
the Phetkāriṇī Tantra, the Puraścaraṇacandrikā,
the Puraścārarasollāsa Tantra, and the auspicious Pañcadaśī.
Picchilā, Prapañcasāra, Haṃsādya, Pārameśvara, Navaratneśvara, Nitya, Nīla, Nārāyaṇīyaka,
Niruttara, Nāradīya, and thereafter the Nāgārjuna-mata.
The Dakṣiṇāmūrtitantra and the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā,
the Dattātreyasaṃhitā and likewise the Aṣṭāvakrasaṃhitā;
the Yakṣiṇī, Yoginī, Yoni, Yogasāra, and its ocean (Yogārṇava).
The *Yoginīhṛdaya*, the unsurpassed *Yogiyājñavalkya*,
the *Yogāmbarodaya*, and the *Ākāśabhairava*;
[the *Rājarājeśvarī*,] Rādhā, Revatī, and the *Rudrayāmala*.
The *Rāmārcanacandrikā*, the *Sāvara* and the *Indrajāla*,
the *Kālītantra*, the *Kāmākhyā*, and thereafter the *Kāmadhenu*; the *Śrīkālīkulasarvasva* and the *Kumārītantra*.
The Kṛkalāsadīpikā and likewise the Kaṅkālamālinī; the Kālottara, the Kubjikā, the Kuloḍḍīya, the Kulārṇava,
the Kalpasūtra known as the Kulamūlāvatāra, and the Yakṣaḍāmara.
The *Sarasvatī*, the *Sāradā*, the *Śaktisaṅgamatantra*,
the *Śaktikāgamasarvasva*, the *Mūrdhāmnāya*, the *Svarodaya*,
the *Svatantratantra*, the *Sammoha*, the *Cīnācāra*, and the *Toḍala*.
The *Ṣaḍanvayamahāratna*, the *Siddhaikavīratantra*, the *Kalpadruma* of the Veda, its creeper (*latā*), and its very essence; the *Tārārahasya*, the *Śrīśyāmārahasya*, and the *Skandajāmalam*.
Having examined numerous tantras such as these, as well as the Purāṇas, the Pañcarātra,
the compendia of Śruti and Smṛti, and other scriptures— just as one gathers jewels from the oceans— I have extracted these gems.
This *Prāṇatoṣiṇī* was composed by Śrī Rāmatoṣaṇa.

The wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpadruma*) grants only that which is thought of; the wish-granting gem (*cintāmaṇi*) [grants] something here and there; and the cow of plenty (*kāmadughā*) [grants] one's desired object.
But this creeper (*vratati*), composed by Śrī Prāṇatoṣaṇa, bestows upon people every fruit to be given on earth as soon as it is seen.
Let not the ignorant person disregard this garland of syllables, radiant by its very nature and composed of various jewels; let him behold it!

Through the compassion of the feet of the true guru, the dull-witted person sees the universe; with a destroyed intellect, he perceives this world directly as Brahman itself. If, through the guru, he becomes possessed of dispassion, then—

O Master! In this shoreless, vast, and formidable ocean of worldly existence—where the winds of desire blow and the high, towering waves surge—be the helmsman for me who am terrified and have taken refuge in a worn-out boat for the sake of attaining my desired goal. [I speak] this to those envious ones who mock me with their vision of faults.
I speak the truth; having heard it, do as pleases you. O venerable ones! With palms joined in humility, I say all these words of the elders and teachers here.
These [verses] have prepared the limbs of this creeper; O wise ones, discern whether there are faults or merits in me.
Those who, like bees at the time of another [season], take up only particles of virtue from a mass of faults as if it were a lotus-stained pond,

let them behold this wondrous creeper fashioned by one such as me— a beautiful and auspicious vine for those who approach it, radiant with jewels, possessing seven stalks consisting of creation, dharma, purpose, desire, devotion, knowledge, and freedom from qualities (nairguṇya). This creeper is variegated...
Adorned with flowers, leaves, buds, fruits, and various types of unopened blossoms,

may this [tree]— variegated with the rays of the sun that are red with the discourses on the meaning of the various sciences— destroy the suffering born of the shadows of words concerning the primary nature of established doctrines for those whose minds are distressed and overwhelmed by the great heat.
This [commentary] was born during the fourth quarter of the current Yuga, which is numbered by the eyes of the elephant (two) within the Vaivasvata Manvantara;

in the year measured by the earth (one), the eyes (two), Dharma (three), and the Yuga (four)—that is, 1324—on the day of Rādha (Vaiśākha), on the third lunar day (triguṇa) of the soft-rayed moon (the waxing moon);
and when the Śaka era, measured by the eyes (two), the Yugas (four), the mountains (seven), and Kāśyapi (twenty-one)—that is, 2471—had passed, on the lunar day of Akṣaya (the twelfth).
There appeared the *Śrī-Prāṇatoṣiṇī*, which delights the lotus-like minds of the wise,
brings satisfaction to the most excellent Brahmin Śrīyuta Rāma, and surpasses the splendor of the moon, the earth, and Sarasvatī combined by its own radiance.

O Speech, you are the delighter of fortune and life, possessed of all virtues, with a body radiant like a diamond-eye; eternally tender, ever-new, and beautiful with the nine poetic sentiments, you dwell amidst planted gardens.
Yet, with a mind intent on wicked purposes, you shall follow this world as an aged form from afar.
O Goddess! Salutations to you, who [overcome] those whose intellects are blinded by the conceit of insignificant matters.
Having offered salutations to the deity who dispels obstacles at the beginning of each section (*kāṇḍa*), I composed seven sections that illuminate with jewels.
This garland, consisting of fifty syllables, possesses infinite forms; it is white as the pure moon, dark as the clouds of the direction of Śiva, and clothed in the raiment of the quarters of space.
May Mālakāntā, who grants desired boons when meditated upon and who is beautiful with her mass of flowing hair, now bring us prosperity.
The primordial, stainless section on the new creation, wherein exists the form of sound—
the source of the investigation into the eternal and the non-eternal, of words, of Viṣṇu, of medicinal herbs, of stars, and of the celestial bodies;
this entire world of moving and unmoving beings has arisen from the elements, and it is the resonance of Brahman that impels the phonemes from within living creatures.
The procedure for writing, as well as the names of the letters and so forth.
For the sake of engaging people in this matter, I have first provided a brief enumeration of some [terms];
let it be known that there are many others as well.
First, the praise of the Tantra and so forth; the cause for the manifestation of the phonemes (varṇa); the manifestation of Śiva and Śakti; the description of their respective states;
the threefold nature of Śakti; and the determination of the powers of Brahmā and the other deities.
Without power (*śakti*), these [entities] would be inert; such is the description of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*).
The eternal form of the Lord is both the Word-Brahman and the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahman*). Thus ends the first section of the first chapter on Creation. || 1 ||
The exposition of the theory of the word-sphoṭa is for the purpose of manifesting the meaning. Two positions—the well-known and the non-eternal—are proclaimed regarding the eternal.
[This includes] the defects of the non-eternal view and the determination of the well-known view.

The refutation of the views that "Brahman is sound" and "Brahman is the meaning of sound" has been presented; likewise, the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) and the established conclusion (siddhānta) regarding the eternal [nature of Brahman] have been described. The body is composed of the thirty-six principles and is endowed with the coverings (kañcukas).
Then there are the digits (kalās) arising from the letters of the moon, fire, and the [other] digits;
likewise, those born of the letters, along with Śakti, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, as well as the medicinal herbs (auṣadhis).
Furthermore, the purpose of the medicinal herbs is the Haṃsa, which is the letter born of transformation (vikṛti).
The manner of its transformation is such that the *haṃsa* arises from the *praṇava*;
likewise, there is an illustration of its persistence within the *praṇava* even when [the phonemes] perish together.
Furthermore, there is another means of proof for understanding the eternity of the phonemes (*varṇas*).
In the two systems of thought, there is the observation of the Vedas as both eternal and non-eternal.
Their eternity is true when established by means of reasoning, perception, and valid cognition.
From the phonemes arise the planets, zodiac signs, and lunar mansions, which consist of the rotation of the wheel.
The determination of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and trees arising from the new moon and other dates;
the observation of faults incurred by cutting even one's own natal tree;
the presiding deities of the constellations and the determination of the origins (*yoni*) of the lunar mansions.
The observation of their mutual opposition in the consideration of husband and wife and so forth,
the determination of the lunar day (tithi) and its lord, and the description of the presiding deity of the lunar day—
thus concludes the second chapter on the germinating of seeds (aṅkura). || 2 ||
The emergence of Sadāśiva and others, the determination of time such as the lava,
the commencement of the creation of the principles (tattvas), the threefold nature of the ego (ahaṃkāra),
the creation from the threefold ego, and the arising of the elements beginning with sound.
The forms of the elemental mandalas, the fourfold creation of the body,
the method of quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa), and thereafter the origin of plants;
then birth from non-plant sources due to sin, and after that, the expiation for that.
(p. 6) The description of the origin of beings born from sweat and the origin of those born from eggs; the praise of the human state and likewise the sequence of birth and death;
everything is born from primordial nature (prakṛti) and dissolves back into it again.
Thus ends the third section on the delimitation of the branches. || 3 ||
The conception of a fetus from the male seed residing within a menstruating woman;
the etiology of menstruation; the process by which the seed enters the womb;
and immediately thereafter, the causes for the birth of a female, a male, or a neuter.
The seed for having many offspring and so forth is the powerful cause for conception;
the entry of the *jīva* (life-principle) therein is the cause for the production of semen and other elements;
and there is the sequence for the production and excretion of sweat, urine, and feces.

The cause of the arising of disease, the sequence of the arising of the elements (dhātu), then the functions of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth, followed by the description of the embryo (kalala) and other stages; this impurity, discrimination, and likewise the sprout of the mass of flesh.
The production of fat, marrow, and so forth; the formation of the limbs and minor members;
the granting of desired boons by the mother; likewise, the determination of the fruits thereof;
the emergence of the skin, ears, and other organs; and the completion of the joints.

The determination of the humors (doṣas) and the affected tissues (dūṣyas), the description of the sense organs and so forth, the determination of the internal organs, the twenty-five principles (tattvas),
the body according to the qualities of the five elements, and the description of the ten vital airs (vāyus).
The description of the channels (nāḍī), the root of the channels, the vessels situated at the gateways, the branches and sub-branches of the channels, and then the determination of their locations;
[the description of] the bones, bone-joints, muscles, and so forth; it is considered that for women, there is an excess of muscles.
The completion of the fourfold non-interruption of the secondary branches. || 4 ||
The names of the winds, the determination of their primacy and so forth,
their respective forms, locations, and functions;
and the movement of the sun and moon when the vital breath (prāṇa) enters the Piṅgalā and Iḍā.
The names of the humors (*doṣas*), the affected tissues (*dūṣyas*), and the digestive fires (*agnis*) are given, followed by the description of the waves and the sheaths.
Thereafter, the manner in which the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) perceives objects is explained,
and the locations of ether (*khādi*) and the other elements within the ears and other sense organs are primarily demonstrated.
The arising of disease occurs when the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) are displaced by wind, bile, and phlegm.
Furthermore, the recollection of past perceptions while situated in the womb is the characteristic of this state.
Regarding the dimensions of the uterus (*garbhāśaya*), that which follows is of three kinds according to karma.
The manner of thought within the womb, and thereafter the state of motionlessness;
the account of the imperishable [soul] residing in the body, the fourteen worlds, and the arrangement of mountains,
continents, planets, zodiac signs, and constellations within that body.
The occurrence of the appearance of drops of blood from the semen and the ovum;
likewise, the abodes of the sun and moon, as well as those of Brahmā and the other deities;
the emergence of the infant from the womb; and the forgetting of what was previously experienced.
At the time of emerging from the womb, however, the suffering of sinners is even greater;
at that time of weeping, there is no perception of sound or form.
Furthermore, the state of the body and the acquisition of a new body occur according to one's karma.
"The enjoyment after death of an action performed in this life is certain"—thus concludes the section concerning those whose form is like a sprout. (5)
When the manifestation of Kuṇḍalinī occurs in fifty ways, beginning with the single [unit], through the undifferentiation of the path of hearing (śruti) into indistinct syllables and speech,
then, being multiplied, there arises in due order the emergence of words, meanings, and so forth.
Fifty names of Kāma and fifty names of Rati follow in sequence;
after that, the names of Gaṇeśa together with his Śaktis;
then the names of the Kṣetrapāla, and thereafter the fruit of his worship and so forth.
From bliss arises the manifestation of the phonemes (*varṇa*); at the end of that manifestation, however, there is forgetfulness.
The locations for the manifestation of the phonemes are the syllables born of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire.
All phonemes are born of the Visarga; this is the description of the eight locations.
The sequence of the pronunciation of phonemes and the determination of the syllables consisting of the five elements; thus concludes the sixth chapter, which takes the form of a hymn of praise.
Then follows the sequence of scripts, which is the cause for manifesting the body of letters upon a leaf;
this includes the deities associated with the phonemes from *a* to *kṣa*,
the prohibition against writing on the ground, and the rules concerning the pen.
Then follows the measurement of the book, the determination of the holes in the book,
the determination of the leaves of the manuscript, and the censure of writing the Vedas;
as well as the difference in deities according to the different ages (yugas), the letters, and the worship of the written text.
The condemnation of the scribe’s acceptance of wages at the commencement and other stages [of the work] concludes the seventh chapter, "The Severing of the Bud. || 7 ||
The names beginning with the syllable *oṃ* and ending with *kṣa*, as well as the flowers that serve as the secret symbols of the Tantra, conclude with the eighth chapter.
The mantras originating from the five faces, as well as the scriptures such as the Tantras, were produced;
thereafter, Gaṇeśa performed the expansion of all the Tantras;
and immediately following that, he established the state of being the seed-syllables for the Mahāmahā-vidyās.
Likewise, there is the determination of the eighteen branches of knowledge and the philosophical systems;
the authorship of scriptures and other works through the immersion in the power of the Lord;
and the investigation into the authors of scriptures, beginning with human beings.
The determination of logic (*ānvīkṣikī*) and the other sciences does not remove the mental sin of householders; rather, the Lord, whose nature is twofold, is the cause of that,
as well as the seed for the introduction of the Tantras, known by the name Pañcavaktra.
The form of the Five-Faced One (Pañcavaktra), the description of the five traditions (āmnāya),
the exposition of the six traditions, the deities of the various traditions,
the fruit of the traditions, and likewise the determination of their swift results.
The determination of the conduct and other practices of the mantras belonging to the various scriptural traditions;
the definitive resolution of the sciences and scriptures according to their exceptions and general rules;
and likewise, the classification of mantras and vidyās based on the distinctions among the deities.
The feminine, masculine, and neuter nature of mantras in the six types of rites;
the fierce and gentle character of mantras, as well as their sleep, wakefulness, and so forth— thus concludes the ninth chapter, on the severing of the filaments.
The determination of defects such as "cutting" (chinnā) and others regarding mantras, along with their remedies;
the characteristics of Mahāmudrā and likewise the form of Yonimudrā;
the characteristics of the throat-seat and how the recollection of the six wheels (ṣaṭcakra) is performed.
Following that, one should meditate upon the chosen deity within the thousand-petaled lotus;
thereafter, the sequence of contemplation proceeds again through the root-support lotus (*mūlādhāra*) and the others.
Then, the subsequent rite consists of the projection of the syllables of the mantra into the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*).
Through practice for one year, that fruit is the attainment of unsurpassed perfection.
For one who is unattached, however, the procedure for recitation consists of the application of the *yonimudrā*,
the placement of the *bhūtalipi*, and the determination of its seers (*ṛṣi*) and other attributes.
Meditation on the Bhūtalipi, followed by the consecration of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā),
the placement of the phonemes (varṇanyāsa), worship, and the ninefold cycles,
as well as the fire-oblation (homa) performed with the Bhūtalipi encased according to the specific desired aim— [these constitute the practice].
When it has been recited one thousand times for the duration of a single month,
then that *mantra*, which grants all accomplishments and is the cause of the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*),
is known by the names of the seeds; this is the consensus of the *Bhūtaḍāmara*.
This name is coextensive with the delimitation of space. || 10 ||
Whatever authority has been upheld by the authors of the *Tantrasāra*, who are suns to the lotus of our lineage, there is no need for anything further here;
all of that, including the mantras, yantras, and so forth, should be consulted therein.

The ritual placement (*nyāsa*), worship (*pūjā*), and other mudrās, as well as hymns (*stava*) and armor-mantras (*kavaca*), along with the consecration of the rosary (*mālā-saṃskāra*) and all such rites, are entirely contained therein; therefore, I shall collect those [elements] not already held there, even if they appear only occasionally in the *Smṛti* tradition.

For the sake of explaining [the work] according to the sequence of the root text, and in order to refute the objections of disputants, I maintain that which was held by him; for in those places where only the intended meaning was shown by that wise master, [I shall expand upon it].
No authority was provided for that; therefore, that authority is now being recorded.

Furthermore, where the Great-Souled One has provided an explanation of the intended meaning of the words, it is [recorded] for the sake of those of dull intellect who laugh at him because they do not understand it.
I shall clarify all of that according to the determination of the meaning of the scriptures.
(p. 9) This sequence is to be understood by the wise in every section:
first there is the seed, rich with new sprouts; thereafter it becomes possessed of divine branches and sub-branches, and from that, the foliage is produced.
From that cluster arose a bud, from that a flower;
the filament emerged, and this sweet fruit was born.
O learned one, through these stages of creation, quickly anoint your pair of eyes and behold everything clearly and without impurity.
Blessed, venerable, excellent, and foremost among those endowed with noble fame;
the abode of steady fortune, possessed of prosperity, and devoted to his own beloved Lord;
Prāṇakṛṣṇa lives long together with the sons of the Blessed One.
In the eighth chapter of the Muṇḍamālā Tantra:
"O Maheśvarī! O lady of excellent complexion! Without the Tantra, without Mantra, and without Yantra, neither worldly enjoyment nor liberation arises."
In the *Matsyasūkta-mahātantra*, in the twenty-four thousand [verse] work, in the upper section, in the first part, in the fourth chapter:
"Viṣṇu is the most excellent among the gods,
just as the ocean is among lakes, just as the Gaṅgā is among rivers, and the Himālaya is among mountains."
Just as the Aśvattha is the best among all trees, as Indra is the foremost among kings, as Durgā is among goddesses, and as the Brāhmaṇa is among the social classes,
so too is the Tantra scripture the most unsurpassed among all scriptures.
Thus ends the praise of the Tantric scriptures.
In the first chapter of the *Vṛhannīlatantra*:
"In whatever house the Tantra resides, there Lakṣmī becomes firmly established."

O Queen of the Gods! O Beloved! A miracle shall occur for one who has taken refuge in the Great Soul at the royal gate, in a cremation ground, in an assembly hall, in the midst of battle, in a solitary place, in terrible waters, or in a region infested with beasts of prey.
Therefore, it must be guarded with every effort and great care. Thus ends the section on the fruit of maintaining the Tantra scriptures in the home,
according to the Matsyasūkta.

"Those [practices] taught in the Tantras and Āgamas must not be rejected through logical reasoning, because they were composed by the Lord; therefore, for the twice-born, the performance of rites prescribed in the Tantras is not to be prohibited by means of dialectical argument.
This is the prohibition against the abandonment of Tantric rites on the basis of rationalist discourse.
In that very same [text]:
"In astrology, in the science of mantras, in medicine, and in Vedic ritual,
one should grasp only the meaning and should not deliberate over corrupt words."
"Mantravāda" refers to that in which there is discourse on mantra; thus, it is the Tantra.
In the *Jyotir-ādi*, there is a prohibition against investigating words;
in that very same [text]:
One should not entertain doubt regarding the Word on the grounds that it is unperceived in some instances;
rather, one should resolve with faith, because of its infinite nature as the form of the Word.
This is also stated in the ninth chapter of the *Nirvāṇatantra*.
The very nature of the Śabdabrahman has emerged from my mouth;
one who desires liberation must not entertain any doubt.
Through doubt, one goes to the Raurava hell along with one's ancestors.
Thus ends the refutation of doubt in the Tantra scripture.
In the second chapter of the Gandharva Tantra:
"In all matters, everywhere—whether Tantric or Vedic—"
Lack of faith is a great defect; one should avoid it with effort.
O Goddess! Faith is declared to be the cause of complete accomplishment.
Thus is the fruit of faith in the teaching.
In the fourteenth chapter of the Mahānirvāṇatantra.
What is the use of wandering to sacred fords, or what is the use of sacrifices and the practice of recitation?
One who knows this great tantra is liberated from the bonds of karma;
he is perfected in all scriptures and is the best among those who know all dharmas.
O Kālikā! He who knows the Tantra is a wise knower of Brahman, a true saint.
Thus is the fruit of the knowledge of the tantra.
In that very place [it is said]:
"Enough with the Vedas, the Purāṇas, the Smṛtis, the Saṃhitās, and so forth;
what is the use of many other Tantras? By knowing this one [reality], one becomes all-knowing."
Thus, even for a single tantra, there is the fruit of knowledge.
In the second chapter of the Gandharva Tantra:
"Now, [the disciple] should be faithful, pure, skillful, free from duality, and one who has conquered the senses;
he should be most devoted to Brahman, a proponent of Brahman, identified with Brahman, and solely intent upon Brahman."
One who is completely free from all violence and devoted to the welfare of all living beings shall be qualified for this scripture; anyone other than such a person is not a practitioner here.
Thus concludes the exposition on the qualifications for the study of the Tantric scriptures.
In the first chapter of the Kubjikātantra.
In the three preceding ages, worship should be performed according to the injunctions of the Śruti and Smṛti;
however, in the Kali age, the wise man should sacrifice to the gods according to the injunctions declared in the Āgamas.
For in the Kali age, the gods do not become pleased by any other method.
Also, in the third chapter of the *Puraścaraṇarasollāsa-tantra*:
"O fair-faced one, in the Kali age, the meditation and mantra taught in the Tantras are highly praised,
as are those declared in the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and the Purāṇas."
O lady with tremulous eyes! It is never praised [to do so] in the Kali age in Bhārata.
And in the second chapter of the Mahānirvāṇatantra:
"O Beloved! In the Kali age, there is no way [to attain the goal] without the path of the Āgamas.
O Śivā! It was previously stated by me in the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and other texts that in the Kali age, the wise man should worship the gods according to the procedure prescribed in the Āgamas."
He who, disregarding the scriptures of the Kali age, proceeds by another path.
"It has no destination—this is the truth, the truth; there is no doubt about it."
Likewise, in the Kali age, the mantras proclaimed in the Tantras are effective and bestow results swiftly;
they are recommended for all rites, such as recitation, sacrifice, and ritual performance.
Those belonging to the Vedic tradition, however, are devoid of potency, like serpents stripped of their venom.
In the Kṛta and other ages, all [mantras] were effective; in the Kali age, they are like corpses.
Just as dolls on a wall, though endowed with all the senses, are incapable of action, so too are other multitudes of mantras.
An action performed with other mantras is like sexual union with a barren woman;
there can be no attainment of fruit therein, for it is merely exhaustion.
In this Age of Strife (Kali), that man who desires success through paths proclaimed by others [will find none].
Thirsty, the fool digs a well on the bank of the Ganges;
there is no other path for the sake of liberation, nor for attaining happiness in this world or the next,
than the path proclaimed in the Tantra for the sake of both liberation and bliss.
Thus ends the explanation of the attainment of results through the rites prescribed in the Tantric scriptures during the Kali age.
In the *Muṇḍamālā*:
"The Guru who speaks the Tantra is Śiva himself;
O Maheśānī! as is the Guru, so is the supreme Guru."
Just as the supreme teacher (Parameṣṭhī) is the highest of all gurus,
and just as the guru who knows the mantras is himself the speaker of the tantras—
thus is the praise of the speaker of the tantras.
In that very same place.
Those people who are fierce and intent on devouring the flesh and bones of those who revile the Tantra, the teacher of the Tantra, and the Tantric practice—
for that very reason, one should never revile a knower of the Tantra.
They do not laugh, they do not revile, and they never speak otherwise at any time.
Thus ends the fault of disparaging the tantras and so forth.
In the first chapter.
Listen, O Goddess! O Mother of the Universe! [This is] the most auspicious of all auspicious things. O Queen of the Gods! One who hears this Tantra shall attain the Nirvāṇa of Brahman.
In the tenth chapter.
O Maheśānī! O beloved! Having heard and understood this King of Tantras, which is the essence of essences, one quickly attains liberation; of this there is no doubt.
In the eleventh chapter.
O Śivā! Whoever should hear this *Muṇḍamālā-tantra*, the supreme cause, which bestows knowledge, liberation, devotion, enjoyment, and happiness— thus, O Goddess, it is the ultimate [teaching],
difficult even for the gods to obtain.
He who knows that which is within the earth is indeed the knower of the ultimate truth.
Thus ends the fruit of hearing the specific tantras.
In the Nirvāṇa Tantra:
Having made his knowledge stainless and his intellect pure,
and having become endowed with great devotion and intent upon the welfare of all living beings,
if he hears this chapter while knowing it to be composed of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman);
Then one attains liberation; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
Whatever fruit is obtained by listening to the eighteen Purāṇas, that is attained by giving gold equal to Mount Meru to the preceptor, who is the very embodiment of Brahman.

O Supreme Goddess! O Śivā! if one who has mastered the Vedas should, with a spirit of devotion, give away the earth consisting of seven continents and abounding in crops, then, O Supreme Goddess, the fruit thereof is indeed manifold.
O lovely-limbed one! If one hears even a single chapter of this tantra, he will certainly obtain a fruit ten million times greater than that result.
Thus ends the description of the fruit of hearing even a single chapter of the tantra.
Without knowledge of the word, everyone is overcome by dullness;
therefore, I shall begin to speak of words that have come into manifestation.
[This is stated] in the first chapter of the *Sāradātilaka*.
From the Supreme Lord, who is the entirety of the manifestation of Being-Consciousness-Bliss, there arose Power (Śakti);
from that, Sound (Nāda); and from Sound, the emergence of the Point (Bindu).
By the phrase "from the glory of Sat-Cit-Ānanda," Rāghavabhaṭṭa maintains that there is no loss of the Lord's essential nature even when he is conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*).
The construction is: "From the All (the Lord) together with Prakṛti, Śakti arose. And so it is stated in that very same work:
The eternal Śiva is to be known as both devoid of attributes (nirguṇa) and possessed of attributes (saguṇa).
He who is devoid of attributes is distinct from primordial nature (prakṛti), while he who is possessed of attributes is remembered as being with parts (sakala).
Thus, there is the explanation that "kalā" is *prakṛti*, [the world] existing together with it.

Now, if it is asked: "How can there be power (*śakti*) again from that which is already accompanied by power?"—this is true; however, that which is of an eternal nature, which existed in a subtle state during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) through the superimposition of consciousness (*caitanya*), becomes possessed of qualities (*saguṇa*) due to the inequality of its constituent qualities (*guṇavaiṣamya*).

It should be understood that this statement by the author of the treatise is made by relying on the Sāṃkhya doctrine, according to which "origination" is used figuratively for either the means of accomplishing the manifold creation consisting of the *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* [evolutes], or for the abiding state of those qualities (*guṇa*).
To this effect, the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa states:
Whenever she manifests for the sake of accomplishing the tasks of the gods,
she is then called "born" in the world, even though she is eternal;
this is also from the *Prayogasāra* cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
Therefore, she who has emerged from that is eternal, all-pervading, and the source of the universe; for she is the origin (*sambhava*) of all things. To this effect, the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā also states:

"By the will of Śiva, the Supreme Power (Parā-śakti) attains oneness with the principle of Śiva (Śiva-tattva); thereafter, at the beginning of creation, she vibrates forth like oil from a sesame seed. Thus it is stated in the first chapter of the *Kubjikā-tantra*.

From that [Bindu] arose Nāda; from Nāda, Śakti was produced. O Maheśānī! She is the form of Nāda, the supreme digit whose nature is consciousness (cidrūpā). And from Nāda itself, O Maheśvarī, Ardhabindu was born.
From the three and a half bindus arises the serpent Kulakuṇḍalī; O Goddess, she is devoid of qualities and yet possessed of qualities, the eternal form of Brahman,
the Goddess whose nature is consciousness, who illuminates all beings.
"The Goddess, whose form is bliss, who illumines the bliss of Brahman"—
thus, the origin of the *bindu* mentioned at the beginning is not contradictory due to the different traditions (*āmnāya*).
That difference in tradition will become clear further on.
Thus is the emergence of Śakti from Saguna Śiva. Of that Śakti, however, there are two states suitable for the creation of Nāda and Bindu.
As it is said in the *Prayogasāra*:

"When that Śakti, awakened by means of Nāda, is oriented toward the state free from affliction (nirāmayapada) and turned toward Śiva, she is then known as having the form of the Puruṣa. Thus ends the distinction of the states of Śakti.
In the *Sāradātilaka*, the world-teacher Lakṣmaṇācārya, a resident of Kānyakubja, has stated that the *bindu* is also threefold by way of its forms as *icchā*, *sattva*, and so forth:
"Consisting of Śiva and Śakti, it is manifest; furthermore, it is divided threefold."
This *bindu* is threefold: consisting of Śiva, consisting of Śakti, and consisting of both.
Its threefold nature is described in that very same source:
"The divisions of that [bindu] are declared to be *bindu*, *nāda*, and *bīja*."
The Bindu is of the nature of Śiva, and the Bīja is Śakti;
their mutual equilibrium is declared as "sama" (equal) by those learned in all the Āgamas.
This is also stated in the Kriyāsāra:

The *bindu* there is of the nature of Śiva, and the *bīja* is remembered as being of the nature of Śakti. From the union of these two, *nāda* arises; from those [two] are born the three powers (*triśakti*).
Thus ends the description of the three *bindus*.
The three powers are described in that very same place:
"From the *bindu* of Raudrī, Jyeṣṭhā was born from the *nāda*, and from the *bīja* [of Jyeṣṭhā], Vāmā arose;
from these were produced the lords of Rudra, Brahmā, and Rāma."
They consist of knowledge, will, and action, and have the nature of fire, the moon, and the sun;
this very statement is also found in the *Śāradā*:
"They are Rudra, Brahmā, and the Lord of Ramā (Viṣṇu)—that is, Śiva, Brahmā, and Nārāyaṇa—respectively."
The meaning is that they have the nature of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), and the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).

For this very reason, these—having the nature of fire, the moon, and the sun—are to be understood as specific states of Śakti alone: the indicators of sound situated within creation, which take the form of the half-moon and the bindu.
By this, it is implied that agency in creation and so forth belongs to power (*śakti*) alone.
Now, one might object: the moon-form [of the Goddess] creates the universe, which exists as both word and meaning, as long as she sustains it;
then, in the form of the sun, she withdraws it all by her own power at the end of the age; yet, how can she ever [withdraw] that Śāradā from within the mind? (p. 14)
"I am forgetting.
Also in the Gorakṣasaṃhitā:
"Will, action, and likewise knowledge are Gaurī, Brāhmī, and Vaiṣṇavī."
That supreme light, which is "Om," wherein power (śakti) resides in three ways, is to be inferred here according to the circumstances:
knowledge is the power of Gaurī, will is the power of Brāhmī, and action is the power of Vaiṣṇavī; thus it is threefold, consisting of these three modes.

Even regarding that [deity] which is about to be described, there are the components of the *praṇava*— beginning with "by the three syllables of the *praṇava*"— consisting of the sun, moon, and fire; namely,
the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*, whose natures are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, as in the passage beginning "from the letter *a*, Brahmā was produced."

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśvara are established in their respective maṇḍalas; therefore, if one objects that there is a contradiction based on the preceding and following descriptions— since in those [other] places the letter *a* in the form of the Sun is Brahmā, whereas here the letter *a* in the form of the Sun is Viṣṇu— the sequence should be understood in accordance with the creation of the objects (*arthasṛṣṭi*), and not otherwise.
Thus it is established according to the manuscript.
However, in the tenth chapter of the *Pūrvakhaṇḍa* of the *Yoginītantra*,
having spoken thus, O Śāmbhavī, that Mahākālī bestowed [this] upon us.
The power of will, action, and knowledge is the means for accomplishing all effects;
the power of will was given to Viṣṇu, the power of action to Brahmā,
and the power of knowledge, which is the embodiment of all powers, was given to me.

Thus, that which was stated— that this is the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) of Viṣṇu— is not contradictory when considered according to the different *āmnāyas*. Likewise, the mutually contradictory statements regarding the forms and so forth of the five *āmnāyas*, the six *āmnāyas*, and their respective individual *āmnāyas* that are about to be described, [are to be understood] through the distinction of *sāttvika* and other qualities, or by means of the different *āmnāyas*.
The description of the creation of the Nibodhikā and others, stating that "these must be established," is found in the first chapter of the *Nirvāṇatantra*:
"In Satyaloka, she is formless, having the nature of great light."
Having cast off the bark of Māyā, she who consists of the universe becomes divided into two;
through the division of Śiva and Śakti, the conceptualization of creation arises. O Pārvatī, in the first [division], a son indeed born, known as Brahmā.
Kālikā said:
"Listen, my son! O Mahāvīra! Perform your marriage with diligence.
Having heard this, Brahmā then spoke these words respectfully.
"Without you there is no mother; O beautiful one, grant me power!
Hearing that, the Mother of the Worlds gave Mohinī from her own body.
She was the second Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), Sāvitrī, the supreme digit (Kalā).
Having obtained her company, perform the expansion of the Vedas;
become the effortless creator of the universe upon the circle of the earth.
In the second [birth], a son named Viṣṇu shall be born, who takes refuge in the quality of goodness (sattva).
Kālikā said:
"Listen, my son, O great hero! Perform your marriage with diligence.
Viṣṇu said:
"By the mere sight of you, a man becomes free from desire. O Mother! What shall I do? O Śivā, grant me a *mohinī* (a deluding power).
Having extracted the power (*śakti*) from her body, she gave it to him.
And for him, O Supreme Goddess, is Kālikā; that great Vidyā, Śrīvidyā, belonging to Viṣṇu. Relying upon her, Mahāviṣṇu protects the entire universe.
In the third [birth], a son was born who was a great yogi, Sadāśiva. Seeing him, Mahākālī, being in her fertile season, became joyful.
"Listen, my son! O great yogi! Take my words to heart."
"Who else but you is a true man, or who else but me is a truly enchanting woman?
Therefore, O Śiva, you who are supreme bliss, perform my marriage!
Sadāśiva said:
"O Mother, it was said that there is no deluder for me without you;
this is true, O Mother of the World! And there is no man without me.
As long as this body remains, I shall not perform the marriage."
"O Mother, if you possess compassion, grant me another body.
At that very moment, Mahākālī gave her [the name] Bhuvanasundarī.
(From the first chapter of the Kubjikātantra.)
Brahmāṇī performs the act of creation, but Brahmā never does;
therefore, O Maheśānī, Brahmā is a ghost (preta), of this there is no doubt.
Vaiṣṇavī performs the act of protection, but Viṣṇu never does.
Therefore, O Maheśānī! Viṣṇu is a *preta*, there is no doubt; Rudrāṇī performs the act of devouring, but Rudra never does. Therefore, O Maheśānī! Rudra is a *preta*, there is no doubt.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others are proclaimed to be insentient;
O Goddess, it has been stated that without Prakṛti they are certainly incapable of all activity.
Thus ends the description of creation and so forth by means of Śakti.
He describes the origin of Śabdabrahman in the first chapter of the Śāradā-tantra: "From the supreme Bindu, as it was being differentiated, the excellent Unmanifest (Avyakta) came into being."

"Those proficient in all the scriptures call it Śabdabrahman. By the phrase "from the supreme Bindu," it is meant that from the first Bindu— which consists of the state of Śakti and which, as it begins to differentiate, is unmanifest in nature, devoid of distinctions such as phonemes, and indivisible— [the universe arises].

The meaning is that only the sound (*nāda*) has arisen. And it has been stated by Durgācārya: "That sound in which the phonemes (*varṇa*), such as *a* and so forth, are not manifested in their specific forms, is called unmanifest (*avyakta*) sound."
It is the undivided, unmanifest, all-pervading sound consisting of *nāda* and *bindu*, whose essence is Brahman; it is merely the first flash of the Supreme Śiva as He is intent on creation.
Thus, its heart is "Śabdabrahman," and likewise is the statement cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:

"From Prakṛti, who is primarily characterized by the power of action (kriyā-śakti) and whose form is the *bindu*, there arose the supreme Śabdabrahman, which is the cause of both word and its meaning. Thus it is also stated in the *Prayogasāra*.

O Goddess, at that time, that inner self, consisting of sound (nādātmā), vibrates by itself; just as [sound], having come into being through the differentiation of positions [of articulation], attains the state of phonemes (varṇatā) when impelled by the vital air, it shall emerge into manifestation from the physical body (piṇḍa).
In the *Śāradātilaka*: "It is my conviction that the consciousness of all beings is the Śabdabrahman;
having attained that [consciousness] which exists in the center of the bodies of living creatures in the form of Kuṇḍalin."

The grammatical connection is as follows: that consciousness, which is of the nature of the *bindu* and whose form is the *kuṇḍalinī*, appearing in the shape of the *praṇava* and residing within the bodies of living beings, manifests—that is, shines forth—in the form of phonemes (*varṇa*) through the distinctions of prose, verse, and so forth. As it is being differentiated, it appears in the form of phonemes.
"What having done?"—the ellipsis being "having reached the organs such as the throat.
And thus, in the *Prapañcasāra*, [Ācārya] Āścarya will say: "That which first arises from the *mūlādhāra* is the *tāra* known as *parā*," and so forth.
Therefore, it should be understood that the creation to be described hereafter proceeds from Kuṇḍalinī.
The twofold nature of Brahman, distinguished as Śabdabrahman and Paramabrahman, is stated in the first chapter of the fifth section of the Kulārṇava.
Knowledge is said to be twofold: that arising from scripture and that arising from discernment.
That which follows the method of scriptural tradition is the *Śabdabrahman*; that which is born of discernment is the supreme *Brahman*.
This is also stated in the sixteenth chapter of the sixth book of the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam*.
"I am all beings, the self of beings, and the creator of beings;
both the Śabdabrahman and the Parabrahman are my two eternal bodies.
Thus [it is said]; and the Śabdabrahman is the form of the supreme sound, as stated in the Bhagavad Gītā:

"Uttering the single-syllabled Brahman 'Om' and remembering Me, he who departs, casting off the body, goes to the supreme goal. Here, "Om" is an indicator for the mere sound; therefore, the Brahman residing in the mouth of the Guru, which is about to be described, is attained.

There is no contradiction with such statements as "by His grace," because the Lord exists everywhere. Furthermore, the meaning of the *praṇava* (Oṃ) is indeed the expressed object, for it is said in such passages as: "The supreme Brahman is remembered as the expressed object, while the *praṇava* is the designator. (p. 17)
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of Bījas and the Manifestation of Words," in the first section of the *Śrīprāṇatoṣiṇī*.
When words have thus emerged from the source (*ākara*), a cave of dispute has arisen in the form of doubt, due to the mutual desire for victory.
Now, there are three views regarding whether sounds (*śabda*) are eternal, non-eternal, or both well-established [as such].
Among these, in the first view, it is well said that sound is Brahman (*śabdabrahman*).
Furthermore, among those who maintain that sounds are non-eternal, there are many, including those who advocate for the internal *sphoṭa*.

Furthermore, those who maintain the doctrine of the external sphoṭa—consisting of both the genus (jāti) and the individual manifestation (vyakti)—debate as follows: "Now, how is a meaning conveyed by a word, given that [the letters] lack the capacity to convey it? For instance, do the letters, which convey the object through their fixed sequence, do so sequentially or simultaneously?"
Not the first [alternative].
For in cases such as "cow" (*gauh*), if the meaning were conveyed by each individual phoneme such as *ga* and so on, the subsequent phonemes would be redundant.
If it is argued that a certain portion of the meaning is conveyed by each phoneme individually, that too is untenable.
For there is no convention for the phonemes *g* and so forth with respect to the parts of a cow or similar objects.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable;
because those perceived at different times cannot exist simultaneously.
For phonemes, which perish as soon as they are uttered, persist only for that brief duration;

nor can there be a cognition of each preceding phoneme persisting into the cognition of each succeeding phoneme, because that would entail their eternity. For this very reason, the following [position] is refuted.

To whatever extent, and in whatever manner, those phonemes whose capacities are well-known are employed in the communication of a particular meaning, they convey that meaning in exactly that way. Therefore,
since there is no distinction between a phoneme that has not yet arisen and one that has arisen and perished— both being non-existent— the cognition of meaning cannot arise from phonemes.
It is possible that the *sphoṭa* is postulated as being manifested by the phonemes (*varṇa*) without being distinct from them.
It is called *sphoṭa* because "the meaning bursts forth" (*sphuṭati*) from it; thus, the suffix *al* is used in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*).
The utterance of the phonemes, however, is solely for the sake of the *sphoṭa*.

If it is argued that since phonemes (*varṇa*) are the manifestors of the *sphoṭa*, a manifestor is impossible through either succession or simultaneity, [we reply: the comprehension of meaning nevertheless occurs; because that [comprehension] would otherwise be inexplicable, the *sphoṭa* is postulated even in respect to the phonemes.
Therefore, from the *sphoṭa* of the phonemes comes the *sphoṭa* of the word (*pada-sphoṭa*), and from that arises the comprehension of meaning. And thus, through both succession and simultaneity—

The comprehension of the sentence-meaning arises from the *vākya-sphoṭa*, which is manifested by the *pada-sphoṭa* due to the impossibility of deriving the sentence-meaning from the individual words alone.
(p. 18) Now, an objection: immediately after the utterance of "gauḥ," we do not perceive anything further that is distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*);
only the phonemes themselves are apprehended.
Therefore, because it is not perceived, they challenge the proponent of the *sphoṭa*, saying that the so-called *sphoṭa*-form does not exist at all, just like the horn of a hare and the like;
"O proponents of the *sphoṭa*, even by means of oaths, your word is not to be accepted."
Who that possesses consciousness would assert that there exists a flower in the sky?
To this, the proponents of *sphoṭa* reply:
"The *sphoṭa* is not apprehended by direct perception."

For instance, following the sequential experience of the three phonemes— the letter *ga*, the letter *au*, and the visarga— in the word "gauh," there arises a cognition of a single, undivided form, namely, "the word. And yet, the three phonemes are not rendered meaningless in that cognition, because the cognition itself is unitary.
Just as the cognition of a cloth, arising from the threads themselves without being distinct from them, apprehends a cloth that is separate from the threads;
so too here, it apprehends another entity distinct from the three phonemes, and that is the *sphoṭa*.
But surely, no other entity distinct from the phonemes is ever perceived? Well then, even a cloth is not perceived as distinct from its threads.
How is it to be accepted that the cloth manifests in the cognition of the cloth? In that case, the *sphoṭa* likewise [manifests].
Now, what is the nature of this *sphoṭa*? Let it be pointed out with precision, as one would grasp a horn, saying "this is it. To this, it is replied:

For whatever is graspable by a particular cognition is indeed cognizable by that cognition alone, and not by other cognitions; therefore, even a cloth is apprehended only by the cognition of "that" (taṭa-buddhi) and not by another cognition. Thus it is.
Just as a cloth, which is a composite whole, is established through direct perception immediately after the experience of its threads, so too the sphoṭa—
manifested by the phonemes— is established through direct perception immediately after the experience of all the phonemes; such is the view of Gopīnātha Tarkācārya.
In the first chapter of the *Śāradātilaka*, the teachers begin to refute those two views:
"Some teachers understand 'Word-Brahman' (*śabdabrahman*) as the meaning of the word, while others understand it as the word itself.
Thus say some teachers.
They call the internal sphoṭa, which is the meaning of the word, the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman).
As it has been said:
"The internal sphoṭa, which is the meaning of the word, is indeed partless, undivided, and of the nature of eternal consciousness."

Other grammarians, however, maintain that *śabdabrahman* is the word characterized as the *vākya-sphoṭa*, which reveals an indivisible single meaning and is awakened by the apprehension of the final word, aided by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of each respective word manifested through the utterance of preceding phonemes.
As it has been said:
"The external form is indeed one, eternal, indivisible from those things manifested, whether it be the *vyakti-sphoṭa* or the *jāti-sphoṭa*.
(p. 19) But if sound were impermanent, then how could it have been taught by various sages and by Mahādeva in the various scriptures for the worship of the Goddess?
How is it that the very same word is spoken in various places at various times? This will become clear further on.
If it is argued that this fault does not apply to the position of eternality because the word itself is eternal, we say no;
for even in the position of non-eternality, there is no contradiction, since the single-natured Goddess of Speech issues forth in the form of words through various speakers.
Whose fault is it? It is due to the diversity of that power (*śakti*).
As for what is stated in the tenth chapter of the first section of the *Yoginītantra*:
"In the midst of that, I beheld a mass of letters, most brilliantly radiant."

"The radiance of ten million suns, the coolness of ten million moons, the blazing splendor of ten million fires—the eternal Supreme Brahman. This statement should be understood as referring to the primordial body residing within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and so forth; otherwise, for those residing within that body...
Even the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) and so forth would be eternal; for within His body, there are indeed cosmic eggs,
and millions upon millions of cosmic eggs of exceedingly vast dimensions.
"O Goddess! They move everywhere at all times; who would be capable of counting them?
This is to be understood from the subsequent words of Śiva.

Now, if you should argue that in your own view it follows that mantras, the Vedas, the Gāyatrī, and so forth, would be non-eternal—and that this is an acceptable consequence (iṣṭāpatti)—[then we reply:]...
"Uttering the single-syllabled Brahman 'Om' and remembering Me"— thus it is stated in the *Gītā*.
The Brahman residing in the mouth of the Guru is attained through His grace.
Thus it is stated in the *Gurugītā*.
And as stated in the sixth chapter of the *Guptasādhanatantra*: "Whatever has been proclaimed by the Guru to anyone, that is designated as Brahman for that person."
"Gāyatrī is the very form of Brahman," as stated in her *Kavaca*, and "the Vedic sentences are not of human origin," as stated by Durgasiṃha.
And it has been said: "The question of whether defects exist or do not exist applies to works of human authorship;
however, since there is no author for the Veda, we have no suspicion of defects whatsoever."

If it is argued that, in various instances, these [words] should be explained as indicating Brahman through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), we reply: this is not so, because such indication is devoid of both conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) and a specific purpose (*prayojana*).
And it has been stated in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*:

"When the primary meaning is obstructed and there is a connection [between that meaning and another], another meaning is indicated— either by convention (*rūḍhi*) or for a specific purpose (*prayojana*)— that function of superimposition is *lakṣaṇā*. Thus, the "primary meaning" (*mukhyārtha*) is the sense understood from the mere hearing of the word.
As stated by Gopīnātha Tarkācārya:
"By the mere hearing [of the word], its purposefulness for that [primary object] is determined;
they consider that to be the primary meaning, whereas that which is established through effort is secondary. (p. 20)
Obstruction (*bādha*), however, is the impossibility of a positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
The indeclinable *yat* is used in the sense of "by which";
it refers to the operation of an action (*kriyā-vyāpāra*).

It is argued that [the word] is superimposed as a cognition mediated by the cognition of the denotable object. However, for those who maintain the conventional view, these phonemes are not eternal, because they lack the characteristics of eternity.
For indeed, the definition of the eternal is: "that which exists and is without cause is eternal."
"Existence" (*sat*) is like a grain of rice (*śāli*) that lacks a cause;
the meaning is that whatever is devoid of a cause is eternal.
If one were to state merely "existence," it would follow as a consequence that even the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of jars, cloths, and so forth would be eternal.
If it were stated merely that [the cause] is "without a cause," it would follow as an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is eternal;
therefore, two qualifications are employed.
As for the phonemes (*varṇa*), however, since they arise in accordance with the sequence of the articulatory organs such as the throat and palate, they ought to be eternal.
Nor are they impermanent, because of the recognition that "this very same sound which was previously perceived is this one.
If it is argued that "this is merely a counterpart to that," even so, there would be the consequence of requiring a different convention (*saṅketa*). As for that convention:
The form of conventional designation (*saṃketa*) consists in the instruction: "From this word, this meaning is to be understood.
Since phonemes (*varṇa*) and so forth perish as soon as they are uttered, the conventional designation perishes as well.
Therefore, these phonemes are neither eternal nor non-eternal.
"But it is well known that [these] have an uninterrupted continuum.
Now, if the phonemes (*varṇa*) are eternal, then how can it be said that "it manifests in the form of phonemes"?
This is not so; you raise this objection because you have failed to understand the intended meaning, for it is as follows:
Sound is of two kinds: resonance (*dhvani*) and phoneme (*varṇa*).
Among the seven notes—*ṣaḍja*, *ṛṣabha*, *gāndhāra*, *madhyama*, *pañcama*, *dhaivata*, and *niṣāda*—resonance manifests independently, apart from the phonemes.
Amarasiṃha also stated that the notes arise from the strings and the throat;
likewise: "The peacock cries out *ṣaḍja*, cows bellow *ṛṣabha*, the goat bleats *gāndhāra*, and the crane warbles *madhyama*."

"In the season common for flowers, the cuckoo sings in the fifth [note], the elephant cries out in the *dhaivata*, and the horse neighs in the *niṣāda*"; such is the statement from the *Saṅgīta* cited by Rāyamukuṭa and others. Thus, even the *rāgas* such as Mālava and so forth are merely sound (*dhvani*) through the differentiation of the modulated notes (*mūrcchita-svara*).
And likewise, at the time of hearing a song such as "This is Mālava" or "This is Vasantā," there would be a cognition among the audience through the distinction of *dhvani*;
for the knowledge of the distinction between *dhvanis* occurs by means of the distinction of tones (*svara*).
"But not in reality. This means that without *dhvani*, a phoneme (*varṇa*) does not manifest.
Its intended meaning is that for the sake of comprehending the object, *dhvani* appears and becomes manifest in the form of a phoneme.
But surely, for the sake of comprehending meaning, even sound (dhvani) manifests while existing in the states of the forms of *parā*, *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*; and thus,
in the case of cows and other animals, a sound proceeds for the purpose of summoning their calves and so forth.
Therefore, it has been stated in the Svaraśāstra:
An infant knows it, a beast knows it, and a serpent knows the essence of song;
Hari knows it, Hara knows it, and Nārada knows it—or perhaps he does not.
If this is said, it is true;

however, cows and the like possess only a limited scope of knowledge consisting in the mere perception of their own sounds, yet they do not possess the cognitions of *dhī*, *medhā*, or *vijñāna*. These, moreover, are not possible without the cognition of phonemes (*varṇa*).
For instance, even knowledge concerning Īśvara does not arise without the word "Īśvara.

In the same way, Brahman— which is indefinable and devoid of attributes— is manifested solely by the word "nirguṇa" (devoid of attributes), just as an object situated in darkness is revealed by a lamp that illuminates it.
For this very reason, it has been remarked by those learned in poetry: "The child knows [only] sound, the beast knows [only] sound, and the serpent knows the essence of song;
but the Lord alone knows the true nature of poetry, and no one else.

Poetry, however, consists of the suggested meaning (*arthavyaṅgya*); therefore, poetry would not exist in mere words consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*). Thus, it is not the case that poetry is merely the denotation of words.
Of that which is devoid of qualities.
Śiva, the eternal, should be known as both being with attributes and being without attributes.

Based on the statement in the *Śārada-śāstra*, "He who is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) is other than *prakṛti*, while he who possesses qualities (*saguṇa*) is remembered as being with parts (*sakala*)," since the castes originate from *prakṛti*, [the term] "other than *prakṛti*" means that He does not exist within them, because He is unconnected with *prakṛti*.
In the first chapter of the Kubjikātantra, however, the latter half is stated differently as follows:
"The eternal Śiva is to be known as both devoid of attributes (nirguṇa) and possessed of attributes (saguṇa).
And from him, indeed, the three bindus were born, which are themselves devoid of attributes."
The Brahmabindu, the Viṣṇubindu, the Rudrabindu, and Maheśvarī.

Otherwise, immediately after perceiving the difference between primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and God (*īśvara*), there would be no perception of the difference of the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) from the qualified (*saguṇa*)—which is the object of the cognition of their union; for this very reason, it is said in the *Śrutisamuddeśa* chapter: "The functions of attributes [are applied] by means of Brahman to Brahman, which is indefinable and attributeless."
How do the Vedas proceed, being directly beyond both the existent and the non-existent?
Thus, even the question posed by Parīkṣit is consistent [with this]. Let the elaboration suffice; I shall now state the subject at hand.
He refutes those two views regarding the word and its meaning according to the *Śāradātilaka*: "By means of the two views, [he refutes] the word and the word-meaning."

Having stated that they [the proponents] do not establish the nature of Śabda-Brahman for those two, because both are insentient, it follows that in the view of those disputants, the establishment of the nature of Śabda-Brahman for those two—namely, the word and its meaning—is not achieved.
He states the reason: "because both are insentient."
This is the intended meaning:

without sound, an object is insentient and impossible to comprehend; who then would cause it to be comprehended? Likewise, without an object, sound is also insentient and incapable of being communicated; whom, then, would it inform? Therefore, [the relationship belongs] to that which is qualified by the nature of both sound and object.
The nature of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman) has been established.
As it is said in the *Adhyātmaviveka*:
"Brahman is without beginning or end; it is the essence of the Word, the imperishable syllable."
"The process of the world is considered to evolve in the form of objects.
Elsewhere it is said: "The wise know that the 'grasping of words' (śabdagraha) is the object cognizable through words;
because objects are not inherently restricted [to specific words], such a [process] is declared to be excellent."
But when that elemental form has arisen, thoroughly interwoven everywhere, it manifests again within the bodies of living beings, expanded for the sake of their purposes.
For this very reason, Śaṅkarācārya [states] in his commentary on the Kalpasūtra:

The universe consists of thirty-six principles (*tattvas*); Śiva, when enveloped by the coverings (*kañcukas*), is the individual soul (*jīva*), while Śiva devoid of coverings is the Supreme Śiva (*paramaśiva*). Thus, the thirty-six principles are divided into the pure, the mixed, and the impure, as follows: Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Śuddhavidyā are the pure [principles].
The *mitras* (associates) are both pure and impure.
The pure ones are as follows: *māyā*, *kalā*, *vidyā*, *vāk*, *ahaṅkāra*, *kāla*, *niyati*, *puruṣa*, *prakṛti*, *buddhi*, and *manas*. The impure ones are as follows:
They consist of the ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose, speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals; and sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; and ether, air, fire, water, and earth.
This has been stated in the Mṛtyuñjaya-saṃhitā:
Enveloped by the pentad of *kalā*, *vidyā*, *vāk*, *kāla*, and *māyā*—along with *niyati*—Śiva becomes the individual soul (*jīva*).

Thus, while there is a difference between Śiva and the soul consisting solely of their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the existence of the *tattvas* within Śiva will be explained in the section on initiation (*dīkṣā*).
The definition of the *kañcuka* (sheath) is as follows, in the *Parāparimalollāsa*:

The cause of this very universal agent’s delusion regarding being a limited agent is the principle known as *kalā*; so the knowers of reality understand. However, for the omniscient one, it would be *avidyā*, the delusion of being a limited knower.
Attachment to sense objects is said to be the passion of the Full (pūrṇa). Time, indeed, is the nature of things, both terrifying and non-terrifying;
it is that which delimits sequence, beginning from a moment (lava) and extending up to the dissolution of the universe (pralaya).

"This must be done by me alone; this must not be done by me"—the cause of such restriction is called *niyati* (fate). Since the pentad of principles (*tattva-pañcaka*) serves as the veil over its essential nature, [it is so designated].
Therefore, this pentad of principles is called the "mantle" (kañcuka); so they say.
Also in the fifth section of the *Kulārṇava*:
"Compassion, shame, fear, sorrow, and disgust as the fifth;
family, conduct, and likewise caste—these eight are proclaimed to be the fetters (*pāśa*)."
Bound by the fetters is the individual soul; freed from the fetters is Sadāśiva.
Thus, the identity of Śiva and the individual soul (jīva) has been stated.
Rāghavabhaṭṭa, however, [argues that] if either the word or its meaning were called Brahman, then the status of being the denotable object of the word "Brahman" would not be tenable.
For the referent of the term "Brahman" consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss;
and it has been stated by the Śruti:
"Brahman is eternal, consciousness, and bliss."
This is not correct;
for it is inconsistent to claim that the nature of the written *kuṇḍalī* is the form of the *praṇava*, and because of the collection of statements stated in the *Viśvasāra* and other texts,
as follows in the *Viśvasāra*:
The Lord Sadāśiva himself declared him to be Śabdabrahman;
that sound is proclaimed to exist within the unstruck (anāhata) cakras.
That great unstruck cakra resides in the hearts of all living beings.
In that regard, the syllable Oṃ is said to be endowed with the three qualities (guṇas). Śiva, Brahmā, and likewise Viṣṇu are established within the syllable Oṃ.
The letter A is Brahmā, and the letter U is of the nature of Being-Consciousness (saccidātmaka).
"The letter *ma* is said to be Rudra"—this is one way of conceiving its meaning;
"the letter *ca* shall be Viṣṇu, and the letter *ru* shall be Prajāpati;
and the letter *ma* shall be Rudra"—such is the determination of the phonemes (*varṇa-nirṇaya*).
And in the first chapter of the *Phetkāriṇītantra*:
"From those very syllables, the forms of Viṣṇu and Śiva arise,
joined with their respective powers (śaktis), in due order."
Thus, fifty forms for each of Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Śakti have been described;
this is also stated in the third chapter of the *Prapañcasāra*.
Since the vowels arising from the Moon (Śaśin) and Fire (Agni) are pervasive syllables that touch the [vocal] tone (*svara*),
and since the Sun (*ina*) is the *sparśa* (the consonant),
thirty-six *kalās* are considered to have arisen from the differentiation of those three.
The vowels belong to the Moon, the pairs of consonants to Saturn, and the musical instruments to Fire;
their respective digits (kalās) are sixteen, twelve, and ten in number.
"In due order" means: sixteen for the Moon, twelve for the Sun, and ten for Fire, making thirty-eight *kalās*.
From the phonemes themselves, through the fivefold divisions associated with the elements, there arise the all-pervading *kalās* numbering fifty. (p. 24)

From those very [syllables] of the *praṇava* (the sacred syllable *oṃ*) known as *tāra*, there arise as many forms of Viṣṇu through their respective powers (*śakti*). From them, along with as many Mothers (*mātṛ*), there arise the forms of Rudra.
And from those very [forms], the fifty medicinal herbs (*auṣadhi*) are said to emerge.
By means of these [mudrās], however, the practitioners of mantra obtain success that grants their desired objects:
Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭī, Rati,
Dhṛti, Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, and the woman Prīti.

The digits born of the vowels—Pūrṇā, Apūrṇā, Amṛtā, Kāmadāyinī, and Svarajā—are described in the sixth chapter of the fifth section of the *Kulārṇava* with the reading "the Mistress of the Kula" (*kulanāyikā*). [These are:
Tāpinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, and Ruci.
Suṣumnā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā;
those beginning with Ka and Bha, ending with Ṣṭha and Ḍa, are declared to be the twelve bestowers of wealth (Vasudās) belonging to the Sun.
[The flames are] Dhūmrārcis, Uṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, and Visphuliṅginī.

Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā, and Havyakavyavahā—these ten kalās, beginning with the letter 'ya' and arising from Fire (Vahni), bestow righteousness (dharma). [Note: Havyavahā and Kavyavahā are listed as distinct names.]
In the Kulārṇava, however,
the reading is: "The ten kalās beginning with the letter 'ya' and starting from the southeast are the bestowers of dharma."
In the *Śāradātilaka*, they are described as "Amṛtā," "Mānadā," and so forth;
they are to be meditated upon as bestowing fearlessness and granting desired objects.
"White, yellow, and red, in sequence"—
thus the specific distinction is stated in the *Prapañcasāra*.

Creation (sṛṣṭi), prosperity (ṛddhi), memory (smṛti), intelligence (medhā), splendor (kānti), fortune (lakṣmī), constancy (dhṛti), stability (sthirā), steadfastness (sthiti), and accomplishment (siddhi)— these ten digits (kalās) are said to arise from the letter *a*. Originating from the letter *a* and born of Brahmā, these digits exist for the purpose of creation.
In the *Śāradā*:
"Born from the letter A, they are Brahmā; they possess the luster of molten gold.
This means they have the color of liquid gold.
These [goddesses], holding rosaries, pairs of lotuses, and water-pots in their hands, are described in the *Prapañcasāra*:
Jarā, Pālinī, Śānti, Īśvarī, Ratikāmikā, and so forth.
Varadā, Hlādinī, and Prīti are the long vowels (dīrgha) born from the syllable Oṃ.
In the case of Śāradā, however,
the long vowels arising from the eight *ta*-group consonants are produced by Viṣṇu from the letter *u*, and they resemble the petals of the *tamāla* tree.
The arms are proclaimed as Abhīti, Vara, Cakra, and Iṣṭa. The digits (kalās) born from the letter *ma* are Tīkṣṇā, Raudrī, Bhayā, Nidrā, Tantrī, Kṣut, Krodhanī, Kriyā, Utkārī, and Mṛtyu.
Arising from the letter *ma*, these digits born of Rudra are for the purpose of withdrawal.
Now, regarding Śāradā:
*ut*, *kārī*, and *mṛtyu*—these are said to be born from the *pa*-group.
"Born from the mouth of Rudra, possessing a radiance like the autumnal moon,
they carry in their arms the gesture of fearlessness, the trident, the skull-bowl, and the boon-granting mudrā.
Thus it is stated additionally.
There should also be four *bindus*, yellow, white, red, and black.
It has been declared by Īśvara that the *bindus* are yellow, white, red, and black.
For Ananta, they are situated in the *ya*-group and resemble the hibiscus flower (*javākusuma*).
"Holding a deer, a sword, and [the gesture of] granting boons with her arms—
thus she is further described in the Śāradā."
"The Kalās, born from Īśvara, arise from the Bindu for the sake of firm retention," so it is said in the Kulārṇava.
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti;
Indhikā, Dīpikā, Recikā, and the supreme Mocikā; Sūkṣmā, Sūkṣmārtatā, Jñānāmṛtā, and Āpyāyanī as well.
Pervasive, of the nature of space, infinite, and born from *nāda*,
these sixteen are said to be born from *nāda* and bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Born of Sadāśiva from *nāda*, they possess white luster.
"With lotus-like hands enriched by a rosary, a book, a string of beads, and a skull"—
thus the fifty *kalās* have been described as bestowing all prosperity;
such is stated in the *Śāradā*.
Thus are the fifty kalās,
according to the *Prapañcasāra*.
Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Govinda, Viṣṇu,
the one named Madhusūdana as the seventh, Trivikrama, Vāmana,
the one called Śrīdhara, and Hṛṣīkeśa following after that.
Padmanābha, as well as he named Dāmodara, joined with Vāsudeva;
and Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha, born from the vowels.
Then [he appeared] bearing the discus, the mace, the Śārṅga bow, the sword, the conch, and likewise the plow.
Muṣalī, he who is known as Śūlin, furthermore Pāśī and Aṅkuśī;
Mukunda, Nandaja, Nandī, Nara, Narakajit, Hari;
Kṛṣṇa, Satya, Sātvata, Śauri, Śūrī, and Janārdana.
Bhūdhārī, Viśvamūrti, Vaikuṇṭha, Puruṣottama,
Balī, Balānuja, Bāla, Vṛṣaghna, Vṛṣa, Haṃsa,
Varāha, Vimala, and Nṛsiṃha— these are the forms [emanating] from the plow (Hala).
The meaning is "from the consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa*.
Furthermore, it is stated in the *Śāradā*: "These [deities] beginning with Keśava are dark-complexioned, holding in their hands the discus, the conch, and the lotus."
Also in the Phetkāriṇītantra:
"All [of them] bear the conch and the discus, possess the luster of clouds, and wear yellow garments;
Keśava and the others have their forms adorned by the Śaktis seated upon their own laps. Thus are the fifty Viṣṇus.
Fame, Beauty, Contentment, Nourishment, Fortitude, Peace, Action,
Compassion, Intelligence, Memory, Faith, Modesty, Fortune, and Sarasvatī—
these are declared to be the powers of the vowels (svara-śaktis), namely Prīti, Rati, and Ramā, in their respective order.
Jayā, Durgā, Prabhā, Satyā, Caṇḍā, Vāṇī, Vilāsinī, Vijayā,
Virajā, Viśvā, Vinadā, Sunadā, Smṛti, Ṛddhi, Samṛddhi, Śuddhi, Bhakti, Mukti, Mati, and Kṣamā.
Ramā, Kledinī, Klinnā, Vasudā, Vasudhā, Parā, Parāyaṇā,
Sūkṣmā, Sandhyā, Prajñā, Prabhā, Niśā,
