Amoghā, and Vidyutā— these are the Śaktis who grant all desires.
Seated upon the laps of their beloveds with smiling faces,
their limbs resembling streaks of lightning and their hands bearing the lotus and the gesture of fearlessness—
thus it is stated in the *Phetkāriṇītantra*.
And they are proclaimed to have lotus-faces with smiles and to possess the luster of lightning;
Kīrti and the others are seated on the laps of their consorts, with hands displaying the lotus and the gesture of granting fearlessness.
Thus it is said.
Thus are the fifty powers of Viṣṇu.
Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananta, Sūkṣma, Trimūrti, Amareśvara, Arghīśa, Bhāvabhūti, Atithi, Sthāṇuka, Hara,
Jhiṇṭīśa, Bhetika, Sadyojāta, and Anugraheśvara.
Akrūra and Mahāsena— these are the forms of the vowels.
Then follow Krodhīśa, Caṇḍeśa, Pañcāntaka,
Śivottama, Ekarudra, Kūrma, Ekanetra, Ahaḥ, and Caturānana.
Ajeśa, Sarvasomeśa, as well as Lāṅgalin and Dāraka;
Ardhanārīśvara, Umākānta, Aṣāḍhin, and Daṇḍin;
those known as Aprimīna, Meṣa, Ālosthita, and likewise Śikhin.
Chagalaṇḍa, Dviraṇḍeya, Mahākāla, and Vālin; Bhujaṅgeśa, Pinākīśa, Khaḍgīśa, Vakreśa, Śveta, Sragvīśa, Nakulīśa, Śiva, and likewise Saṃvarttaka.
These Rudras are remembered as being red in color, holding tridents and skull-bowls.
Thus are the fifty Rudras.
Pūrṇodarī, Virajā, and thereafter Śālmalī; Lolākṣī, Vartulākṣī, and Dīrghaghoṇā are proclaimed;
likewise Sudīrghamukhā, Gomukhī, and Dīrghajihvā.
Kuṇḍodarī and Ūrdhvakeśī, as well as Vikṛtamukhī;
thereafter Jvālāmukhī should be known, followed by Ulkāmukhī, Suśrīmukhī, and Vidyāmukhī— these are the powers of the vowels (svaraśaktis).
Mahākālī and Sarasvatī are endowed with all supernatural powers (*siddhi*);
Gaurī is the lore (*vidyā*) of the three worlds, and after that follows the accomplishment of mantras (*mantrasiddhi*).
Ātmaśakti, Bhūtamātā, and likewise Lambodarī are thus remembered.
Drāviṇī, Nāgarī, and further Khecarī and Mañjarī; then Rūpiṇī, Citriṇī, Kākodaryā, and Pūtanā;
there are also the two Yoginīs Bhadrakālī and Śaṅkhinī, as well as Garjinī.
Kālarātri, Kubjinī, Kapardinī, and Vajraṣā;
Jayā, Sumukheśvarī, Revatī, and thereafter Mādhavī;
Vāruṇī and Vāyavī are declared, followed by Vidāriṇī in battle.
Then, together with Alakṣmī, who is pervasive and endowed with Māyā—
these [goddesses] seated upon the lap-thrones of Rudra, their forms crimson with vermilion,
their lotus-like hands adorned with red lotuses and skull-cups.
The meditation on the weapons and so forth is likewise for both the left and the right in all cases.
Thus end the fifty powers of the Rudras.
Sandalwood, red sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, ushira, roga, water, and saffron.
Kakkola, jāti, māṃsī, murā, coraka, granthi, rocanā, patra;
pippalī, bilva, guhā, aruṇatṛṇa, kalā, raṅgāhvā, kumbhī, vallinī;
śolū, ambara, kāśmarī, sthirā, abja, and darapuṣpikā.
Mayūraśikhā, plakṣa, agnimantha, siṃhī, kuśāhva, darbha,
kṛṣṇadarapuṣpī, rohiṇa, cuṇḍaka, vṛhatī, pāṭala, citra, tulasī, apāmārga,
śatamakhalatā, dvirephā, viṣṇukrāntā, mūṣalī, and añjalinī.
Dūrvā, Śrī, Devī, Lakṣmī, and Sadābhadra— these are said to be the first [of the series]. Then, according to the sequence of the letters, there are the medicinal herbs.
Due to the various distinctions of the *gulikā* (pill) and *kavāya* (decoction) preparations, these bestow all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
Sandalwood is well-known;
*kucandana* is red sandalwood.
Aguru is well known;
karpūra is *rasakarpūra*;
uśīra is the root of *vīraṇa*.
The disease is leprosy;
the water is a young girl;
the saffron is saffron (Crocus tinctorius).
*Kakkola* is well known as *kākolī*. *Jāti* is a specific type of flower. *Snatāmāṃsī* is *jaṭāmāṃsī*.
*Murā* is *māṃsī*.
*Corā* is *corapuṣpī*;
it is called *ḍholakalambī* in the Gauḍa dialect.
*Granthi* is commonly known in Bengal as *gāṭhiyānī*;
*rocanā* is turmeric;
*patra* is *tejapatra* (cassia leaves); and *pippala* is the *aśvattha* tree.
The *vilva* is well known;
*guhā* is *jayantī*;
and *aruṇatṛṇa* is *pṛśniparṇī*.
Phalāraṅga is known as *kāmarāṅga*;
*kumbhī* is *gāmbhārī*;
and *vallinī* is *tāmbūlī*.
Śolvaṃbara is well known as Cholaṅga;
kāśmarikā is kaśeru;
sthirā is balā.
*Abja* is *dujjala*, which is commonly known as *hijala*.
*Darapuṣpikā* is the *tilapuṣpa* flower.
*Mayūraśikhā* is a specific type of *apāmārga*, commonly known as *supāṅā*.
The Plakṣa is the Vaṭa;
the Agnimantha is the Gambhāri;
the Siṃhī is the Kaṇṭakārī.
Kuśā is the well-known kuśāhva;
darbha is a specific type of kāśa;
and kṛṣṇa is pippalī.
Darapuṣpī is indrayava;
rohiṇa is kuṭukī;
cuṇḍuka is kukubalyā.
Vṛhatī is well known;
pāṭala is commonly known as pāralī;
tulasī is well known.
*Apāmārga* is well known;
*śatamakhatā* is the *indralatā*;
*dvirepha* is the *bhṛṅgarāja*.
Viṣṇukrāntā is aparājitā;
mūṣalī is tālamūlī;
añjalinī is known as lājālu or lajjāvatī.
Dūrvā is well known;
Śrīdevī is grain;
Lakṣmī is śatamūlī.
Sadārudrajaṭā and Bhadrā (also known as Bhadraparpaṭī) are medicinal herbs.
The purpose of the medicinal herbs has also been stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa as follows:
Whichever mantra it may be, pills prepared from the medicinal herbs corresponding to its syllables,
in a number equal to those syllables, grant the accomplishment of that mantra.
With such a pill, there is consecration, fire-offering, tasting, and anointing.
And worship of that likewise bestows accomplishment; it cannot be otherwise.
Thus ends the description of the fruits of medicinal herbs.
Also, in the first chapter of the Kāmadhenu Tantra:
The Mātṛkā, consisting of the letters from 'a' to 'kṣa', exists in the form of seed-syllables;
it possesses the visarga and the bindu, and its two junctions (sandhis) constitute the body of Brahman.
The visarga is Prakṛti, and the bindu is Puruṣa.
He possesses a double intention and is the differentiator of the two.

"From the *varṇa* (syllable/sound), O Goddess, Brahmā is born, as well as Viṣṇu, Prajāpati, and Rudra, the agent of the world’s dissolution. Thus [is described] the nature of all those to be worshipped, beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu, as well as all the *kalās* and medicinal herbs."
This is because [Brahman] arises from the Praṇava—which is the very nature of Brahman—consisting of its five rays: A, U, M, Bindu, and Nāda, and so forth.

Alternatively, even if one accepts that by the word "Praṇava" (used through the relationship of signifier and signified and by way of indication) Brahman, which is the signified of the Praṇava, is meant, the aforementioned defect remains exactly as it was.

According to the various authorities cited in the *Śāradā-tilaka*, the *Viśvasāra-tantra*, and the *Prapañcasāra*, it is the very components of the *praṇava* that are the generators of all things, and not specific components of Brahman;
for how else could the origin of all things proceed from them? (p. 29)
But surely, Brahman is not merely the agent of origination; rather, it is that which is determined to be the cause of origination, sustenance, and dissolution.
And thus says the Śruti cited in the Vedāntasūtras:
"That from which these beings are born, by which, once born, they live, and into which they enter upon passing away—that is Brahman."
If it is asked how [the Praṇava] can be so, since it is merely the progenitor of the Praṇava,

the answer is: it is true that the causality of the Praṇava is clearly understood from observing that Brahmā and others, who arise from the rays of the Praṇava, are the agents of creation and so forth.

Now, as for the objection: "If the syllable *praṇava* possesses the nature of Brahman, how can other phonemes do so?"—this too is a weak argument, because those [other phonemes] are also composed of sound (*dhvani*), being modifications of the *praṇava*.
And likewise, in the first chapter of the Prapañcasāra:
He spoke thus regarding the root-syllables, the modifications of the syllables, and even the further modifications of those modifications;
as well as the various mantras derived from them and their diverse applications,
both Vedic and Tantric.
The root-syllable is *haṃsa*.
The modification of the syllables consists of the sequence from the letter *a* to the letter *kṣa*.
The modification of the modification consists of the conjunction of letters and so forth.
By that [word], they were split, having reached division; the rest is easy to understand.
Thus, in this manner, the connection [of the sentence] is: Kāla spoke to Brahmā and to all [others].
As for *haṃsa*, it is a type of modification (*vikāra*).
In the fourth chapter, the seed-syllable named *ha* is of the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*);
from it arise the six waves (*ṣaḍūrmayaḥ*), as well as the four qualities (*guṇa*) originating from *repha* (the letter *r*),
beginning with wind and ending with earth, together with the qualities such as touch.
The instruments (karaṇas) are also four: the aggregate (saṅghāta) and volition (cetanā).
Thus, six qualities of the letter *ha* have been proclaimed by the wise in due order.
Furthermore, the six letters beginning with *a* and ending with *u* arise from these very six.
From the various divisions, the four vowels beginning with *ṛ* have arisen from the great-souled letter *ha*; the others are known as those arising from *ra*.
The group of six letters, beginning with *e* and ending with the *visarga*, has been extracted.

From the letter *ha* and from the six limbs—this [system] possesses sixteen limbs. From these limbs were born the sixteen vowels that pervade all; from them arose all the other letters. Therefore, they know this to be the root.
That *tāra* exists as the very seed-syllable (*bīja*) established within living beings alone. By this, the entire universe—including all stationary things—is pervaded.
It is described as *nāda*, *prāṇa*, *jīva*, *ghoṣa*, and so forth.

This [syllable] is designated as *māyā* in three ways: by means of signs determined as masculine, feminine, and neuter; as the letter *ra*; and as the seed-syllable (*bīja*). [The goddesses associated with it are:
Śānti, Śrī, Sannati, Kānti, Lakṣmī, Medhā, and Sarasvatī.
Through her own conceptualized states— patience, nourishment, stability, tranquility, knowledge, and so forth—
which denote her own purposes and assume various modifications,
the virtuous know this very one, who moves within the heart, as Kuṇḍalī.
That goddess constantly utters the melodic sound of the *bhṛṅgī*;
the wise know her form in many ways according to their own disposition.
She is to be known in every respect as Kuṇḍalinī, who indeed follows the path of the Suṣumnā.
Because it is the seed of the world of moving and non-moving beings, that [state] is indeed the *vi-ja* (the seed).
Through the union of the root with the *bindu*, there arises the state of hundredfold bliss (*śatānanda*).
From the union of the letter *u* and the letter *ā*, accompanied by the letter *ra*, there is the production of these two.

Because he arises from that which is called the syllable *ha*, he is designated by the word *hari*. His state of being *hari* (the remover) is due to that very fact, as is my own state of being the Self of all.
Through his emergence from this *bindu*, at its conclusion he is called *so'ham* (I am That).
The person (puruṣa) is said to be accompanied by the ego (ahaṅkāra), while that [other principle] is remembered as primordial nature (prakṛti).
This power (śakti) is considered to be Ajapā; likewise, she has a right and a left side.
The right part is the Bindu, while the left part is the Visarga.
By that, the two parts known as right and left are distinguished as male and female.
The *bindu* is said to be the Puruṣa, while the *visarga* is considered Prakṛti.
The *haṃsa* consists of the soul (*pums*) and primordial nature (*prakṛti*); this entire world is composed of that.
Having known her own form to be that of the Soul (*pums*), she attained the state of "I am He" (*so'ham*).
He alone is called the Supreme; he is the *manu* of this Great-Souled One.
Having elided both the letter *sa* and the letter *ha*, one should apply the euphonic combination (*sandhi*) known as *pūrvarūpa*; thus it becomes the *praṇava*.
From the final portion of the *tāra* [Oṃ] when divided, the elements beginning with space (*kha*) arise; then, from the middle portion, [the other elements arise].
And from the primordial elements and sounds, together with mantras, they arise in the world due to prior existence;
in some places, the reading is "all together" (samastāḥ).
This is also stated in the second chapter of the Viśvasāra.
There, two swans—male and female—are considered to have arisen;
there, the letter *ha* is declared to be the Puruṣa (Spirit), and the letter *sa* is remembered as Prakṛti (Nature).
These two pervade the entire universe, like fire pervading wood.
The word *kṛtaka* means "ashes.
Just as fire pervades the flame, so too do these two pervade the universe; this is the meaning.
Even without a word explicitly indicating a simile, such as in the expression "the boy is fire," a simile is nevertheless perceived.
When one attains that state, then one is known as "I am That" (so'ham).
He alone is the Supreme Brahman, the immutable source of the world's sprout.
All the gods, as well as the Vedas, the quarters, the winds, the sun, and so forth [are He].
The divisions of space, time, and the kalpas are likewise of that very nature;
O Goddess of the Universe, they go to dissolution within that when speech perishes.
Within that, creation always proceeds, and within that, even today, it abides.
That alone is the supreme Brahman; it arises through the sense of "I am That" (so'haṃbhāva).
When the two identical letters have been elided, one should then indicate the conjunct letter;
this is what was declared by the Lotus-born One as the *praṇava* within all letters.
O Dear One! Brahman, which consists of supreme bliss and is manifested as the Śabdabrahman, resides within the center of one's own body as the essence of all mantras.
Thus, in the Rudrajāmala, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa, in the twenty-second chapter.
The three gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—are a single form; fashioned as my own body, they create, protect, and destroy. Born from the Praṇava, these are always the creators of obstacles to yoga.
One should take refuge in the letter *A*, the color of Brahmā, the form of sound, of great luster,
eternally contained within the *praṇava*, and the fulfillment of yoga;
and [one should take refuge in] the letter *U*, the color of Viṣṇu, the Lord who pierces through sound.
One should take refuge in the *kumbhaka* of yoga, which is the essence (*sattva*) contained within the *praṇava*.
The syllable *makāra*, the form of Śambhu, is the living soul that has emerged from the wind.
One should take refuge in the place of dissolution, the time situated within the end of the *praṇava*.
This phoneme (varṇa), through its division, is conceived as the *praṇava*.
From the *praṇava* arises the *haṃsa*; that *haṃsa* is "I am He" (*so'haṃ*), which is the Supreme. That "I am He" is knowledge, the Great Knowledge, difficult even for yogins to attain.
He who meditates upon this continuously shall indeed become supreme.
The syllable *Haṃ* is the Person (Puruṣa) by its own nature, and the syllable *Sa* is Primordial Matter (Prakṛti).
One should know this *Haṃsa* as that which pierces the solar orb.
When that knowledge of "I" (so'ham) arises precisely through the reverse order, then one who has gone to the Sun becomes a Siddha, worshipped by Vāsudeva.
After that, having elided the letter *ha* and the letter *sa*, [the mantra is complete].
"After that, one should perform the *sandhi*; this *praṇava* is the great mantra.

This is because the manifestation of all [elements], beginning with the syllables, is seen from the *praṇava*. For this very reason, he will state the name of the *praṇava* as "the progenitor of all living beings" in the section on the designation of letters (*varṇābhidhāna*).

Now, it has been stated that the *praṇava* denotes Brahman, but is not Brahman itself; rather, the entire phenomenal creation (*sṛṣṭiprapañca*) proceeds precisely from Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Śakti, and Īśvara, who are denoted by the five components of the *praṇava*: the syllables *a*, *u*, *m*, *nāda*, and *bindu*.
For this very reason, Puṣpadanta has also said: "O Giver of Refuge! one praises You, both collectively and individually, with the word 'Om'.
And elsewhere it is said: "The Supreme Brahman is to be realized; the Praṇava is remembered as its designator."

It has been stated that the denoted object (vācya) is Brahman, but not that the denoter (vācaka), the *praṇava*, is so; therefore, [one might argue] that the phoneme (*varṇa*) is non-eternal. If this is raised, we say no, because it contradicts the *Kalpasūtras*;
for each respective *Sūtra* states that words consisting of phonemes are eternal.
This is the intended meaning:

sound is indeed of two kinds, consisting of resonance (*dhvani*) and consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*). Regarding these, some maintain that the one consisting of resonance is impermanent because it is not perceived [as persisting].
But they, regarding sound as arising solely from the striking of clay drums and the like, claim that what consists of phonemes (varṇa) lacks the nature of sound (dhvani);
this is extremely weak, for sound is of two kinds: wave-like and resembling the opening bud of a Kadamba flower.
The first [type of resonance], by means of the analogy of waves, gradually awakens the nearby form of the self-sound for each letter in succession and thereby conveys the meaning;
the second, however, like a kadamba bud, awakens the self-sound itself in an unmanifest form while it is still at a distance.
It is not denotative, like the sound "haṭṭādi";
however, that which consists of phonemes (varṇas) is indeed eternal, as it is stated in the *Mātṛkodaya*:
The Lord is the author of the Vedas, and the great sages are the authors of the Purāṇas;
since no author is heard of for this [Mātṛkā], she is therefore Svayambhū (Self-born).
Also in the Jāmalam:
The state of Brahmā was attained by Brahmā, and the state of Viṣṇu by Viṣṇu himself.
Also in the *Parākrama*: "Indeed,
by the blessed devotees of Maheśvara who possess the recognition of their own true nature,
they become liberated while living (jīvanmukta) merely through that self-recognition."
By this, the eternality of the mantras is demonstrated;
thus it was explained by the venerable Śaṅkarācārya in his commentary on the *Kulamūlāvatārakalpasūtra*.
In reality, however, as stated previously, that which is expressed (the denoted) is the Supreme Brahman, but not [merely] Brahman.
But has not the eternity of the Veda been demonstrated by the two statements, "The Vedic sentences are non-human" and "Because there is no author of the Veda"?
If so, how can God be the author of the Vedas?

If it is argued that the statements such as "the Vedas have a state of being produced" and "the seed of the Vedas and so forth will be explained" are consistent with both the fact that mantras are produced and the eternity of mantras, this is true;
however, the authorship of the Vedas by God is accepted in the sense of His being their illuminator, not in the sense of being their producer.
And likewise, in the fourth chapter of the Bṛhannīlatantra:
"O daughter of the mountain, know for certain that the Veda is indeed Brahman itself!
O beautiful one, the Veda proceeds of its own accord; there is no author of it.
In ancient times, the Veda was likewise sung by the Blessed Lord to Svayambhū."
From Śiva down to the sages, they are the rememberers of this [scripture], not its creators;
indeed, Kṛṣṇa and the other celestial beings are merely its revealers.
As for that which is found in the thirteenth chapter of the first *rātra* of the *Nāradapañcarātra*, in the hymn of praise to Sāvitrī:
By the statement, "I am Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas; Brahmā (Vidhi) is the progenitor of the Vedas;
I bow to that very Creator who is beyond the three qualities," it is not asserted that he has Sāvitrī as his mother or that Brahmā is his progenitor.
That too must be understood as making him an expander [of the Vedas], based on its syntactic unity with the previously stated injunction: "Having obtained her company, expand the Veda.
Otherwise, [the meaning would conflict with] the first verse of the *Bhāgavata*: "By him, from the heart of Brahmā... [referring to the Vedas obscured by darkness at the end of the age].

Otherwise, the verse from the eighteenth chapter of the fifth book— which states, "He who, assuming the form of a human horse, took back [the earth] from Rasātala for the sake of the poet who entreated him; salutations to Him whose efforts are never in vain"— would be rendered meaningless.

It is impossible for Brahmā, the self-born progenitor of the Vedas, to receive instruction from another or to obtain them through the request of another. Therefore, the logical connection is as follows: assuming the form of a horse with a human head (Hayagrīva), he recovered and retrieved from the subterranean realm (Rasātala) the Vedas that had been eclipsed and stolen by Tamas in the guise of a Daitya for the sake of Brahmā, who was being entreated [for their return].

In that case, how is it explained by Śrīdharasvāmin in the first chapter of the sixth book [of the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*], where it says: "We have heard that the Veda is Nārāyaṇa himself, the Self-existent"? Herein, he has provided the following commentary:

The Veda has arisen from Nārāyaṇa; he himself is its direct manifestation, and thus it is called "self-existent" (svayambhū), for it exists by itself through his mere breath. Accordingly, the Śruti states: "This which is the Ṛgveda is the breath of this Great Being."
Also in the Kāmadhenu Tantra:
Beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with 'kṣa', she herself is the supreme Kuṇḍalinī;
she, whose essence is the phonemes, certainly gives birth to the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings.
O beautiful one! She is likewise the various scriptures, the Purāṇas, and the Itihāsas.

"O beloved! The Vedas, the Smṛti scriptures, and whatever else there may be—all this is born from the Imperishable (akṣara) and consists of the Supreme Brahman. According to this statement, Kuṇḍalinī gives birth to the Veda; she is that which will be described as the three abodes (dhāmatraya).
The scriptural passages beginning with "of the Vedas" and so forth, as well as the statement regarding the eighteen branches of knowledge (*vidyā*) and so forth, are thus consistent.
It is true that all of this can be reconciled by relying on the Vedānta doctrine;
however, according to that system, everything is indeed impermanent except for the Lord alone.
The statement beginning with "apauruṣeyāṇi" (they are not of human origin) is stated in accordance with the Mīmāṃsaka school;
thus, everything is faultless.
In reality, however, the Goddess consists of all the Vedas and likewise consists of all mantras, and so forth.

Furthermore, the eternity of the Vedas and the mantras is established as the very proof [of their authority] because the Kuṇḍalinī— whose nature is consciousness, who is described as Śabdabrahman in the forthcoming Śāradā-tantra, and who consists of both sound and meaning— is composed of the Vedas and so forth.
If it is asked, "In that case, what is the status of the aforementioned scriptural statement?"— it is not so;
for the meaning is that the Veda is the breath of the Great Being, the Lord in the form of Virāj, and thus the Veda's quality of being produced does not follow.

Furthermore, if those who rely on the commentary of Śrīdhara Svāmī were to accept that [the Lord] is produced, then the Lord in his Varāha form—who appeared through the breath of Parameṣṭhin—would necessarily be born from Parameṣṭhin.
The proof for this is found in the thirteenth chapter of the third book: "Parameṣṭhin, however, [was situated] in the midst of the waters... and so forth.
"Having beheld the Great Earth," thus beginning, [he said]: "May He from whose heart I have become a servant ordain for me.
O sinless one!
As he was meditating thus, there suddenly emerged from the cavity of his nostril a boar the size of a thumb.
"O Bhārata! While he was looking on, [the body] became healthy and in an instant grew to the size of an elephant; that was a great wonder," such were the words of Maitreya.
Thus ends the account of the origin of the various scriptures;
the origin of the planets and other celestial bodies from the primordial sound (varṇa) has also been described.
In the fourth chapter of the *Prapañcasāra*.
Then, this Sun is the lord of the vowels; Mars is the lord of the *ka*-group;
Venus is the lord of the *ca*-group; Mercury arises from the *ṭa*-group;
Jupiter arises from the *ta*-group; and Saturn arises from the *pa*-group.
This moon, born from the *ya*-class [of consonants], is thus endowed with seven qualities.
In the Viśvasāra-tantra, it is stated that the planets possess the nature of presiding deities over the groups arising from the final Mātṛkā.
For example: O Queen of the Gods! I shall tell you the deities of the seven groups.
The son of the Earth (Mars), who is red in color, is considered the deity of the *ka*-group.

The Lord of the *ka* group is known as Kavi; the wise one (Budha) is remembered as the lord of the *ca* group; the Preceptor of the Gods (Bṛhaspati) is the lord of the *ta* group; Śanaiścara is the lord of the *pa* group;
likewise, Candra is the lord of the *ya* group; and the Sun is the deity of the vowels (*svara*).
In the *Prapañcasāra*.
From the colors of its modifications (vikāra) are born the twelve zodiac signs (rāśi).

Through these, accumulated over time in units such as degrees (lava), there occurs the movement of the wheel (cakragati). Likewise, the stability of the world depends upon the movement of the wheel within the constellations (ṛkṣa), the zodiac signs, and so forth.

I shall describe the form of the wheel as it is bound by the zodiacal signs. One should construct the circle of signs with its internal and external divisions. On the terrestrial wheel itself, Aries and the others are to be understood as pertaining to the human realm.
The zodiac sign called Aries (Meṣa) is understood by those beginning with the first [vowel] and ending with *ī*;
Taurus (Vṛṣa) is formed by those ending with *ṛ* and *ḷ*, and Gemini (Yugma) follows from three [vowels].
Thus, after the arising of the sign Aries, Taurus is produced by the three ending with *ṛ*.
The grammatical connection is that there is a pair with the three [letters] ending in the letter ḷ.

From *e* and *au* was born the sign Karkaṭa; from *o* and *au* arose Siṃha. From the letters *ś*, *v*, *r*, *ṇ*, *k*, *e*, *bh*, *y*, and *s*, Kanyā is considered to have been born. And from the six groups *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, and *ya*, [the remaining signs] were produced.
The zodiac signs beginning with Capricorn (Vaṇik) and ending with Pisces (Mīna) arise from the expansion of Śakti;
together with the four letters beginning with Ya, the letter Kṣa belongs to Pisces.
Thus ends the description of the creation of the zodiacal signs according to their colors.
The lord of the field is also present there.
In the four signs beginning with Taurus, the lords of the houses are Mars, Venus, Scorpio, and Virgo; in those of Mercury, Cancer;
likewise, Leo for the Moon and Taurus for Jupiter; and Sagittarius, Pisces, Capricorn, and Aquarius are declared to be the lords of the houses for Saturn in strength.
And this sequence has been shown regarding the water-jar (kalaśa).
Thus ends the description of the lords of the zodiac signs (rāśyadhipa).
Then, situated above that, there is likewise the circle of the earth;
and that [circle] upon which the lion and others reside is the fixed path of the ancestors.
And situated in the portion above that is one's own circle, which is also of such a nature.
But he is the wielder of the bow, the center of the divine wheel;
thus is the description of the wheel of the mass of the three worlds.
Likewise, from these very same groups, the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) arise;
and that [group] also becomes twenty-sevenfold through the differentiation of syllables. From these two [groups], Aśvinī was born, and then Bharaṇī and Kṛttikā.
From the three vowels [a, i, u] comes Rohiṇī; from the four following them [ṛ, ḷ, e, ai] come Mṛgaśīrṣa and Ārdrā; from the two ending with those [o, au] comes Punarvasu;
the combination of the two nasals [ṅ, ñ] alone constitutes the yoga for Revatī, which is treated separately.
Kṛttikā corresponds to *ti*, and likewise Āśleṣā to *ṣṭha*; Maghā belongs to the two letters *gha* and *ṅa*.
Then, from the three *pūrva*s come *tta*, *cha*, and *ja*; similarly, from the three *uttara*s come *jha* and *ña*.
From Hasta comes *ca*, Citrā *ṭa* and *ṭha*, and Svātī arose from the letter *ḍa*.
From Viśākhā, Ṣaṇḍa was born; likewise, from those [stars], Anurādhikā arose.
From Dhakāra came Jyeṣṭhā, and from Napapha came the one named Mūlā. Then another, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, was born, and Śravaṇā is likewise considered to have arisen.
Then there is the one called Śraviṣṭhā, likewise Śatabhiṣā for the two Yavas;
the name Proṣṭhapad is for the two Vaśas, and they are remembered as following after the Vasus. Thus ends the description of the creation of the lunar mansions according to their classes.
When this letter *kṣa* indeed dwells together with these two letters *ka* and *ṣa*, then the conjunction of the moon and the sun is perceived as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*).
From *ka* and *ṣa* comes *bhava*; from us two, *ka* and *ṣa*, there is the union that is *abhava*.
From that, the letter *kṣa* was born; its presiding deity is Nṛsiṃha. That [letter], together with the letters *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha*, went to the final *prauṣṭhapada*.
Thus is the account of the origin of the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*).
Another practice is the recitation of one's own respective mantra on the days of the lunar mansions (nakṣatra) and the weekdays.
Therefore, the presiding deities and other details for these days are now described.
Thus ends the description of the recitation on the days of the lunar mansions and weekdays.
The trees known as kāraskara, āmalaka, udumbara, and jambu; khadira, kṛṣṇa, vaśa, pippala, nāgarī, hiṇa, palāśa, plakṣa, kāmboṣṭha, dhiya, arjuna, and vikaṅkata.
The Vakula, Saraja, Sarja, Vañjula, Panasa, Āmra,
Kakubha, Śamī, Kadamba, Nimba, Āmra, Madhuka, Antādi, and other such trees—
desiring long life, one should never cut down a tree belonging to one's own asterism.
In this context, the word "should" expresses both the agent's own purpose and the logical reason;
thus, one should neither cut [oneself] nor cause [another] to cut.
Thus ends the prohibition against cutting down trees belonging to one's own natal asterism (*nakṣatra*).
The Aśvins, Yama, Dhātṛ, Śaśin, Rudra, Aditi, Surejya (Bṛhaspati), and Sarpas;
Pitṛs, Aryaman, Bhaga, Dinakṛt (Sūrya), Tvaṣṭṛ, and likewise the Maruts, Indra, and Agni;
Mitra, Indra, Nirṛti, Jala (Varuṇa), the Viśvedevas, Hari (Viṣṇu), and likewise the Vasus.
Varuṇa, Ajapāda, Ahivradhna, and Pūṣan are the deities of the lunar mansions.
Thus ends the description of the deities of the lunar mansions.
Mounting a horse, an elephant, a snake, a serpent, a goat, a cat, a ram, a tortoise, a crucible, a mouse, a bull, a buffalo, a tiger,
a tigress, a doe, a lordly man, a beast, a monkey, a woman, or a horse;
Martya, Gokariṇī, and Sādhukathitā are the constellations of birth in their respective order.

Thus concludes the results of describing the origins from the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). There is enmity between the cow and the tiger, the elephant and the lion, the horse and the buffalo, the dog and the mongoose, the monkey and the ram, and likewise between the cat and the rat.
Having understood through worldly convention that there is also something else [to be considered] regarding effort and so forth,
those seeking auspiciousness should always avoid this for a husband and wife, as well as for a king and his servant.
Due to their state of eternal enmity, when these two are joined, they form a dual compound characterized by both unity and neuter gender.
From these [days], the lunar dates (tithis) beginning with Pratipad and so forth are the limits of non-existence.
In this system, two and a half lunar days (tithis) constitute one zodiac sign (rāśi).

Thus, the thirty lunar days are divided into twelve distinct signs. Furthermore, these same signs are again divided into two types according to the distinction between the first and the last halves of each lunar fortnight.

A fortnight (*pakṣa*) consists of fifteen days; the first, beginning with the first lunar day (*pratipad*), is known as the bright (*śukla*) fortnight. Likewise, the other fortnight, beginning with the first lunar day of the dark half (*kṛṣṇa-pratipad*), should be understood as such.
This concludes the description of the origin of the fortnights.
Although the names are identical, due to the waxing and waning of the moon, the lunar days (tithis) are not equal throughout both fortnights;
nevertheless, they attain thirty divisions.
[The lords of the days are] Agni, Aśvin, Umā, Savitṛ, Vighna, Nāga, Guha, Savitṛ, Mātṛ, and Durgā.
Kakubh, Dhanapati, Viṣṇu, Yama, Harapati, and Candra are, in order, the lords of the lunar days (tithis).

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the World as a Collection of Syllables Containing the Explanation of Brahman as the Nature of Word and Meaning," in the first section on Cosmogony of the *Śrī-Prāṇatoṣiṇī*.
Thus, in order to highlight its preeminence, the creation of sound (*śabda-sṛṣṭi*), which was mentioned first as the "other end" (*aparānta*), has been described.
Since the [higher levels of speech] such as Paśyantī cannot be described without the creation of the body (*śarīra-sṛṣṭi*),
the Teacher now begins the description of that [creation] in the first chapter of the *Śāradātilaka*.

Then, from Śambhu, whose nature is the bindu and who is bound by time, and from him whose nature is *kalā*, there was born Sadāśiva, the witness of the world and all-pervading. From Sadāśiva arose Īśa, and from him Rudra was born.
From him [Viṣṇu] comes Viṣṇu, and from him Brahmā; such is their origin.

Regarding this matter of creation, the subsequent birth of Rudra and the others occurs in the form of objects (artha-rūpeṇa), whereas their prior birth was in the form of sound (śabda-rūpeṇa); therefore, there is no tautology.
*Kalā* is *māyā*, because she is produced from that [source].
The term *kālabandhoḥ* means "from the one whose nature is sound (*nāda*), who has time as his companion"—that is, from the source of creation during time which is without beginning or end.
By these two qualifiers, it is stated that both *prakṛti* and *kāla* persist even during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*).
Therefore, the permanence of these two is relative, whereas the permanence of the *puruṣa* is intrinsic, because the destruction of everything culminates in the *puruṣa*.
For this very reason, it is said in the *Viśvasāra*:
"The moments (*nimeṣa*) and so forth, as well as *māyā*, the days, and likewise the nights."
(38) The fortnights, months, seasons, as well as the solstices, years, the yugas, the measure of the yugas, and likewise the intervals between the Manvantaras—
all this, up to the great dissolution (mahāpralaya), is remembered as being of the nature of the Bindu.
By this, the dissolution of time in the form of creation has been stated.
However, in the context of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), by the word "bandhu" in the phrase "of the kinsman of time," the causality of time is indicated.
And so, as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:

That which begins with the *lava* and ends with the *pralava*, manifested through the power of *tamas*, is this time (*kāla*) which serves as the instrumental cause for the birth of entities and their receptacles; such is the measure beginning from the *lava*.
In the first chapter of the *Prapañcasāra*.

The time required to pierce a single leaf within a cluster of lotus petals with a fine needle is known as an *alava*. Thirty *lavas* constitute a *truṭi*, and they know that thirty such *truṭis* make up a *kalā*.

The *kāṣṭhā* is to be understood as a gradual measure; that same *kāṣṭhā* is equal to a *nimeṣa* (the blink of an eye) and is also said to be equivalent to the snap of a finger. A *mātrā* is traditionally defined by eight of those [snaps].
It is the duration of time in which one's own hand [can travel] around one's own knee-circle.
That measure is equal to a single breath;
thirty-six hundred breaths are known as one ghaṭikā.
Two nāḍikās constitute a muhūrta, and thirty of those make up a day and night.
Thirty of those days and nights make a month, and twelve of those months [make a year].
This human year is a single day and night for the dwellers of heaven.
Likewise, a divine year is to be known as consisting of three hundred and sixty such divine days and nights; and by those divine years, [the lifespan of the gods is calculated].
Twelve thousand distinct [cycles] constitute one Caturyuga;
O Śatānanda, ten thousand of those are considered to be one day of yours,
and your night is said by those who know time to be of equal duration.
By thirty such days and nights you reach a month;
by twelve such months a year is reckoned for you;
and you live for a hundred such years.
"Your life is my breath; thus it is impelled by Time. Thus [it is said]. However, in the *Tithitattva*, within the section on the *saṃkrānti* (transits) as recorded in the *Smṛti*:
A fourth part of a short syllable is called a *truṭi*.
Two *truṭis* are declared to be a *lava*, and two *lavas* are a *nimeṣa*. Eighteen *nimeṣas* constitute a *kāṣṭhā*, and so on, up to what is known as *saṃvarta*, *pralaya*, and *kalpa*.
Time has been defined by Amarasiṃha, and its status as a causal factor (*nimitta*) is demonstrated by the preceding statement. (p.
39) Also, in the first chapter of the *Merutantra*, [it says] regarding the lifespan of Indra:
Having stated the measure by another method, it is said that a day of Brahmā consists of as many Indras as there are Indras.
That which is meditated upon as Mahāmāyā by me is the emergence of its teaching.
"By as many Indras" means by fourteen in number.
The day of Brahmā is the *prapañca* (the phenomenal world), while his night is the *kumbhaka* (the state of suspension).
Thus, one *ghaṭikā* of hers is recorded as one year of the Creator. Brahmā lives for a hundred such *ghaṭikās*, like a mere insect.
For one fortnight Satī was of fair form, while Pārvatī was dark;
Hari lived for only a single season, and Sadāśiva for one year.
In this manner, she indeed became the wife of Mahākāla for a hundred years.
"Having repeatedly cast off the body like a snake sheds its skin, [it becomes] ever-new"—this is the determination of time.
Thus, while the creation of objects (*arthasṛṣṭi*) has been introduced, he begins to speak of the creation of the principles (*tattvasṛṣṭi*).
In the first chapter of the *Śāradā-tantra*, however:
From that manifest, transformed, and supreme object which is the root cause,
there indeed arose the principle of Mahat, consisting of the qualities and the internal organ.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: from the *śabdabrahman* (the Word-Brahman), which is a transformation and is oriented toward creation, the *mahattattva* (the Great Principle) was produced.
This is because the entire creation has that as its root-form; thus, it arises from the unmanifest (*avyakta*), the supreme reality, in the form of the *bindu*.
Of what nature is it? It consists of the qualities (*guṇas*) of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
The intention is that the fourfold internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), consisting of mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), and consciousness (citta), is one and its cause is also one.

Because the effect is metaphorically designated by the name of the cause, it is said to be of the same nature as that cause. Thus, scripture also states: "From Prakṛti comes Mahat; from Mahat comes Ahaṅkāra."
Also in the Vāmakeśvaratantra as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
From the unmanifest form of the Śabdabrahman, the cause of all things,
the principle of intellect (buddhitattva) was born to express the manifest quality of sattva.
In the Sāṃkhya system, the principle of the Great One (mahattattva) is designated as the principle of intellect (buddhitattva).
In the first chapter of the Śāradā[-tilaka].
From that [Mahat] arose the threefold ego (ahaṅkāra), which is the differentiation of creation.
From the *vaikārika* ego arise the ten *vaikārika* deities:
Dik, Vāta, Arka, Pracetas, Aśvin, Vahni, Indra, Upendra, Mitra, and [Kāma].
From the Taijasa [ahaṅkāra], the sense organs arose through the sequential application of the subtle elements (tanmātras);
from the Bhūtādi ahaṅkāra, the five gross elements were born.
Also cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
That ego (ahaṅkāra) is threefold, according to the distinction of the qualities such as sattva and the rest:
the vaikārika is named sāttvika, the taijasa is remembered as rājasa, and the bhūtādi is tāmasa; and these separately brought forth the principles and so forth.
(p. 40) According to the principle that designations arise from predominance (*adhika*), the specific distinctions such as *sāttvika* and so forth have been stated.
In reality, however, the three *guṇas* exist in all three [categories] in varying degrees of deficiency and excess, even in that which consists of Śiva and Śakti and the like.
It should be understood accordingly:
from the *vaikārika* [sattvika] ego arise the presiding deities of the senses and the moon;
from the *taijasa* [rajasic] ego arise the five organs of perception, the five organs of action, and the mind.
From the primary element (bhūtādi), the subtle elements (tanmātrāṇi) were born.
And likewise, as recorded by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
From the *vaikārika* [sattva] arise the eleven beginning with space (*dig*),
which are traditionally known as the presiding deities of the sense organs;
and there is the other principle, the mind (*manas*), which possesses conceptualization and deliberation.
From Taijasa alone arose the ten sense organs, each according to its own class;
from Bhūtādi arose the five subtle elements (tanmātras), and from that [Bhūtādi] subsequently arose the gross elements.
And the subtle elements (tanmātras) are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
From the subtle element of sound arises space;
from the subtle elements of sound and touch arises air;
from the subtle elements of sound, touch, and form arises fire.
From the subtle elements (tanmātras) of sound, touch, form, and taste, water arises;
from the subtle elements of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, earth is produced.
This has been stated in the first chapter.
From sound arises ether; from that, through touch, air; from those two, through form, fire; from these three, through taste, the waters; and from all these four, through smell, the earth.
Thus the five elements, beginning with ether, arise in sequence as possessors of their respective qualities.
But as for the Brahmajñāna-tantra and the Nirvāṇa-tantra:
From space arises wind; from wind is produced the sun; from the sun is produced water; from water is produced the earth.
The earth dissolves into water;
water dissolves into the sun; the sun dissolves into wind; and wind dissolves into space.
From the five principles (pañcatattva) creation arises; within each principle, a principle dissolves.
And it is stated in the Śruti as well.
Therefore, from Brahman ether was produced; from ether, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth;
from earth, plants; from plants, food; and from food, the person—thus the creation of the elements from the elemental constituents has been described.
Thus ends the manner of the origination and dissolution of the five elements.

The logicians (Tārkikas), however, declare that sound and the other qualities belong to ether and the rest. The Sāṃkhyas also hold that sound is the quality of ether; sound and touch are the qualities of air; and those two, along with form, are the qualities of fire, together with taste.
Those [qualities] belong to water along with its odor, and those to earth.
Also in the Īśānasaṃhitā cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"Space has sound as its sole quality; wind has the qualities of sound and touch;
fire is held to have the three qualities of sound, touch, and form. (p. 41)
Water possesses four qualities—sound, touch, form, and taste;
earth possesses five qualities—sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.

In reality, however, through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*), each of the five elements contains all five qualities, just as the three *guṇas* (sattva, rajas, and tamas) exist within each individual element.
Therefore, pungent substances, clothing, and so forth are perceived by the sense organs of earth and the rest, such as the nose.
This concludes the description of the qualities of the five elements.
The maṇḍalas of the elements are described in the first chapter of the Śāradātilaka.
The wise know that the sphere of heaven is circular, marked with six dots;
that of the wind is triangular and endowed with a svastika; that of fire is joined with a half-moon;
that of water is a lotus; and that of earth is square.
Also in the *Prapañcasāra*:
"The [mandala] of space is circular and endowed with six dots; that of air is a triangle with a svastika;
the solar orb is endowed with a lotus and a half-moon; the watery [mandala] is a circle; and that of earth is a triangle with a thunderbolt."
Or, as it says in the Viśvasāra:
The mandala of space is said to be circular and is agreed upon by all;
the mandala of wind is hexagonal, that of fire is triangular,
that of Varuṇa is octagonal, and the supreme mandala of earth is square.
Thus, having considered "it is so" or "it is not so," three opinions have been recorded therein.
The purpose of this, however, is the knowledge of forms regarding questions,
and the direct perception of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), the *āyāma*, and the *bhūta-udaya*.
And the accomplishment of all six rites will be explained further ahead.
Thus end the maṇḍalas of the elements.
The forms of the elements are also described in the Śāradā-tilaka.
The sky is clear, the wind is black, fire is red, water is pure white, and the earth is yellow;
thus the wise know the five elements according to their respective substrata.
Rāghavabhaṭṭa says it means "clear" and "white";
"viṣadam" means "white."
And likewise, in the *Prapañcasāra*:
Space is characterized by vacuity; wind is prone to movement; fire is possessed of heat;
water is endowed with taste; and earth is dense. These possess the appearances of white, black, reddish-pink, bright white, and yellow respectively. "Vacuity" means a hole or aperture.
"Siti" means black;
in reality, however, it refers to that which is clear, stainless, and blue—
this will become evident in the context of the inquiry.
In his view, by means of the inquiry "Is it white?", [one concludes] "it is not black. The intended meaning is that the cavities and so forth are known through [the perception of] space and the rest.
"Based on their respective substrates" means they are based on their own respective causes.
The creation of the fourfold body consists of the five elements as described by the Sun and the Moon.
In the first chapter of the *Viśvasāra-tantra*.
From the earth, medicinal herbs are born; from medicinal herbs, food is produced. Therefore, O Goddess, that [food] shall then become semen, which brings all happiness.
From that semen, O Goddess, the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) of the moon and the sun comes into being.
This entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is composed of the moon and the sun;
"moving" refers to that which is locomotive, and "unmoving" to that which is stationary.
In the first chapter of the Śāradātilaka.
This entire world, consisting of the moving and the non-moving, is composed of the five elements.
The non-moving is divided into many kinds according to the distinctions of mountains, trees, and so forth.
The moving, however, are divided into three types: those born from sweat, those born from eggs, and those born from the womb.

By the phrase "consisting of the five elements," both the theory of tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) and the theory of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*) are indicated. In that regard, according to the theory of tripartition, even in the bodies of those gods who are composed of fire (*taijasa*), half the portion consists of fire, one-fourth of earth, and one-fourth of water.

In the view of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*), however, fire consists of four parts, while each of the other elements contributes one-eighth part; this is likewise stated in the *Tattvaviveka*, the fifth chapter of the *Pañcadaśī*.
He speaks as follows in order to define quintuplication for the sake of establishing the production of the gross body and so forth:
For the sake of its enjoyment, for the enjoyment of further objects of experience, and for the birth of its own body,
the Lord effects the quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa) of each element, beginning with ether; the Lord is one who is endowed with the six qualities, such as sovereignty and the rest.

The sixfold group of qualities beginning with sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) has also been described as consisting of complete sovereignty, power, fame, splendor, knowledge, and dispassion. As it is stated in tradition: "Sovereignty, power, fame, splendor, knowledge, and dispassion—of these six, the term *bhaga* is used."
By the term "samarasya" (of equanimity), the eightfold sovereignty beginning with *aṇimā* is indicated; therefore,

because the Lord possesses qualities superior to those of Īśvara— who consists of the quality of *tamas*— the Lord’s superiority is established through His nature as consisting of the three qualities (*guṇas*) in equilibrium, such as *sattva*.
However, the name "Bhagavat" does not belong to that which consists of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* as mere existence.
Wise men should reflect that if it were so, that designation would not be applicable to you, who are composed of the three *guṇas*.
On the contrary, the Supreme Lord [manifests] again and again for their enjoyment—that is, solely for the enjoyment of those individual souls (*jīvas*) and for the objects of enjoyment.

For the birth of its offspring, for the enjoyment of food, drink, and the like, and for the production of the fourfold class of bodies— such as those born from a womb— it causes each of the five elements, beginning with space (*viyat*), to undergo quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*).
That which was not composed of five parts is thereby made to become composed of five.
Having divided each of the two [groups] into four parts again,
by joining each with its own second part and the second part of the other,
there are five times five.
Alternatively, there are six parts of fire, and the tenth part each belongs to earth, water, air, and ether.
Thus, even in our own earthly bodies and those of others, there are six parts of earth, and the tenth part each belongs to water and the other elements; as it has been stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
One should divide each of the elements, such as earth and the rest, into two parts.
Taking one part from each, one should then divide it again into five portions.
One should then sequentially merge each of these portions with each of the [other] elements.
Then, for that which has become space (*ākāśabhūta*), there are indeed six parts belonging to itself;
the four parts beginning with air (*vāyu*) enter into the elements beginning with air themselves.
And thus, because of the predominance of the parts of space and air among the sky-dwellers (*khecarāṇām*), they [move] in the sky.

The movement of house-lizards and the like is due to the predominance of the space-element (ākāśa-bhāga); the movement of elements such as earth and the like is due to the predominance of the air-element (vāyu-bhāga), resulting in movement everywhere and a lack of stability.
Thus ends the quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa).
In the first chapter of the Prapañcasāra.
When primordial nature (prakṛti), impelled by time, consists of the qualities (guṇas) and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa),
the fourfold body of a living being arises, distinguished according to the differences in its mode of birth:
the sprout-born (udbhijja), the sweat-born (svedaja), the egg-born (aṇḍaja), and the fourth, the womb-born (jarāyuja).
The body, which consists of the qualities and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), is fourfold, distinguished according to the different modes of birth for living beings:
the sprout-born (udbhida), the sweat-born (svedaja), the egg-born (aṇḍaja), and the fourth, the womb-born (jarāyuja).

The meaning is that when *prakṛti*— which has the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as its quality and is impelled by time— is present, the body of a living being (*jantu*) arises through fourfold distinctions of origin, such as the "sprouting" (*udbhijja*) and so forth.
The definition of the "sprouting" type has already been stated.
In the first chapter of the Viśvasāra-prapañcasāra.

That which emerges after breaking through the earth is designated as *udbhijja* (born from a fissure), being a stationary being (*sthāvara*) characterized by trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth. The manner of their production is [explained] according to the text cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
Immobile beings are to be known as those that sprout forth, taking the form of grasses, shrubs, and the like.
In that process, the earth, moistened by waters and heated internally,
being stirred by the wind, attains the state of a seed.
And so it has been said: seeds that have been moistened with water attain swelling, softness, and the state of a root;
from that root arises the sprout, and from the sprout comes the production of leaves.
From that, the leaf-nature arises; from the stalk, again, the bud.

its location is in the middle of this [body], always adorned by a lotus;

In the world of truth (satyaloka), Mahākālī is embraced by Mahārudra;
she is as vast as a chickpea in form, yet her nature is that of the moon, sun, and fire.
She is joined with the beginningless Puruṣa, and those who are portions of Him are designated as individual souls (jīva).
O Goddess, just as sparks flash forth from a blazing fire,
when the supreme bindu falls from that [state] onto the earth,
it immediately becomes endowed with power (śakti), O Goddess.
Thus ends the description of the manner of the conception of the embryo;
such is the manner of its arising from semen and blood according to the *Yogārṇava*.
That vital wind, having entered into the middle [of the body], divides the life-sustaining food that has been eaten into two parts— separating the food and the water. That wind is the *prāṇa* wind.

Also in the fourth chapter of the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Yogiyājñavalkya: "The life-sustaining breath (prāṇa), residing within the belly, shall separate those foods— whether they be nourishing or already consumed—
which have been suddenly mixed together by them."
The method for performing the separation [of the elements] is found in the *Yogiyājñavalkya*.
Furthermore, having reached the water in the fire, the food and other substances remain above the water;
then the apāna breath itself, together with the vital air (māruta),
proceeds toward the flame situated there within the center of the body.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: having caused the water to reach the fire, and having placed the food and other substances upon that water, by means of that very *prāṇa* wind, the *apāna* wind reaches—that is, attains—the flame situated within the body.
And thus, it will be stated primarily that [the process] is "impelled by the *prāṇa*" and "by the persistence of the *prāṇa*."
In reality, however, the meaning is that it is impelled by the very breaths of prāṇa and apāna.
By the apāna wind, the fire gradually increases;
then, O best of Brahmins, it blazes within one's own body in the center of the family (kula).
Thereupon, the flaming fire is impelled by the prāṇa.
Then, situated within the stomach and resting upon the water,
the food together with its condiments burns while supported by the liquid.
Then he caused it to fall into a deep sleep by means of water heated by fire.
And in the Yogārṇava:
Having placed water above the fire and that food upon the water,
one's own vital breath (*prāṇa*), staying beneath the water, gently causes it to sweat.
Stirred by the wind, the fire makes the water exceedingly hot.
That food is then cooked on all sides by hot water;
once cooked, it becomes twofold: the waste matter separately and the essence separately.
Excrement is impurity.
The method for the production of the *rasa* therein is found in the second chapter of the *Prapañcasāra*.

Furthermore, even food consisting of the six tastes that has been brought to the path of the throat becomes sweet through the influence of *śleṣman* (phlegm) when it is accompanied by it. In this regard, [the six tastes are:
sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent.
The six tastes are said to be derived from the transformation of the elements and to reside in substances.
Sweet, sour, pungent, and bitter.
In that same manner, having reached the stomach, it subsequently proceeds to the bile-receptacle.
The intention is the flaw.
Then, by following that [fire], it attains a pungent state;
likewise, here, being closely joined with the internal [heat], it is cooked by the water of bile.
The transformation of water and other elements through cooking is described in the *Yogiyājñavalkya*.
Sweat and urine would be water; rasa would take the form of semen;
and feces would be food, O Gārgī! Prāṇa would make each of these distinct.
In the *Prapañcasāra*.
That vessel called the grahaṇī is shaped like a handful or a closed fist.
The vessel is the channel.
Below that, the primary fire (pradhānāgni) is impelled by the equalized breath; for the wise know this place to be the root-support (mūlādhāra).

This primary fire is distinct from the fires located in the humors (doṣa) and the bodily constituents (dūṣya); it is the digestive fire (jaṭharāgni), renowned as being in the form of the submarine fire (vaḍavānala).
And likewise:
"As it is being digested, the wind (vāyu) carries away the juice (rasa), which is distinct [from the waste], as well as the blood and other constituents.
Therein, the wind separates the fecal matter (kīṭṭa) and collects it individually in the duodenum (grahaṇī)."
As that [feces] accumulates, it repeatedly fills the *viṇā* and the *grahaṇī*.
Filled with that excrement, she releases a contraction;
"with excrement" means with impurity (*mala*).

Feces are expelled through the anal canal; when that is digested, water [is likewise expelled]. Then, like the sweat of the limbs, the wind (vāyu), having pervaded the interior by means of subtle openings of Śiva, fills the bladder; once full, it releases its contents in a stream.
The receptacle for urine, curved like a bow, is called the bladder (*vasti*).

They say that "urine" (*mūtra*) is water that has emerged from the bladder due to the movement of wind (*vāyu*). When these two channels are afflicted by the humors (*doṣa*) through the consumption of unwholesome things, [disease arises].
There occurs the manifestation of urinary disorders such as prameha and mūtrakaṣṭa, as well as grahiṇī and other ailments.
In the *Suśruta* as interpreted by Rāghavabhaṭṭa: "Skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen—these elements all arise from one another, having been cooked by the heat of the *pitta*. (p. 53)
By this, it is stated that each preceding factor is the cause for each succeeding one;
and so it is said in that very same [text]:
The nutrient essence (*rasa*), situated within the channels, is intensely cooked by the bodily heat;
from that which is being cooked, two further transformations arise:
blood is produced, completely enveloped by a membrane.
The bodily constituents (dhātus) arise in succession, being ripened by the fire of their respective internal digestive organs (koṣāgni).
In the Yogārṇava:
The vital breath (prāṇa) slowly fills those channels with that essence;
once filled, they completely nourish the body from all sides.
In the Yogiyājñavalkya [Smṛti]:
Together with the *samāna* wind, the vital air (*māruta*) circulates through the body in the form of breath, pervading the nutrient essence throughout all the channels;
and through the nine apertures of the void, it effects the discharge of feces and urine.
All the winds act continuously within the bodies,
producing inhalation, exhalation, and coughing, impelled by the functions of the vital breath (prāṇa).
This evacuation of feces, urine, and so forth is the function of the downward-moving wind (apāna).

The functions of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, such as movement and so forth, are considered to be the work of *vyāna*. The work of *udāna* is said to be that which causes the elevation of the body and the like.
The nourishment and other such functions within the body are proclaimed to be the work of *samāna*.
The function of Nāga is said to be belching and other such qualities;
that of Kūrma is the closing of the eyes and so forth; that of Kṛkara is hunger and thirst;
and O best of Brahmins, the function of Devadatta is proclaimed to be yawning.
All the rites for Dhanañjaya, beginning with *poṣa*, have been proclaimed;
those for the Vāyus, beginning with *snāta*, will be described hereafter.
Thus ends the explanation of the origin of semen, blood, and so forth.

In the *Yogārṇava*: "Indeed, the mother's water-carrying channel is pierced; it is called 'supreme' because it carries the essence provided by the mother to the embryo within the channels situated at the navel."
In the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī*:
"In one night there is *kalana*; on the fifth day, a bubble;
blood in ten nights; and a lump of flesh on the fourteenth."
In the Prapañcasāra.
The impurity arising from yoga is called *mārīya*; the impurities of *pauruṣa* and *kārmaṇa* are [also included]. That which is called *āṇava* is proclaimed as the union of those two impurities.
Within these two impurities lie the twenty-four principles (*tattvas*) in their subtle forms.
In that regard, having first quickly performed the *yoga*, the wind of the embryo (*garbhamāruta*) agitates and then causes it to grow; this is to be connected with what was stated previously.
That [embryo] is moistened and boiled by the internal winds, fire, and waters.
On that very day, it was mixed together and made the size of his mother's thumb.
"Measured" (sammita) means measured by the size of the mother's thumb nail.
(p. 54) In the Yogārṇava as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
On the twentieth day, the flesh becomes thick and the state of a solid mass is attained;
on the twenty-fifth full day, that mass develops into sprouts.
But in the Śāktānanda it is said:
"When a full month has passed, the lump of flesh sprouts."
Thus it is stated in that very same [text]:
"In the beginning, the seed is produced; the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is suddenly the sprout.
In its center is Mount Sumeru, bearing the form of a skeletal staff."
The abode of all moving and non-moving beings, including the gods and others, as well as of all living creatures, is within Mount Meru; moreover, the individual soul (jīva),
shaped like the flame of a lamp, always resides in the heart.
Just as a hawk tied with a string is drawn back even though it has flown away,
so too the individual soul (jīva), bound by the qualities (guṇas), is drawn by the out-breath and in-breath (prāṇa and apāna).
In the second chapter of the *Yogiyājñavalkya*, however, it is said: "In the midst of that is the navel; from the navel arises the wheel (*cakra*).
It possesses twelve spokes, and by it the body is supported."
Driven by merit and demerit, the living being revolves in this wheel,
just as a spider moves within the midst of its web of threads. "Lūtika" refers to the spider (*ūrṇanābha*), which is well known by the name *mākara-sā*.
The soul's movement is merely its circling around the navel, whereas its actual place of residence is the heart alone;
therefore, there is no contradiction with the previous statement.
In the Yogārṇava:
When two months are fully completed, the marrow of the head is produced;
the marrow and bone [are formed] in three months, and the hair and skin in the fourth month.
Regarding these months, a specific detail is stated in the *Adhyātmaviveka* as follows:
In the first month, a state of liquidity called *kalala* arises;
in the second month, however, it becomes a solid mass (*ghana*), a fleshy lump (*peśī*), or a thickened swelling (*arbuda*).
These are, respectively, the initial stages for males, females, and hermaphrodites.
In the third [case], however, the five sprouts are considered to be the hands and so forth, ending with the head.

In these three texts, the threefold division mentioned regarding the emergence of the sprout is not contradictory, whether understood through the distinction between the body, Mount Meru, and its parts, or through the distinction between different Vedic traditions (āmnāya).
At that time, the limbs, minor members, and parts would exist simultaneously, even in their subtle forms.
In the fourth month, the manifestation of those parts arises;
his heart, born of the mother, longs for sense objects. Therefore, one should fulfill the mother's desires for the sake of the embryo’s prosperity.
The wise call that woman who possesses two hearts "Dohadinī" (one with pregnancy-longings).
From the non-granting of these longings, deformities and other defects of the fetus arise;
if the mother does not obtain the desired objects, the son is born afflicted by distress.

If [the woman] sees a longing for these things during her pregnancy, the fetus will be: wealthy if she longs for wealth; an enjoyer of pleasures if for enjoyments; handsome if for ornaments; most righteous if in a hermitage;
devoted to the gods if she sees a deity; and cruel if she sees a serpent. (p. 55)
By eating the flesh of an iguana, one becomes sleepy; by eating beef, one becomes strong.
By [eating] buffalo meat, however, one gives birth to a son with red eyes and hairy skin.
In the fifth stage, the embryo (*piṇḍa*) has fully developed, partaking in the nourishment of flesh and blood.
In the sixth [week], there is the distinctness of the bones, sinews, channels, and so forth, as well as the nails and hair;

the two *bala* (strengths) also become fully developed. In the seventh, however, the skin is not yet complete. In the eighth, the skin and the ears appear, and this *ojas* (vital essence) arises from the heart.
But in the Jñānabhāṣya, however:
In the fifth month, the cavities of the ears, eyes, and nose, as well as the throat and abdomen, are formed;
in the sixth, the mouth and feet; and in the seventh, all the limbs.
Then, in the eighth month, the joints reach full completion.
This also is as before.
Starting from the testicles and the skeleton down to the root of the anus,
the thirty-two knots of knowledge and realization constantly increase.
In the first chapter of the Śāradā-tantra.
Then, nourished by food, drink, and other provisions brought by his mother, he possessing a body of reality (tattva-deha) gradually grows day by day, week by week, and month by month.

"Tattvadehavān" means having a body composed of the twenty-four principles (*tattvas*). "Attaining manifestation through his own senses while being affected by the *doṣas* and *dūṣyas*" refers to this: wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*kapha*) are the *doṣas*, and the seven bodily constituents (*dhātus*) are the *dūṣyas*.
Thus concludes the exposition of the elements.
In the *Śāradā*.

The organs of knowledge (jñānendriya) are the ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose, and so forth. The objects of the organs of knowledge are traditionally held to be sound and the rest; the organs of action (karmendriya) are likewise [to be understood].
"Sound and the rest" refers to sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
The wise call them speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals;
namely, the mouth, hands, feet, anus, and sexual organ.
These are associated with speaking, grasping, moving, excretion, and pleasure.
Speaking, grasping, moving, releasing, and experiencing pleasure are declared to be the objects of the organs of action; the internal organ belongs to the self.
In the first chapter of the Viśvasāra.
I shall describe the qualities of the sense organs; listen, O lotus-faced one!
Form is declared to be the object of the eyes, and sound that of the ears; scent is to be known in the nose, and touch is said to be in the skin.
Seizing is said to be in the two arms; taste is said to be in the tongue. Emission is to be known in the secret organ; bliss should be in the generative organ.
Moving is in the pair of feet; speaking is in the lotus of the mouth.
Thus concludes the exposition of the sense organs and their objects. The author of the Śāradā-tantra clarifies the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
The mind (manas), the intellect (buddhi), and the ego (ahaṅkāra) are proclaimed as the consciousness (citta).
Herein, the mind consists of conceptualization and discursive thought;
the intellect is that which effects the determination of all states of being.
Ego (ahaṅkāra) is that which is endowed with the conceit of being a knower;
it is the non-conceptual mind (nirvikalpaka-citta).
As it has been said: "This is the supreme power (śakti), whose nature is that of the seed, and whose characteristics have been described."
Engaging in both conceptualization (*saṅkalpa*) and discursive thought (*vikalpa*), it becomes the mind (*manas*);
likewise, assuming the form of the intellect (*buddhi*), it effects the determination of all objects.
Through the conceit "I am the knower," that very same [faculty] is designated as the ego (*ahaṅkāra*).
"That very [reality], which is non-conceptual in nature, is indeed the essence of the mind;
thus, though it is one alone, it is perceived in many ways, like a dancer. So too says the Śruti:
"The mind conceives, the intellect determines, the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra) identifies with the 'I', and consciousness (cetas) perceives.
This is also stated in the *Prapañcasāra*.
Then, through the further increase of that supreme radiance, she of great power becomes the mind (*manas*).

When, however, she performs the functions of conceptualization and discrimination, and when she again reaches a definitive conclusion, she is designated as the intellect (*buddhi*). And when her activity is directed toward the knower as the self, she becomes the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).
Then, when she is measured within, their mind has determined the object.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
The organs of perception, the elements, and the mind— these sixteen are the modifications (vikāra). The five elements, ego-consciousness (ahaṅkṛti),
the unmanifest (avyakta), and the great principle (mahat)— these eight, along with the subtle elements (tanmātra), are the primary natures (prakṛti).
Those who know the principles understand that the seven transformations (vikṛti) are accompanied by ego-consciousness (ahaṅkāra).
This is the final meaning of the statement: "There are sixteen modifications (vikāra), eight primary natures (prakṛti), and seven transformations.
As it has been said: "The root-nature (mūlaprakṛti) is not a transformation; the seven, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), are both natures and transformations."
The group of sixteen, however, is a modification; it is neither primordial nature (prakṛti) nor a further modification—so say those who know the principles (tattva).
These twenty-four principles, ending with primordial nature, together with the person (puruṣa), constitute the twenty-five.
This has been stated in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā:
Beyond the twenty-three principles (tattvas), primordial nature (prakṛti) is said to be supreme;
they declare the Puruṣa, the twenty-fifth, to be beyond that nature.
Or rather, those who know the principles understand it thus.
The meaning is that because these are included within the [twenty-five] principles (tattva), those who know the principles have assigned them these designations.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
The drop (*bindu*) consists of the nature of Agni and Soma because it possesses the nature of both.
Semen is the form of Agni, and blood is the form of Soma;
since it consists of those two, the meaning is that the drop possesses the nature of both. (p. 57)
This has been stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa as follows:

The Moon consists of sixteen digits (kalās), the Sun of twelve digits, and Fire is endowed with ten digits; [the Self] enjoys thirty-eight digits. At present, these exist here for the purpose of conception.
By that [process], the entire world of moving and non-moving beings, consisting of Agni and Soma, is sung;
through the yoga of the fractional parts (kalāṃśaka), the birth of the embryo occurs.
In the first chapter of the Brahmajñānatantrodaya.
Śiva said:
Bone, flesh, and nails, as well as the channels and the skin—
these are declared to be the five qualities of earth, as spoken by one possessing the knowledge of Brahman.
Likewise, excrement, urine, semen, phlegm, and blood [are the qualities of water].
Water is said to have five qualities, as spoken by Brahmajñāna:
laughter, sleep, hunger, delusion, and laziness. Fire is said to have five qualities, as spoken by Brahmajñāna.
Holding, moving, throwing, contracting, and likewise expanding—
these are declared to be the five qualities of wind, as spoken by the knowledge of Brahman.
Desire, anger, greed, shame, and delusion as the fifth— these are declared to be the five qualities of ego (ahaṃkāra).
It was spoken by means of the knowledge of Brahman.
As cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"Bone, flesh, skin, sinew, and likewise hair as the fifth—
thus the earth, which is solid in nature, is said to be fivefold."
Saliva, urine, semen, blood, and marrow as the fifth—
these five qualities of water are proclaimed to be forms of Rudra.
Hunger, thirst, fear, sleep, laziness, and patience likewise [are his forms].
These qualities, characterized by thirst, are proclaimed to belong to fire.
Support, expansion, digestion, contraction, and extension—
these five qualities of wind are established in the form of action.
"Passion and hatred, as well as shame, fear, and likewise delusion—
these are declared to be the five qualities of space, which is called 'the void' and is of the nature of emptiness.
Thus ends the description of the origin of the five elements, beginning with bone.
In the Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī.
The vital winds are Prāṇa, Apāna, Samāna, Udāna, and Vyāna;
then there are Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya.
These ten qualities are said to belong to the self that is under the control of all the vital breaths (prāṇas).
In the Śāradātilaka.
The sun is known as the right portion, and the moon is the left side.
They know there to be ten channels (*nāḍīs*); among them, three are proclaimed as principal.
*Iḍā* is in the middle of the left body, while *Suṣumnā* and *Piṅgalā* are on the other [sides].
Among those, the middle channel (nāḍī) has the nature of Agni and Soma.
Here, the iḍā is situated below the left testicle; curved like a bow, it extends to the left nostril.
Similarly, the piṅgalā is situated below the right testicle; curved like a bow, it extends to the right nostril.
The meaning is that Suṣumnā is situated within the spinal column;
this will become clear further on.
Likewise, in the *Prapañcasāra*:
"Above, [the channel] is raised by the vital air (*marut*); from that, moreover, arises the pair of impurities (*mala*).
The channel, which consists of both [impurities], extends downward; it is long and straight."
With her face turned downwards, there would be a pair on each of her two sides;
on both sides, that is, on both flanks,
those channels (nāḍīs) are completely obstructed, while seven other channels are considered to remain.
In that context, the first channel is called Suṣumnā;
that which is on the left is known as Iḍā, and the one on the right is considered Piṅgalā.
Likewise, there is a certain channel with an opening directed outward that is attached to the mother's heart; through it,
the fetus attains nourishment like a field through an irrigation canal,
being gradually sustained by the bodily constituents produced from the essence of the mother’s food.
Through gradual increase, the supreme light attains the state of the individual soul (kṣetrajña).
That impurity (mala), together with the field-knower, along with the elements, the qualities,
and further with defects and the objects of corruption, is designated as "jantu" (the living being).

The aforementioned collection of the five elements, together with the mere *kṣetrajña* (knower of the field) and the impurities such as the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), is called a "living being" (*jantu*). This is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*). Of what nature is it? It is "with qualities" (*saguṇa*), meaning endowed with the qualities of *sattva* and so forth; or it is "with defects" (*sadoṣa*), meaning possessed of wind, bile, and phlegm.
Endowed with impurities and arising from the seven constituents—
such is the characteristic of a living being.
That pair of testicles is manifest in a male, but not in a female;
in a neuter, however, some manifestation of it is observed here. "The pair of testicles" refers to the pair of scrotal sacs.
In the first chapter of the *Niruttaratantra*.
O Goddess, the flow of the channels (nāḍīs) is like that of the lotus-root within the womb of the lotus, just as [the embryo is] within the egg of a bird.
Therein, seventy-two thousand channels have arisen;
"kañjasya" means the lotus, and "yoni" refers to its source or place of origin, namely the lotus-root (śālūka).
The principal channels that carry the vital breath are traditionally said to be ten:
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā as the third;
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Pūṣā, and Yaśasvinī.
Alambuṣā, Kuhu, and Śaṅkhinī are recorded as the ten [nāḍīs].
Thus, the wheel consisting of nāḍīs is to be understood within the wheel of powers (śakticakraka).
That which is the Suṣumnikā situated between the Iḍā and the Piṅgalā—

And this [central channel] should be known as consisting of the three qualities (guṇas), having the nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. Possessing the quality of passion (rajas), it is called Vajrā; Citriṇī is conjoined with the quality of goodness (sattva); and possessing the quality of darkness (tamas), it is the Brahmā-nāḍī—according to the sequence of their distinct functions.
Likewise: "The wind should be known as consisting of the sun, and the mind as consisting of the moon.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna are the vital breaths."

That which is connected to the left testicle, embracing the *suṣumṇā*, rests upon the right wheel; curved like a bow, it stays in the heart. Passing through the interior of the mechanism of the left shoulder, it reaches the right nostril.
Likewise, [the breath] situated in the right groin goes to the left nostril; as stated in another tantra:
Having emerged from the Suṣumṇā, it has gone and taken recourse to the right testicle;
having joined with the left side, it has reached the center of the instrument (yantra) and arrived at the opening of the right nostril, O Daughter of the Mountain!
"The left [channel] is interwoven with the mandala, non-different from the right nostril.
The nature of these two is stated in the *Yogārṇava*:
"Iḍā has the luster of a conch or the moon; she is situated on its left."
