"Piṅgalā, having a white and red luster, rests upon the right side.
According to another tantra, "The moon is situated in the iḍā, and the sun in the piṅgalā.
The meaning is that among these, the suṣumnā is the principal one.
And it is said in the venerable *Tattvacintāmaṇi*:
Outside Mount Meru, on the left and right, reside the Moon and the Sun; in the center is the Suṣumnā channel, composed of the three qualities (guṇas) and having the nature of the Moon, Sun, and Fire.
Furthermore, elsewhere it is said that the Suṣumnā stands in the middle, supported by the spinal column of those two, reaching as far as the Brahma-aperture.
Furthermore, the names of others are also mentioned in the Śāradā:
Gādhārī, the one called Hastijihvā, as well as Pūṣā and Alambuṣā.
Yaśasvinī, Śaṅkhinī, and Kuhu—these are the seven nāḍīs;
their state and nature are described in the Yogārṇava.
On the back of the iḍā, however, is the gāndhārī, resembling the throat of a peacock;
extending from the left foot to the end of the eye, it is celebrated as gāndhārī. The nāḍī called hastijihvā, which resembles a blue lotus, is situated in front of it.
Pūṣā, resembling a dark blue cloud, rests upon the right side from the crown of the head down to the big toe; she is on the back of the Piṅgalā,
extending from the eye to the sole of the foot on the southern side.
Yaśasvinī is conch-colored and resides in the eastern region; Piṅgalā is likewise situated in the east. Śaṅkhinī is considered to be located between Gāndhārī and Sarasvatī.
Suvarṇavarṇā, whose colors range from the feet to the top of the head, is situated on the left side.

In the southern portion, extending from the big toe to the top of the head, Kuhū, Rāvaṇā, Sarasvatī, Viśvodarī, and Śaṅkhinī are considered to be present; these too are mentioned as being primary. And it has been said:
These are very numerous, but among them fourteen are said to be the principal ones:
Suṣumnā, Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Kuhū,
Sarasvatī, Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Rāvaṇā, and Yaśasvinī.
Viśvodarī, Śaṅkhinī, then Pūṣā, Yaśasvinī,
and Alambuṣā.
In the Jñānabhāṣya cited in the Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī.
Iḍā is considered to be in the left nostril, and Piṅgalā in the right; Suṣumnā is at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), Gāndhārī in the left eye,
Hastijihvā in the right, and Pūṣā in the right ear.
Yaśasvinī is to be known on the left, and Ālambuṣā is considered to be at the mouth;
Kuhu should be at the base of the penis, and Śaṅkhinī above the head.
Thus, these ten channels remain, taking their stand upon the gates.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space—
these five have attained stability both externally and internally.
Thus, immediately after the description of the primary channels, the channels in the form of branches have been described.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:

Infinite channels have arisen; among them, the Suṣumnā exists within five joints—namely, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūraka, Anāhata, Viśuddha, and Ājñā. Therein, the completion [of the path] extends from the lowermost knot upwards, reaching as far as the uppermost knot.
They are infinite because they are impossible to count. As it has been said:
"O Sulocanā, [they arise] from the previously mentioned Suṣumnā situated in the center."
Originating from the navel, heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows,
and the joints, some vessels face downward, some face upward,
and others extend horizontally; among them, there are more than three hundred thousand.
The principal channels are said to number fifty thousand.
Within all of them, the powerful vital breath, Vāyu, is present on every side.
But in the Viśvasāra:
From the navel arise the channels that nourish the field of the body;
the *iḍā* is situated on the left side, while the *piṅgalā* is considered to be on the right.
In the middle, the *suṣumnā* is to be known as having the nature of the moon, the sun, and fire.
"Endless channels have arisen from her in the five joints"—

this which was stated [previously] as originating "from the navel" is for the purpose of nourishing the body through the movement of the *rasa* (nutrient fluid) and so forth, and not for the purpose of knowledge, meditation, and the like; this is within the context of the practice of the winds (*vāyu*).
I shall clarify this. (p.

61) Even the *Brahmajāmalam*, held within the *Narapatijayacaryā* and *Svarodaya*, speaks of the *kuṇḍalinī* at the navel for the sake of nourishing the body, just as it says: "The great power, *Kuṇḍalinī*, resides in the channels (*nāḍī*) in the form of a serpent."
From there, ten channels go upward and ten likewise go downward; two channels each extend horizontally, numbering twenty-four in total.
Beyond these, there are seventy-two thousand subtle principal channels.
Within the great power of Kuṇḍalinī, these root channels arise;
from them, subtle-mouthed channels that nourish the body are produced,
numbering seven hundred and seven.
There are ten principal channels, and ten are the carriers of the vital winds.
In the first chapter of the *Yogiyājñavalkya* as well, beginning with the navel-cakra:
"The channel situated in the middle of the *kanda* is celebrated as the *suṣumnā*;
all other channels stand surrounding this cakra."
O Gārgī, among all the channels as well, fourteen are the principal ones.
"Gārgī" is Yājñavalkya's address to his wife.
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Suṣumnā, Sarasvatī,
Vārūṇī, Pūṣā, Hastijihvā, Yaśasvinī, Viśvodarī, Kuhu, Śaṅkhinī, and Payasvinī.
Alambuṣā, Gāndhārī, and these fourteen principal [nāḍīs];
among them, three are the most prominent, and among those three, one is the most excellent.
That Suṣumnā, the sustainer of the universe, is said to be on the path to liberation.
O Gārgī! Suṣumnā is established in the middle of the bulb (kanda).
By means of that bone in the middle of the back, it is situated at the crown of the head.
Indeed, the Vaiṣṇavī Suṣumnā is situated on the path to liberation.
Iḍā and Piṅgalā are indeed on its left and right sides;
the Moon and the Sun move within Iḍā and Piṅgalā respectively.
One should know that the Moon is in Iḍā and the Sun is in Piṅgalā.
The moon is said to be of the nature of *tamas*, while the sun is said to be of the nature of *rajas*.
The portion of the sun is poison, and likewise, the portion of the moon is nectar.
These two [together] constitute everything below that, throughout all time, consisting of night and day.
Suṣumnā is the enjoyer of time; this is declared as the secret.
Sarasvatī and Kuhu are situated on the two sides of Suṣumnā.
Gāndhārī and Hastijihvā are on the rear and front sides of Iḍā.
Yaśasvinī and Pūṣā are located on the back and the front [of the face], while Piṅgalā is on the back; Kuhu and Hastijihvā are in the middle, with Viśvodarī situated there.
Between Yaśasvinī and Kuhu, Vāruṇī is established.
The illustrious Sarasvatī is situated between the Pūṣā and [the other] Sarasvatī;
and the Śaṅkhinī is situated between the Gāndhārī and the Sarasvatī.
And O best of Brahmins, the Alambuṣā is situated below the middle of the kanda.
In the eastern part of the Suṣumnā, Kuhu is situated from the navel down to the perineum;
she is to be known as moving both downward and upward, being Vāruṇī and all-pervading.
Yaśasvinī is held to extend from the southern [side] down to the big toe.
O my beloved! Know that Piṅgalā goes upward to the tip of the right nostril;
Pūṣā is at the end of the right eye, well behind Piṅgalā;
and likewise, O Gārgī, Payasvinī is held to reach the end of the right eye.
Likewise, Sarasvatī is proclaimed as the Hastijihvā extending upwards;
O best of Brahmins, Śaṅkhinī has ascended upwards from the left ear;
and Gādhārī is situated on the left side of the Iḍā, reaching as far as the corner of the left eye.
The *iḍā* is situated in the middle part, extending to the left nostril;
likewise, the *hastijihvā* is held to extend to the big toe of the left foot.
The *viśvodarī*, however, is that channel situated in the middle of the abdomen.
O highly fortunate one! Alambuṣā, Vāyumūlā, and likewise Ūrdhvagā—these others have arisen, as well as other auspicious ones;
just as they are on the leaf of the Aśvattha tree, so too are they upon the petals of the lotus.
O one rich in asceticism! All these channels must be understood in this way.
Thus ends the description of the origin of the channels (*nāḍī*) in the *Ādhyātmaviveka*. In this [system], the number of channels in the body is three hundred and sixty.
Dhanvantari has declared that there are exactly three hundred bones here;
there are two hundred and ten joints of the bones.
Two thousand [parts]—consisting of muscles, ligaments, vessels, and joints—are recognized.
There are nine hundred ligaments and five hundred muscles;
in women, there are twenty additional ones located in the breasts and the pelvic region.
Furthermore, there are nine million and twenty thousand veins and arteries.
Thus, there would be nine hundred and fifty-six and a half.
Thus ends the account of the production of the bones and other [constituent parts].
In the seventeenth chapter of the Rudrajāmala.
(63) "There are thirty-five million hairs on a human being,
and from all the openings of the channels, drops of dharma flow forth.
Thus ends the description of the locations of the channel-openings.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Human Body Consisting of the Annamaya-kośa," in the first section (Sargakāṇḍa) of the Śrī Prāṇatoṣiṇī.
Thus, following the description of the channels and so forth, the section on the vital winds (vāyu) is now described, as it is appropriate in this context.
In the Śāradātilaka.
The vital breath (prāṇa), having risen from the mūlādhāra, pervades that body by means of those [channels].
Here, ten winds are proclaimed, and ten fires are remembered.
By means of those channels.
That very body which has been experienced as a body.
The names of the winds are given in that same place:
the five vital airs beginning with *prāṇa* are proclaimed by the names Nāga, Kūrma, Dhanañjaya,
Kṛkara, and Devadatta.
"Prāṇa and the others" refers to prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna.
This is also stated by Yājñavalkya in the fourth chapter:
"Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna."
Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya—
these ten vital airs (vāyu) circulate through all the channels (nāḍīs). Among these, the five beginning with Prāṇa are known as the primary ones.
Among them, O best of men, these two—prāṇa and apāna—are the most principal;
of these two, prāṇa alone is always the primary one for all living beings.
Their forms and locations are described in the *Yogārṇava*:
"The form of Prāṇa is proclaimed to resemble sapphire;
it resides between the mouth and the nose, in the center of the heart, and in the middle of the navel."
Some say that the abode of the vital breaths is even in the big toe.

This *apāna* wind carries away food that has been consumed, as well as semen, urine, and excrement; therefore it is called *apāna*. This *māruta* (wind) resembles the *indragopa* insect and is like a cloud at twilight.
And it [is located] in the penis, the anus, the thighs, the groins, and the knees.

The penis (*meḍhra*), the *liṅga*, the anus (*pāyu*), the rectum (*guda*), the two thighs (*ūru*) in their well-known form, the groin (*vaṅkṣaṇa*) at the joint of the thigh, and the knee (*jānu*) in its well-known form;
the *indragopa* is a specific red-colored insect,
known as the *kāpāsiyāpokā*.
It resides in the calves, the abdomen, the hollow of the nape, and at the root of the navel.
Vyāna is born from a hundred vyānas; it provokes all diseases. (p.
64) It resembles great silver and acts as the cause for taking up necklaces.
"Great silver" means gold.
The meaning is: one who performs the act of taking up the necklace, that is, one who grasps the food.
Between one's own eyes and ears, at the waist, and also at the ankles—
the waist is well known;
the ankle is the joint of the foot.
The wind named Udāna resides continuously here in the nose, the throat, and the region of the buttocks;
it causes the lower lip and the mouth to quiver, provokes agitation in the limbs and eyes,
and agitates all objects.
Having the color of lightning-fire, he causes one to rise from bed and take a seat;
he dwells in the joints of both the feet and the hands.
When drunk, eaten, or smelled, it [subdues] blood, bile, phlegm, and wind.
The wind named Samāna leads [the vital energies] equally throughout the limbs;
resembling cow's milk in appearance, it is established throughout the entire body.
And in the Yogiyājñavalkya [Smṛti] as well.

They say that the abode of the vital breath (prāṇa) is between the mouth and the nose, in the center of the heart, and in the center of the navel; some say it is also in the big toe. Below and above the Kuṇḍalinī, the vital breath rests on all sides.
Some indeed say that the abode of the apāna wind is in the anus, the middle of the thighs, the knees, the abdomen,
the testicles, the hips, the shanks,
or the navel; however, the apāna wind stands between the two supports of the anus.

In these locations, udāna constantly shines like a lamp; it resides in all the joints, as well as in the feet and the hands. Samāna, having pervaded everything, remains established throughout all the limbs.
But Rāyamukuṭa says:
He says: "Prāṇa is in the heart, apāna is in the anus, samāna is in the region of the navel, udāna resides in the region of the throat, and vyāna pervades the entire body."
Regarding the "udgāra" (eructation), it is said to be like a dark blue cloud.
The tortoise remained with its eyes opened, possessing a luster like that of crushed collyrium.
Kṛkara is characterized by hunger and is reddish-brown, resembling the color of the Java flower.
In its manifestation, Devadatta resembles pure crystal.
Likewise, Dhanañjaya was of the color of great silver in the herd.
On the forehead, the chest, the shoulders, the heart, and the navel— in the skin and bones—
the five winds beginning with Nāga are firmly established together.
But in the first chapter of the Viśvasāra [Tantra]:
Prāṇa, located in the heart region, has a luster like that of a ruby;
apāna, in the secret region, is said to be like an indragopa insect;
and samāna, in the region of the navel, is white in appearance like cow’s milk.
Udāna is proclaimed to be smoke-colored and located in the region of the throat;
Vyāna exists in all the limbs in the form of light.

In accordance with this statement, the distinction between the form previously mentioned as being "worn by Rāyamukuṭa" and the form stated in the present statement— which was previously cited— should be reconciled through differences such as those found in various scriptural traditions (āmnāya).
But the author of the Prapañcasāra, however, [states]:
The one called Dhanañjaya performs various kinds of breathings within this body;
because he is the worldly wind (laukikavāyu), he does not leave the deceased.
Therefore, in the Viśvasāra it is said:
"When he desires sexual union, then he should engage in sexual union;
at that time, the wind Dhanañjaya collects the seed within the womb."
"Having placed [the breath] on the path of the wind, one should cause it to enter once again"—thus it is said that the movement of the embryo proceeds from the *dhanañjaya* wind.
However, others have stated that there are four additional winds, as follows:
"The *vairambhaṇa*, the *sthānamukhya*, the *pradyota*, and likewise the *prakṛta*."
"In that [system], the Vairambhaṇa and other winds fall under the control of all the winds," as stated in the *Brahmajāmala* cited in the *Narapatijayacaryā-svarodaya*.
The movement of the vital air (vāyu) within the center of the body is clearly perceived by the wise through the three channels (nāḍīs): Piṅgalā, Iḍā, and Suṣumnā.
The moon resides in the Iḍā channel, while Piṅgalā carries the sun.

Suṣumnā is the form of Śambhu, and Śambhu has the nature of the Haṃsa. The letter *ha* is said to be the exit, while the letter *sa* is for entry. The letter *ha* shall be the form of Śambhu, and the letter *sa* is called Śakti.
The specific details regarding this will be stated further ahead,
in the second chapter of the Śāradā-tantra.
The short vowels are situated in Piṅgalā, while the others are joined in Iḍā;
those four which are neuter should be known as residing in the middle of Suṣumnā.
Herein is the method: at the moment when the bodily wind begins its entry from the left nostril into the right nostril, [it remains] for a certain time...

When time flows through both [nostrils] simultaneously, that is the time of the commencement of the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*); at that time, the pair of short vowels consisting of *ṛ* and *ḷ* arises.
Likewise, when [the breath] moves from the right nostril to the left nostril, that is the time of the commencement of the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*); at that time—
The pair of long vowels, ṝ and ḹ, arises;
this has been stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"Starting from the seven notes, those four which are neuter arise when the vital breath (prāṇa) rests in the Suṣumṇā at the transition of the solstices."
In the Jāmalam.
The moon, in the form of *śakti*, resides as the flow of the left channel (*vāmanāḍī*);
whereas the sun, in the form of *śambhu*, resides in the flow of the right channel (*dakṣanāḍī*).
Thus ends the description of the winds situated within the body.
In the *Śāradā* [Tantra]:
The ten fires are dissolved within the body in the doshas and dūṣyas;
their names, as recorded by Rāghavabhaṭṭa, are as follows:
Jṛmbhaka, Dīpaka, Vibhrama, Bhramaśobhana, Āvasathya, Āhavanīya, Dakṣiṇāgni, Anvāhārya,
and Gārhapatya— these are the ten fires.
The description of the ten fires is based on the elision of the middle term (*madhyapadalopa-samāsa*), interpreting "bhrama-śobhana" as "one who is beautiful with delusion."
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
Hunger and thirst belong to the vital breath (prāṇa); memory belongs to the mind (manas);
sorrow and delusion belong to the body; old age and death are the six waves.
Also in the Prapañcasāra:
"Hunger and thirst, sorrow and delusion, old age and death—
these are the six waves residing in the attributes of the vital breath, the intellect, and the body."
A specific state that produces distress among waves.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
From the father's semen come the sinews, bones, marrow, and skin; from the mother's blood come the flesh and the eyes.
From the father's semen come the sinews and so forth;
from the mother's blood come the skin and so forth.
It is declared in the second chapter of the *Prapañcasāra* that [the body] of all embodied beings consists of six sheaths (*ṣāṭkauṣika*) within all bodies.
Marrow, bone, and sinew arise from semen; skin, flesh, and blood arise from blood. Thus, the body of embodied beings consists of six sheaths (ṣāṭkauṣika).
However, by those who know the Vedānta, five sheaths are described in another manner, as follows, on the full moon day:
In the eighth chapter of the *Pañcakośaviveka*, Vidyānandasvāmin states:
"The body, born from the semen produced by the food consumed by the parents, grows through food alone;
it is composed of food (*annamaya*) and is not the Self, because it did not exist prior [to conception] and will cease to exist afterwards."
In the expression "pitṛbhukta," by means of the grammatical device of *ekaśeṣa* (retaining one of two identical terms), the meaning "born from the food consumed by the mother and father" is obtained.
The phrase "by means of food"—that is, by means of nourishment such as milk and so forth—"prior to birth" is the understood remainder.
After death, because of its absence—that is, because of the absence of a body—it [does not exist].

That which is present throughout the body, which constitutes its strength, and which is the initiator of all activities, is the vital air (vāyu) consisting of prāṇa; it is not the Self (ātman), because it is devoid of consciousness. During deep sleep it is dissolved, and upon the awakening of the body, it extends from the body to the tips of the nails.
The intellect (*dhī*), accompanied by the reflection (*chāyā*) of the Self, does not itself possess the designation "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*);
this is the remainder of the sense.
The internal organ (*antarindriya*) undergoes modification through its states as agent (*kartṛtva*) and instrument (*karaṇatva*).
"Consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the mind (*manas*) are these two, internal and external, respectively.
Herein is the commentary of Rāmakṛṣṇa Paṇḍita:

"Now, since there is no difference between the mind and the intellect (*buddhi*) in their status as internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), [they are distinguished] by way of their forms as consisting of mind (*manomaya*) and consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*)."

Anticipating the objection that the conceptualization of two sheaths (*koṣa*) as consisting of mind (*manomaya*) and consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) is untenable, [the author] states—beginning with "by way of being the agent," etc.—that the distinction between them is indeed possible because of the existence of a difference based on their respective natures as agent and instrument. (p.
67) The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is the internal sense-organ, exists in the form of an agent by way of both being the agent and the instrument.
"And by means of the form of the ear" (*karṇarūpeṇa*) means that it would undergo modification or transformation.
These two—the agent and the instrument—become what are designated by the terms "intellect" (*vijñāna*) and "mind" (*manas*).
And these two exist in a relationship of being internal and external to one another.
Therefore, the meaning is that the existence of two sheaths is logically established.
The internalized state [of consciousness] beginning with the letter *ka* partakes in the reflection of bliss;
during the enjoyment of merit and upon the cessation of that enjoyment, it dissolves in the form of sleep.
Now, in order to demonstrate that that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is not the Self, he states its nature in the verse beginning with "kācit" and so forth.

During the enjoyment of merit—that is, at the time of experiencing the fruit of meritorious actions—a certain mental modification (*dhīvṛtti*), being turned inward, partakes in the reflection of bliss; it bears the reflection of the bliss that is the very nature of the Self.
That same [modification], upon the cessation of enjoyment—the termination of the experience of the fruit of meritorious actions—merges in the form of sleep; it becomes dissolved.
The intention is that this "vital function" (*vṛtti*) is what constitutes the *ānandamaya* (sheath of bliss).

By this, those six sheaths mentioned by experts in the Tantras— namely, the marrow-sheath, bone-sheath, sinew-sheath, skin-sheath, flesh-sheath, and blood-sheath— are subsumed by the knowers of Vedānta as being included within the *annamaya* (food-sheath) itself.
Furthermore, four additional sheaths have been mentioned—namely, those consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*), consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), mind (*manomaya*), and bliss (*ānandamaya*).
From this, it follows that this body consists of ten sheaths.
Thus concludes the exposition on the sheaths of the body.
In the Prapañcasāra.

The grammatical connection is that digestion occurs sequentially among the bodily constituents (dhātus), beginning with rasa and ending with semen. From the digestion of semen, the eighth stage of old age arises spontaneously as a distinct state.
At that time, for the individual soul (kṣetrajña), that which is sought is its sole support,
just as oil is for a lamp, or as the flash of lightning is for a cloud;
it is like the fire within a jar enclosed by many openings.
Just as light spreads forth possessing the power to illuminate what is nearby,
so too, although the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) of great splendor is enveloped by the body,
his respective faculties expand toward the apprehension of their own respective objects.

Just as at the time of a lamp’s ignition, the oil or other fuel spreads out toward the flame for the sake of its burning and comes forth of its own accord; or as the cloud approaches at the moment of the lightning’s flash;
or as when fire enclosed within a jar with many holes consumes ghee.

The meaning is that the lights— possessing the power of near-illumination and endowed with the power of proximate manifestation— increase and spread forth through the sense organs as instruments for the respective perception of objects by the Self, which is enveloped by the body and situated within the ten sheaths (kośas).
(p. 68) Although the meaning is perfectly clear in the reading "as oil" (sneham), it is nevertheless explained as follows:

Just as the light of a lamp [spreads] toward its oil, just as the light of lightning [spreads] toward a cloud, and just as the light of fire enclosed within a vessel with many holes [spreads] toward the ghee, so too do the lights of the self [spread] toward the apprehension of their respective objects.
The meaning is that they spread forth.
By the use of the plural number in the expression "they increase" (*saṃvivarddhante*), it is indicated that even at a single moment, many objects are grasped by many sense organs.
For this very reason, one whose gaze is turned inward has severed the bond resulting from looking toward external objects.

May some indescribable state of Śambhu’s grace be ever present before me— a state in which my mind has attained the unimpeded bliss of the Supreme Brahman through mature spiritual exaltation, my inner self is perfectly serene, and my speech is sweetened by the arising of various divine emotions, and my face is ever smiling.
Thus begins the prayer of the matured yogin of the Kula tradition.
The statement from the *Kulārṇava* to be cited later—“inner vision, outward eyes,” and so forth—is well-supported.
It is also said by the Vaiṣṇavas:
“Even a wise man, though moment-to-moment intent upon objects one after another, does not become deluded regarding the lotus-feet of Mukunda.”
"Even when under the sway of singing, dancing, movement, and rhythm, she remains mindful of protecting the water-pot upon her head, like an actress"—
this and other such instances are established by direct perception; yet someone may simultaneously scratch their own body, send another on an errand, and look at something else as well.

By this, let the wise carefully examine and deliberate upon the view of certain thinkers—whether praiseworthy or not—that we do not admit the existence of a cognition that has both as its simultaneous objects; enough of this elaboration.
Let us return to the subject at hand.
The teachers state in the *Prapañcasāra* the manner in which the five elements abide within the sense faculties.
Space in the ear, air in the skin, fire in the eye,
water in the tongue, and earth in the nose— thus proceeds the manifestation of objects.
Space is the ether (*ākāśa*), air is the wind (*vāyu*), water is the liquid (*jala*), and earth is the ground (*pṛthivī*).
This, however, has been stated by way of predominance;
in reality, it has already been explained that all five elements exist within each of the five [elements] according to the previously described process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*).
When bile (*pitta*) thoroughly dissolves the wind (*marut*) that has become liquefied, [it causes fever].
At that time, the *dhātu* gradually melts the blood and the *lasīkā* in an instant.
Once melted, that which is called *tulasī* increases through the pores of the skin;
likewise, sweat flows forth externally everywhere in droplets.
When the phlegm (kapha), driven by wind (marut) and bile (pitta), becomes stagnant and then flows forth—
either moving upward or rushing out rapidly as vapor—
it produces a disorder characterized by phlegm that fills the ear canal.
Or one may produce swellings such as gaṇḍamālā in a living being through the power of karma.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
Having become thus within the womb, remembering the auspicious and inauspicious deeds of his previous birth, he remains there in a state of suffering, his body concealed by the fetal membrane.
In the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī*:
"In the ninth month, the embodied soul residing within the womb remembers everything with its heart;
dwelling in the city of the nine gates, it passes the time slowly."
As for the manner of its position, it is stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"With palms joined at the forehead, resting against the mother’s back,
with limbs drawn together, it dwells within the womb on the right side."
The channel (nāḍī) resting on the left side is considered to be the neuter, while that resting in the middle is considered the male.
In the Viśvasāra: "The aperture arising from the region of the womb, and beyond that the root of the navel—
those who know all the tantras call that the *garbhāśaya* (uterus)."
The *kalala* indeed remains there, and from that the embryo is produced;
by the application of karma, the Creator ordains its formation according to its own nature.

The individual soul (*jīva*), conditioned by the adjunct of ignorance (*avidyopādhika*), enters the womb out of a desire to experience the fruit of previously accumulated karma— that is, karma accumulated in previous and even earlier lives—
driven by the longing to enjoy the results of past actions.
The remainder [of the verse] states:
"What is the nature of the fruit of prior karma? It is that which was previously acquired," and so forth.
This is the intended meaning.

Karma is threefold: accumulated (*sañcita*), commenced (*prārabdha*), and future (*āgāmi*). Among these, the destruction of the accumulated is effected by means of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*), medicinal herbs, and so forth; and that of the future is through austerity (*tapas*).

For this very reason, Gopīnātha Tarkācārya formulated the definition of a *śiṣṭa* (an authoritative person) as one who possesses the destruction of defects that is not contemporaneous with the antecedent non-existence of those defects.
There is no other way for the *prārabdha* (commenced karma) to be exhausted except through experience (*bhoga*).
Therefore, he describes the entry of the individual soul (jīva) into the womb for the sake of experiencing that fruit;
and it has been stated that the exhaustion of prārabdha-karmas occurs only through experience.
In the Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī.
Having fully known all that was done, both good and evil, in his previous birth, he entered the womb with his feet upward and his face downward,
into that motionless and terrible-looking place.
In this motionless, pitch-black darkness, terrible to behold and fearsome,
I practice the auspicious knowledge that carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra.
Having thus become a long-practiced yogi, I shall be liberated and go to that state.
Thus, the living being situated within the womb, afflicted by the torments of the womb and having attained the characteristic of consciousness, constantly contemplates this within the mind.
In the Viśvasāra:
At that time, the embryo, remaining thus, stays motionless for a moment while recollecting the auspicious and inauspicious deeds of its previous birth; it certainly becomes immobile because,
without the presence of the fifty syllables within the body, it is unable to emit sound and other [sensations] through the mouth.
The manifestation of the Śabdabrahman is said to be their womb and their abode in that very place:
"In former times, O Goddess, in the Kṛta age, on Kailāsa, the best of mountains."

O lotus-faced one! Through the yoga of meditation, I meditate upon your pair of feet; may my perfection be attained therein at the end of the age. There, the sound of hand-cymbals became filled with supreme bliss for me.
At that very moment, O Goddess! a drum, adorned with the Brahman of Sound, arose there for the increase of my joy;
it resounds through the union of substance with the resonance whose essence is both sound and meaning.
Endowed with the fifty letters and adorned with *nāda* and *bindu*,
the *mātṛkā* consisting of the fifty letters is established within the *cakras*.
The mantra is supported by the six *cakras*, and the *mātṛkā* resides within the bodies of embodied beings.

In the foundation (ādhāra), the genitals, the navel, the heart-lotus, the root of the palate, and the forehead; in the two-petalled, sixteen-spoked, twenty-two-petalled, ten-petalled, twelve-spoked, and four-petalled [cakras];

at the end of the abode (vāsānta), in the middle of the child (bāla), and in the region of the throat accompanied by the letters ḍa, pha, ka, ṭha, and sa, as well as the vowels and the letters ha and kṣa in the middle of the bow (kodaṇḍa).
Let the one of stainless intellect perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) for the sake of accomplishing the perfection of *nyāsa*.
Regarding the locations of the fourteen worlds within the body, it is stated in the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī*:
"The netherworlds (*pātāla*), the mountains, the worlds, and the nine planets beginning with the Sun."
The seven worlds beginning with Bhūrloka, the heavens, and the Nāgas—all these reside within the body of every embodied being. I shall now describe their locations to you:
one should know that below the feet is *Tala*, and above that is *Vitala*.
The wise one should perceive Sutala at the knees, A-tala in the crevice of the joints,
Talātala in the middle of the anus, Rasātala at the base of the penis,
and Pātāla at the joint of the hips, extending from there to the feet.
The Bhūrloka is at the region of the navel, and the Bhuvarloka likewise in the heart;
the Svarloka is at the region of the throat, and the Maharloka is in the eyes;
the Janaloka is above that, and the Tapoloka is on the forehead.
Satyaloka is within the great womb, as are the fourteen worlds.
Meru is situated at the apex of the triangle, Mandara at the upper corner,
Kailāsa at the right corner, and Himālaya at the left corner.
Vindhya is Viṣṇu, and above that are these principal mountain ranges (kulaparvatas).
O Maheśānī! Jambūdvīpa is situated in the place of the bones;
Kuśadvīpa is in the flesh, and Krauñcadvīpa is in the veins.
Śākadvīpa is said to be located in the blood at all the joints of living beings;
above that is Śālmalidvīpa, and Plakṣadvīpa is in the mass of body hair;
Puṣkaradvīpa is in the navel, and immediately following that is the ocean.
The salt ocean is likewise in the urine; the milk ocean is in the semen;
the ocean of curd is in the marrow; above that is the ocean of clarified butter;
the ocean of fat is said to be in the marrow-fluid (vasā); and the sugarcane ocean is the blood of the hips.
The blood is said to be the river of wine; thus the seven oceans have been described.
Now listen, O Pārvatī, as I shall speak of the mandala of the planets:
the sun is situated in the wheel of sound (nādacakra), and the moon is in the wheel of the point (binducakra).
Maṅgala is said to be in the eyes, and likewise Soma’s son (Budha) is in the heart;
Guru is in the belly, and Śukra is likewise in the semen;
then Mandu (Śani) is situated in the navel, and Rāhu is likewise situated in the mouth.
The feet, the hands, the banner, and the circle of sacred sites (tīrthamaṇḍala) within the body are described in the Viśvasāra.
The zodiac signs beginning with Aries are situated in the body in sequence: on the head, face, arms, heart, and abdomen;
then on the hips, bladder, genitals, thighs, knees, shanks, and feet.
Now hear their forms.
They are respectively red, white, green, pale-red, and pale-yellow; variegated, blackish-yellow, and reddish-brown; tawny, speckled, and lotus-colored;
and green and dark-blue.
"Sitetaraḥ" means black (*kṛṣṇa*).
"Piśaṅga" is a mixture of blue and yellow.
"Karvura" is well known [as variegated].
Vabhru is Kapila.
One should assign Aries, Taurus, Gemini,
Cancer, and Leo; Virgo, Libra,
Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces to the limbs, preceded by the syllable *Oṃ* and followed by *namaḥ*.
Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, and Rohiṇī;
likewise Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, and Punarvasu after that;
Puṣyā, Āśleṣā, Maghā, and Pūrvaphalgunī after that.
Uttarā-phalguṇī, Hastā, Citrā, and the one following it; Svātī, Viśākhā, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Mūlā following that;
Pūrvā-āṣāḍhā, Uttarā-āṣāḍhā, Śravaṇā, and likewise Abhijit.
Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, Pūrvabhādrapadā, Uttarabhādrapadā, and ending with Revatī are thus proclaimed.
[These are assigned] to the head, the pair of eyebrows, the two eyes, the two ears, the nose, and the two cheeks.
On the two lips, on the rows of teeth, on the tongue, at the base of the neck, on the pair of breasts, as well as on the sides of the chest, in the region of the navel,
on the hips, on the back, in the private parts, and again on the two feet.
One quarter consists of two constellations (nakṣatras) and effects the transformation of the zodiac signs (rāśis).

As for the purpose of stating the zodiac signs and constellations in relation to the body: the intention is that at the time of a query, when the querent asks while placing his hand on a certain limb, whichever sign falls upon that limb, one should determine the [person's] caste and other attributes by means of that sign.
The placement of the constellations (rāśinyāsa) and the placement of the lunar mansions (nakṣatranyāsa) for Śrīvidyā have been described by this very [text].
In the *Jñānabhāṣya* extracted from the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī*:
"From semen blood is produced; from blood arises the *bindu*.
From *prāṇa* wind is produced; from *apāna* comes the fire of time (*kālāgni*)."
The navel is produced from semen; from semen arises fire.
From the *apāna* [wind] is born the Fire of Time (*kālāgni*), which resides in the region of the navel in the form of the submarine fire (*vaḍavāgni*) that digests food.
These ten fires, situated within the elements of wind, bile, and phlegm, are produced from semen. Thus, the origin of fire is stated twice according to this distinction.
From the flesh arises the production of excrement, and from that also comes the marrow;
the tongue and the nose of embodied beings are produced from the semen.
From the blood arise the eyes, both the left and the right.
From the vital breath (prāṇa) arises the void, as well as the two nostril apertures.
In the sixth chapter of the *Tattvasāra*.
Īśvara said:
The moon, the sun, and likewise fire; the ten channels (nāḍīs) in the body;
the five vital winds (vāyus) residing in the body, as well as the mind and the bindu.
The six cakras and the spinal column (merudaṇḍa), as well as Uḍḍīyāna,
Jālandhara, Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagrīva, and Śrīhaṭṭaka.
In the first chapter of the Nirvāṇatantra.
O Pārvatī! The cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) has the form of a living being and possesses various bodies;
indeed, that cosmic egg is said to be the physical form consisting of the gross, the subtle, and so forth.
O Goddess! Mount Meru is in the center, and there are seven principal mountain ranges (kulācala).
Indeed, the mountain named Sumeru extends from its base to its summit; O Maheśānī, situated two finger-breadths below the upper region of Meru,
lie the seven worlds in succession, beginning with Bhūrloka.
"O Supreme Goddess, seven netherworlds (pātāla) remain at a distance of two finger-breadths," as stated in the *Tattvasāra* on page 73.
Prakṛti and Puruṣa, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva,
as well as the rivers, the oceans, and the fourteen worlds—
whatever qualities exist within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), they all abide within this body.
O lady of pure smiles, I shall briefly declare all of this to you:
situated upon the summit of Mount Meru, the Moon, endowed with sixteen digits (kalās),
pours down a stream of frost-like moisture day and night, facing downward.
The moon, which flows in various ways, is indeed a drop of nectar (*pīyūṣabindu*);
by means of the center of the jewel-drop (*binduratna*), the perfection of the body (*dehasiddhi*) is produced.
O beautiful one, it resembles the *javā* flower in the region of the bladder.
Pervading the root of the *śaṅkhinī*, the Sun resides within embodied beings;
the Sun consists of twelve *kalās*, while Fire consists of ten *kalās*.
Within the bodies of all embodied beings, it is eternally the digester of food and other substances.
The moon rains down frost, while the sun always causes drying;
when joined together, the vital breath (prāṇa) remains stable, but upon their separation, death occurs.
The solar ray is always above in the limb, while the lunar nectar is below.
Those who know yoga understand the practice of *kāmarūpa* to be yoga;
and one becomes a *saṃyogin* yogi through the single union of *prāṇa* and *apāna*.
*Prāṇa* is said to consist of the moon, and likewise, *apāna* consists of the sun.
The meeting of these two in the middle is the passion (*rajas*) that is the cause of disease.
Having firmly bound *uḍḍīyāna*, one should perform exhalation (*recaka*) and inhalation (*pūraka*).
Through the union of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, there occurs the conjunction of *samāna* and *udāna*.
In Kāmarūpa, one attains union with the three: prāṇa, apāna, and samāna.
Uḍḍīyāna is said to be between the two powers at the navel;
Jālandhara is to be known in the bladder; Kāmarūpa is within the womb;
Pūrṇagrīva is between the eyebrows; and Śrīhaṭṭa is above the palate.
Likewise: Brahmā resides in the center of the navel, Keśava in the center of the heart, and Śaṅkara is to be known as being in the head; these three locations bestow liberation.
Thus ends the description of the sacred sites (*tīrtha*) and so forth within the body.
In the Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī.
In the meantime, O Goddess, amidst the peril of being within the womb of all beings,
in the ninth or tenth month, the creature— afflicted with fever— is expelled through an opening by powerful winds of birth, like an arrow shot from a bow.
The meaning is that she is afflicted by pain.
Even though she has fallen, she does not know [her husband], and even when fainted,
she does not recognize her lord because of the pressure on the vaginal opening caused by the force of the birth-wind.
All the knowledge that was contemplated within the heart in the womb has been forgotten.
In that regard, there is an excess of affliction for sinners at the time of birth; this has been stated in the second chapter of the *Prapañcasāra*:
(p. 74) Now, for those embodied beings who have committed evil, there is great effort required to emerge from the womb;
the course of karma for human beings is exceedingly diverse in its workings, as was the thought of Nalinodbhava, that is, Brahmā.
He becomes intensely agitated, his limbs tremble with yawning,
he breathes heavily and violently, and out of fear he desires to weep;
for that sound called *parā*, which first arose from the *mūlādhāra* and later reaches the heart, now perceives [the object].

The intellect is called the intermediate (madhyamā). Then, for a living being who desires to speak, the conjunction of phonemes— driven by the vital air and bound within the *suṣumnā*— arises in the mouth as the manifest speech (*vaikharī*).
Since even the crying of an infant immediately after birth consists of indistinct phonemes, [the author], while describing the manner in which phonemes arise,
has shown the general production of all letters from Kuṇḍalinī:
"Due to the lack of differentiation in the path of the channels, there is no manifestation of the phonemes therein."
As long as there is the distinction of the throat, head, and other locations for the manifestation of phonemes, from that [source],
when the state consisting of mind, ego, and intellect arises with the thought "I am born," then the innate nature of the living being,
preceded by consciousness, begins its gradual development.

Then he forms an attachment first for his mother and father, and subsequently for his kinsmen. Having drunk her breast milk many times, he does not cry when he sees his mother nursing; thus there arises between them a mutual bond.
In the Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī.
These five are also created for the embodied being while still in the womb:
lifespan, karma, wealth, knowledge, and death itself.
Furthermore, there are the stages of childhood, infancy, adolescence, and youth.
Beyond this, however, are the youth and the mature; then the very mature, the old, and beyond that the very old;
as well as the grey-haired and death—these are proclaimed to be the stages of life.
Thus ends the exposition of the eleven stages.
Even immediately after death, one is reborn in that very same place.
Thereupon, by virtue of his own karma, he goes to hell or to heaven;
through the actions of his birth, he is born as a god, a human, an animal, a bird, a worm, or even as an immobile being.
Likewise: "A living being is born through karma and perishes through karma alone;
when the body has perished, that karma leads him to obtain another body."

Just as a calf finds its mother among a thousand cows, so do good and evil deeds follow their doer. This is stated to dispel the doubt: "How can there be the experience of a deed in the hereafter, given that the deed perishes so quickly?"
This has been stated with an illustration in the Kulārṇava, in the first chapter of the fifth section.
(75) Whatever action is performed here, its fruit is experienced there in the next world; just as the fruit of a tree whose roots have been watered is seen upon its branches.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Human Birth," in the first section of the *Śrī-Prāṇatopiṇī*.
Now, the *Prapañcasāra* demonstrates the method of the origin of the castes (*varṇas*) in their proper sequence.
When that Kuṇḍalinī, due to the lack of clarity in the channel of the mouth and nostrils, utters indistinct syllables and speaks in an unclear manner,
then she vibrates within the Mūlādhāra and repeatedly encircles the Suṣumnā.
When that Kuṇḍalinī, due to the lack of evenness and impurity in the passage of the mouth and ears,
utters indistinct syllables— that is, an unclear sound— in which the syllables are unmanifest (the word "sound" being understood from the context),
meaning she produces such things as the speech of a young elephant, then she vibrates and resounds at the Mūlādhāra and within the Suṣumnā.
The grammatical construction is "it coils repeatedly.
The nature of Kuṇḍalī has been described in the Śāradātilaka.
Then she, whose nature is consciousness, all-pervading, and universal in form,
having approached the presence of Śiva, became the source of the manifestation of the qualities of eternal bliss.
The connection with the subsequent word is "she remains" (*tiṣṭhati*).
By the phrase "in the presence of Śiva," it follows that she is denoted by the term *śakti*; therefore, the qualifiers are used in the feminine gender.
Although there is non-difference between Śiva and Śakti due to their being one essence, nevertheless, having accepted a conceptual distinction, [the text proceeds].
It has been stated that [this occurs] in the presence of Śiva.
This has been stated by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta:
And Śakti desires identity with the possessor of power (Śaktimat) in the form of manifestation;

there is a constant identity between these two, like that between fire and its burning power. She in whom the qualities (guṇas) arise is "Guṇodayā," and she is eternal bliss (nityānandā). Thus, she is both Nityānandā and Guṇodayā.
Unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, all-pervading, encompassing all objects, and auspicious—

this is considered the Supreme Power (Parā Śakti) through its division into the higher and the lower. Although there is a certain Supreme Power and a certain Lower Power, even through that division, this [Lower Power] is indeed the Supreme Power itself.
As it is said in the Bhagavad Gītā: "Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind,
intellect, and ego— thus is my nature (prakṛti) divided eightfold."
But know that this other nature of Mine is superior, O mighty-armed one! It is the individual soul (jīva), by which this entire world is sustained.
To Śāradā.
Dancing with ease within the lotus-heart of yogis.
The meaning is: directly, according to reality.
In the foundation, which is the root-center (mūlādhāra) of all beings— that is, of all living creatures— she flashes forth with the form of lightning.
The Goddess stands encompassing everything by way of the spiral of a conch shell (*śaṅkhāvarta*).
The meaning is that just as the spiral within a conch shell stands encompassing the conch itself, so too does she stand encompassing all of Śiva.
Having attained the splendor of the limbs of coiled serpents,
the Goddess is composed of all the Vedas, composed of all mantras, auspicious,
composed of all principles (tattvas), manifest, subtler than the subtle, and all-pervading.
The All-pervasive One (vibhu) is impossible to know by measure.
The Goddess, the mother of the three abodes, is the very nature of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman).
"The three abodes" refers to the forms of the moon, the sun, and fire.
She consists of forty-two syllables and has the form of fifty syllables.
The meaning is that "forty-two" refers to that which consists of the mantra of the earthly letters (bhūtalipi),
while "fifty" refers to that which consists of the Mātṛkās. Multiplied by the universal body— that Kuṇḍalinī, the supreme deity— once awakened by the Universal Self, she gives birth [to all things].
The world consists of mantra.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: when [the alphabet] is multiplied by all its limbs and all its phonemes and joined with one another, it gives birth to and reveals the world consisting of mantra.
In the *mūlādhāra*, a channel exists coiled like a serpent; because it resides in the center of that [region], it is called *kuṇḍalī*.
This energy (*śakti*) is multiplied into one [form] as the impeller of the entire universe.
By the inclusion of both terms "the entire" and "universe," it is indicated that she is the producer of both sound and meaning.
The seed-syllable of the Vedas, the seed-syllable of Śrī, the seed-syllable of Śakti, and that of Manobhava (Kāma).
Prāsāda, Tumburu, Piṇḍa, Cintāratna, Gaṇeśvara;
Mārtaṇḍabhairava, Daurga, Nārasiṃha, Varāhaja; Vāsudeva, Hayagrīva, Bīja, and Śrīpuruṣottama.
And at that time, she certainly produces other seeds as well,
when that consciousness becomes doubled in form:
the two supreme selves of identical color, namely sound and meaning, or day and night.
Then this supreme goddess creates both Prakṛti and Puruṣa;
whatever else exists in this world, each of those was born from her.
With all her limbs composed of the three guṇas, she is the embodiment of consciousness, the consort of Śiva.
He brought forth the Traipura mantra, the Śaktivināyaka mantra,
the three-syllabled mantra beginning with *pāśa*, the Traipuṭa, the Caṇḍanāyaka,
the Saura, the Mṛtyuñjaya, the Śakti, the Śāmbhava, and the Vinatāsuta.
Vāgīśī is the three-syllable mantra; she is Nīlakaṇṭha, the remover of poison.
She is the mantra tripled by the Goddess, the three worlds, and the three qualities (*guṇas*).
She is the three abodes of the Vedas, the triad, and the auspicious three phonemes.
The Goddess [bestows] Tripuṣkara, the vowels, and the triad of triads beginning with Brahmā.

"Tripuṣkara" refers to the three sacred fords (tīrtha) according to their status as superior, middling, and inferior. "Svarān" refers to the acute (udātta), grave (anudātta), and circumflex (samāhāra) accents.
The three times of Fire, the triad of Śakti, the great triple mode of existence,
the three channels, the threefold aims of life— whatever else is considered to be threefold, that she is.
Also in the second chapter of the Prapañcasāra:
One should multiply by two, four, five, six, seven, eight, ten,
and likewise by twelve and fifty, in sequence.
Whenever one multiplies by three, then the All-pervasive Lord (Vibhu) is in a state of tripled manifestation.
The power (śakti), whose nature is the resonance of the fire of time (kālāgni-nāda), is perceived as having a hidden form;
then those of great learning call that "the Savior" (tāra) and the "nature of space" (vyomātman).
Others speak of that very same power as "Hara" and as the "Self" (ātman).
She is the three qualities (guṇas), she is the three humors (doṣas), she is the three colors, she is the triple Veda, and she is that [triple world];

she is the three worlds, she is the triple form (trimūrti), she is the three lines—she is distinguished as such. Because she delivers these, she is the Savior (Tāra); she is Śakti because her power is held by Him.
When she, who moves through the stations beginning with the Subtle (sūkṣma), is multiplied fourfold,
she then becomes the vocal [power] of the states beginning with waking and of the instruments.
When she is multiplied fivefold, she is divided into five groups of five.
And likewise of the five syllables, of the phonemes, and of the vital airs— namely,
the vital airs such as prāṇa and the rest.
When that [line] is multiplied sixfold, it pierces Koṣoma and Ira;
then, it pierces the one called Ṣaḍguṇita and the Moon. When it is multiplied sevenfold, it likewise [pierces] Tāra and Hṛllekhā.
It exists separately through seven divisions beginning with *a* and ending with *śānta*.
The letter *a*, the letter *u*, the letter *m*, as well as the *bindu*,
the *nāda*, the *śakti*, and the *śānti*— these are proclaimed as the divisions of the *Tāra*.
The letter *ha*, the letter *ra*, the vowel *mā* (the long *ā*), as well as the *bindu* and the *nāda*,
and likewise *śakti* and *śānti*— these are declared to be the divisions of *śakti*.
From these seven limbs of hers, the universe is divided into sevenfold.

When that [number] is multiplied eightfold by means of the world-systems, mountains, continents, netherworlds, oceans, planets, lords of sages, the elements and so forth, as well as other such categories distinguished by the number seven, it then becomes differentiated into its constituent natures (*prakṛti*).
When the channel (*nāḍī*), multiplied tenfold, pierces the vital points (*marmans*) and the directions and so forth—
even when increased by twelve and so on— it is then conjoined with the form of the Sun of the zodiacal sign (*rāśyarka*);
it expresses the mantra known as the "twelve-syllabled" as well as the vowels.
Then that mantra, numbering as many [syllables] as she, consists of her powers multiplied by those qualities;
when she, the Goddess, becomes multiplied fiftyfold, differentiated into fifty phonemes,
and further multiplied by her fifty constituent parts, she then possesses a divine state established within her own self.
The meaning is that, through contact with the sound arising from the cavity of the path of Suṣumṇā, that Power impels the fifty letters one by one in succession;
that is, through contact with the resonance emerging from the aperture of the Suṣumnā path, she impels the fifty letters.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
Multiplied by fourfold qualities, the Śāmbhavī bestows bliss;
at that time, she forms the four syllables of the Moon-lotus (the Sun).
She forms the fourfold group of Gaṇeśas and the fourfold group beginning with the Self (Ātman).
The Ojā-pīṭha, the worship and so forth, the fourfold group beginning with Dharma,
the elephants starting from the petals, O Goddess, and whatever other tetrad there may be—
the Consort of Śambhu, who bestows all goals, is fivefold multiplied [in these].
Tripurā is the five-peaked [mantra]; her two sets of five syllables constitute the Five Jewels (*pañcaratna*) of the Great Goddess, which bestow the fruits of all desires.
The five-syllabled [mantra] belongs to Maheśa, and the five-colored [mantra] belongs to Garuḍa.
The five arrows that cause delusion, the five objects of desire, the five celestial trees, the five vital winds beginning with prāṇa, the five colors of the Great Lord (Maheśvara),
the five forms, the five kalās, and the five Brahmans— the Ṛgvedic verses— [are] in sequence.
This supreme Śakti, whose form consists of the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas, creates;
multiplied sixfold, that Goddess bears the six-syllabled mantra—
the six-peaked Tripurā-mantra and the six-syllabled Gāṇapatya-mantra.
The six-syllabled mantra of the Moon (Śiva), the six-syllabled Nṛsiṃha-mantra,

the six seasons beginning with spring, the six presiding lords of qualities such as fragrance (Āmoda), the six treasuries consisting of the essence of the waves, the six powers beginning with Ḍākinī, and the six paths (adhvan).
The Yantra, multiplied sixfold by Śakti, gave birth to the six supports (ādhāras).
Whatever is sixfold in this world, all that belongs to the Supreme Goddess.
Multiplied sevenfold, the Eternal One (Nityā) possesses a body half of which is Śaṅkara.
The seven-syllabled mantra of Tripurā, the seven-syllabled Vināyaka, the group of seven *vyāhṛtis*,
and that seven-syllabled Sudarśana;
[these correspond to] the worlds, the mountains, the gods, the bodily constituents (*dhātus*), the sages, the seven planets, and the elephants.
The fuel-sticks are reckoned as seven, and the tongues that consume the oblation are seven;
whatever else is of sevenfold nature, all that was born from her. The Power multiplied eightfold is the two eight-syllabled [mantras] of Śiva.
The eight-syllable mantra of Hari, the supreme two-syllable mantra of Śakti, the eight-syllable mantra of Bhānu, the eight-syllable mantra of Durgā, the eight-syllable mantra of the Supreme Self,
and the eight-syllable mantra of Nīlakaṇṭha which has Vāsudeva as its essence.
The divine Kāmārgala Yantra, the Devīyantra, and the Ghaṭārgala; the auspicious eightfold perfumes that reach the hearts of the goddesses and gods;
[and] Brāhmī and the others, all the Bhairavas, the Mūrtis, the Āśās, and the Vasus.

The great goddess has eight seats (pīṭhas) accompanied by the eight groups of eight; she is the primordial nature (prakṛti), and [one should worship] in sequence the [eight] obstacles beginning with Vighna and Vakratuṇḍa,
the qualities beginning with aṇimā, the nāgas, and the forms of fire beginning with Yama.
Then she expands everything else in the world, which consists of eight aspects;
the eternal one, multiplied ninefold, then gives birth to the mantra composed of that.
Maheśvarī, whose nature is the *tattva*, is the group of nine consisting of the *śakti-tattvas*.
There is a group of nine for the seat-energies (pīṭhaśaktis), the nine aesthetic sentiments beginning with the erotic (śṛṅgāra),
the nine gems beginning with ruby (māṇikya), and the nine groups [of letters].
There is a group of nine for the life-breath messengers (prāṇadūtīs), and the auspicious mandala of nine.

Whatever ninefold nature exists in the world, all of that rises up within her; she is the tenfold transformation of Śambhu, the future destroyer of the suffering of existence. The ten-syllable mantra of Gaṇapati and the ten-syllable mantra of Tvaritā [are contained herein].
Tripurā is the ten-peak mantra; that is the ten-syllable mantra of Tripurā.
The ten-syllable mantra belongs to Sarasvatī; that is the ten-syllable mantra of Yakṣiṇī.
The mantra consisting of Vāsudeva is the ten-syllable mantra of Aśvārūḍhā.
By name, she is the mantra of Padmāvatī, the mantra of Vāyu, and the ten-syllabled [mantra];
she is Maheśvarī, whose form is the essence of the ten principles (tattvas).
She is the group of ten women and, in due order, the ten incarnations of Viṣṇu.
Whatever tenfold group of world-protectors or whatever else he creates,
that [group] is elevenfold when multiplied by consciousness;
it consists of the world and is the eleven-syllabled mantra of the primordial power, known as the Rudraikādaśinī.
The omniscient Goddess Vāṇī utters the eleven Rudras in sequence from the eleven-spoked [wheel],
and when multiplied, she utters twelve in sequence;
likewise, Maheśā and the others utter the Nityā-mantra and the mantra whose essence is Vāsudeva.
The zodiac signs, the suns, the forms of Hari, and the twelvefold yantra—
all that is similar to these was produced within her.
In the *Padārthādarśa* cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
[the syllables] multiplied thirteen times constitute the Vāgīśvarī-Aśvārūḍhā mantra, the Viśvedevas, and so forth;
multiplied fourteen times, they constitute the Vāsudeva-Gopāla mantra, the worlds (*bhuvana*), and so forth.
The *nityā* of the Trident-bearer, multiplied fifteenfold, consists of the mantra, lunar days (*tithi*), and so forth;
multiplied sixteenfold, it consists of the *cakra*, mantra, vowels (*svara*), *kalā*, and so forth.
Regarding "vowels" (*svara*): this refers to those beginning with *a* and ending with the *visarga*.
Multiplied seventeen times, it consists of the *laghu-pañcamī*, the *tārā-vidyā-mantra*, and so forth; nineteen times, the *kṛṣṇa-dharā-mantra* and so forth;
and multiplied twenty times, the *ratna-dhāra-māmaheśvara-mantra* and so forth.
Multiplied twenty-one times, it produces the numerous names, mantras, yantras, and so forth;
multiplied twenty-two times, it produces the mantras of Kṛṣṇānnādhipati, Sumukhī, and others;
and multiplied twenty-three times, it gives birth to the Laghuśyāmā, the Puruṣottama-hṛdayaṅgama-mantra, and others.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
Then the Gāyatrī of Savitṛ becomes beautiful, consisting of twenty-four principles; the Gāyatrī of Śambhu is of the nature of sound;
the Gāyatrī of Viṣṇu is the Gāyatrī; and the Gāyatrī of Tripurātman is likewise.
The Gāyatrī belongs to Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and the Gāyatrī is the consort of Śambhu.
Within that Supreme Self, the twenty-four principles (tattvas) were present;
even there, it should be understood that there is something else.
The omnipresent one, consisting of all mantras and multiplied by thirty-two varieties,
gives birth to the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra, the great Nārasiṃha mantra,
and the great mantra of the high-souled Varuṇa beginning with *lavaṇa*.
She [recited] the Hayagrīva mantra, the Durga mantra, the Varaha mantra, and the Vahninayaka mantra; the great mantra of the Lord of Ganas, the mantra of the Commander of the Army,
the mantra of Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and the garland mantra of Manobhū (the God of Love).
The *triṣṭubh* [verse] of Vanavāsinī, the great mantra named Aghora,
the mantra of the Son of Devakī, the mantra of Śrī Puruṣottama,
the Śrī Gopāla mantra, the Bhūrmā mantra, and the Tārā mantra— in this sequence.
She gave birth to the great mantra of Mahālakṣmī, the mantra of Bhūteśvara,
the mantra consisting of Kṣetrapāla, and the mantra that wards off calamities;
she also gave birth to the Mātaṅginī-vidyā, the Siddhi-vidyā of auspicious origin.
Multiplied by this sequential yoga,
she who is beloved of Śiva arranges the thirty-six Śaiva principles;
she also gives birth to other auspicious mantras and yantras.

In this context, what has been stated— that she "gave birth" (*ajījanat*) and so forth— is intended either in the sense of being a manifestor (*prakāśakatva*) or in the sense of dependent origination (*pratīti*).
Otherwise, what was previously stated, namely that she "consists of all the Vedas" (*sarvavedamayī*), and so on, would be untenable.

Since all [phonemes] consist of the limbs of Kuṇḍalinī in the form of Mātṛkā, their birth and so forth are contradictory; this should be discerned with great skill by the wise through mental reflection.
The teachers state the sequence of the origin of the syllables in the Śāradā:
The Mistress of the Universe, multiplied at her root by forty-two, gives birth to Kuṇḍalinī, the all-pervasive one who consists of the Śabdabrahman.
From that comes Śakti; from that, Dhvani; from that, Nāda; and from that, Nibodhikā.
From that arose the half-moon, from that the point (bindu), and from that emerged Parā.
The grammatical connection is as follows: at the root, in the *mūlādhāra*, the *viśvanāyikā* Kuṇḍalinī, multiplied by forty-two,
gives birth in this sequence to the garland of phonemes consisting of the *bhūtalipi* mantra composed of forty-two elements, beginning with the letter *a* and ending with the letter *sa*.
He states the sequence with the words "the power" (*śaktim*).
The construction is as follows: that Kuṇḍalinī gives birth to power (*śakti*); from that power, sound (*dhvani*) arose;
and from that sound, and so forth, should be understood.

And this sequence [is as follows]: in the production of all phonemes (*akṣara*), that very [power], having entered into *sattva* and being permeated by *rajas*, is the state of the phoneme (*akṣara*) denoted by the term "sound" (*dhvani*); that same [power], when permeated by *tamas*, is the unmanifest state denoted by the term "resonance" (*nāda*);
and that same [power], due to the predominance of *tamas*, is denoted by the term "intellect" (*nibodhikā*). It is that very [power].
Because of the abundance of the fear of reality, she is denoted by the term "half-moon" (ardhendu). As it is said in the *Padārthādarśa*:

"Proclaimed by the power of the will-force (*icchā-śakti*) and illuminating the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), that power, which is the Lord, takes the form of the individual soul (*puṃrūpiṇī*) and, called the power of action (*kriyā-khyā*), creates."
That very same *bindu*, having moved to another location, becomes known as Parā and the others;
[these are] Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī, which is the birthplace of sound.
Among these, Parā is at the root (mūlādhāra), Paśyantī is in the Svādhiṣṭhāna, Madhyamā is in the heart, and Vaikharī is in the mouth.
As it has been said in the *Padārthādarśa*:
The subtle Kuṇḍalinī, whose nature consists solely of light, resides in the center;
because it is beyond the range of the ears, she rises upward from there.
Self-luminous and perceiving, she takes refuge in the Suṣumṇā.

That very [power], having reached the heart-lotus, becomes the central channel (madhyamā) in the form of sound (*nāda*). Thenceforth, it consists of mere internal discourse (*sañjalpa*), moving upwards without division.
That same [power] resides in the chest, throat, and palate, and is situated in the head, nose, and mouth.
Vaikharī speech is produced by the movement of the tongue, the root of the tongue, and the lips; it encompasses all phonemes,
generates the manifold expansion of sound, is perceived by the ear,
and consists of the nature of will, knowledge, and action, being of the form of light and composed of the qualities (guṇas).
In this sequence, Kuṇḍalinī emits the garland of phonemes,
consisting of forty-two units from the letter *a* to the letter *sa*.
Multiplied by the fifty gateways, she [emits] the garland of fifty phonemes.
The *kalās* (energies), differentiated according to their respective colors, sequentially give birth to the Rudras and the others.
The *kalās* and the Rudras have been previously mentioned. By the word "and others" (*ādi*), the fifty *kāmās*, the *kāma-śaktis*, the Gaṇeśas, their *śaktis*, and the Kṣetrapālas are also included.
The names of the Kāmas as held by Rāghavabhaṭṭa are as follows:
He who grants desires at will, the beautiful one, the radiant one, the enjoyer of desires;
he who moves at will, the desirous one, the lover, the increaser of desire;
Rāma, the delightful one, the charmer, the lord of delight, and the beloved of Rati.
Lord of the night, beloved of Ramā, sporting one, wanderer of the night;
Nandaka, Nandana, Nandin, and furthermore, the delighter of others;
wielder of the five arrows, friend of Rati, flower-bowed one, possessor of the great bow.
Bhrāmaṇa, Bhramaṇa, Bhramamāṇa, and another, Bhrama;
Bhrānta, Bhrāmaka, Bhṛṅgī, Bhrāntācāra, and Bhramāvaha; Mohana, Mohaka, Moha, and indeed Mohavardhana.
Madanī, Manmatha, Mātaṅgī, Bhṛṅganāyaka,
Gāyanī, Gītija, Nartaka, Khelaka,
Unmatta, Mattaka, Vilāsa, and Lobhavardhana.
He has the luster of a pomegranate flower and is joined by Śakti on his left side.
All the fifty Kāmas are described as gentle, wearing red garments, and bearing flowers, arrows, dice, and bows; they are adorned with all ornaments.
And the names of those powers are also mentioned in that very same place.
Rati, Prīti, Kāminī, Mohinī, Kamalapriyā, Vilāsinī, Kalpalatā, Śyāmalā,
Śucismitā, Vismitākṣī, Viśālākṣī, Lelihānā, and Digambarī.
Vāmā, Kubjādharā, Nityā, Kalyāṇī, Mohinī, Madanā— the best of goddesses— Lāpinī, Mardinī, Kalahapriyā, as well as Kākṣī, Sumukhī, and thereafter Nalinī.
Jayinī, Pālinī, Śivā, Mugdhā, Savibhramā,
Cārunetrā, Sulolā, Dīrghajihvā, Ratipriyā, Lolākṣī, Śṛṅgiṇī, Pāvanā, and likewise Mādanā.
Mālā, Haṃsinī, Viśvatomukhī, Nandinī,
as well as Ramaṇī, Kānti, Kalakaṇṭhī,
Vṛkodarī, Meghaśyāmā, and Ruṣonmattā— these are declared to be the fifteen [Mothers].
The Śaktis, resembling saffron in hue and adorned with all ornaments,
holding blue lotuses in their hands, should be meditated upon as capable of attracting the three worlds.
Therein are fifty Gaṇeśas and their Śaktis:
Vighneśa, Vighnarāja, Vināyaka, Śivottama,
Vighnahṛt, Vighnakartṛ, Gaṇa, Ekadanta, Dvidanta, and Sudantaka.
Gajavaktra, Nirañjana, Kapardin, Dīrghajihvaka, Śaṅkukarṇa, Vṛṣabhadhvaja, Gaṇanāyaka, Gajendra,
Sūryakarṇa, and he who is known as Trilocana.
Lambodara and Mahānanda, Caturmūrti and Sadāśiva; Amogha and Durmukha, as well as Sumukha and Pramodaka;
Ekapāda and Dvijihva, and Sūravīra, Śiva, and Āmukha.
The Bestower of Boons, Vāmadeva, Vakratuṇḍa, Dviraṇḍaka;
the Leader of the Army, the Village Chief, the Intoxicated, the Sober, and he whose vehicle is the Intoxicated;
the one with matted hair, the Shaven-headed, the Sword-bearer, the Most Excellent, and the Bull-bannered.
Bhakṣyapriya, Gaṇeśa, and he known as Meghanāyaka;
Vyāpin and Gaṇeśvara—these are declared to be the fifty leaders of the Gaṇas.
Resembling the young morning sun, they have elephant faces and three eyes.
Holding a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in their hands, they are endowed with power.
Hrī, Śrī, Puṣṭi, Śānti, Kṣānti, Sarasvatī,
Svāhā, Medhā, Kāntikāmīnī, Mohinī, Naṭī, Pārvatī, Jvalinī, Nandā, Suyaśas, and Kāmarūpiṇī.
Ugratejovatī, Satyā, Vighneśānī, and Surūpiṇī.
Kāmadā, Madajihvā, Bhūti, and Bhautikā are white;
Ramā is said to be the consort (mahiṣī), as are Bhañjinī and Vikarṇayā.
Bhrūkuṭi, Lajjā, Dīrghaghoṇā, and Dhanurdharā are likewise [white].
She is known as Yāminī, Rātri-saṃjñā, Kāmāndhā, and Śaśiprabhā;
she is Lolākṣī, Cañcalā, Dīpti, Śubhagā, Durbhagā, and Śivā;
she is considered to be Garbhā, Bhaginī, Bhoginī, and Subhagā.
Kālarātri and Kālikā are remembered as the fifty Śaktis;
they are radiant with all ornaments, seated upon the laps of their beloveds, and exceedingly beautiful.
With red lotuses in their hands, they should be meditated upon as wearing red garlands and garments, and glowing with a crimson hue.
Thus, there are forty-nine Śaktis of Gaṇeśa;
and there are forty-nine Kṣetrapālas, as stated in the section on Kṣetrapālas in the *Prayogasāra*.
Forty-nine divisions of Kṣetrapāla have been proclaimed;
they are differentiated by the various seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the Mātṛkā and by differences in name.
First is Ajara, then Apakumbha, and after that Indrastuti.
Iḍācāra, Ukta-saṃjña, Uṣmāda, Ṛṣisūdana, Samukta, Luptakeśa, Kṣepaka, Ekadaṃṣṭraka, Airāvata, Oghabandhu, and likewise Rogādhīśa.
Añjana, Astravāra, Kavala, Kharukhānala,
Cāmukhya, Ghaṇṭādoṅmanas, Caṇḍavāraṇa,
Chaṭāṭopa, Jaṭālākhya, Ṛddhīvas, Jaḍa, and Cara.
Ṭaṅkapāṇi, as well as another, Aṣṭhānabandhu, and Ḍāmara; Ḍhakvāvāra, Ūṇavāṇa, Taḍiddeha, and Sthira;
Dantura, Dhanada, and also Anattiktānta and Pracaṇḍaka.
Phaṭkāra, Vīrasaṅgha, Śṛṅga, Meghabhāmura,
Yugānta, Cauhyava, Lambauṣṭhī, Vasu, Śukananda, the one named Ṣaḍāla, Śunānāha, and Vṛka.
These divisions have been fully described as having their source in the syllables of the *mātṛkā*.
The purpose for explaining the *kṣetrapālas* has been stated in that very same place.
Whichever letter among the letters of the name-mantra is seen first within the *mātṛkā*, there in that very place resides this Kṣetrapālaka;
there, as a distinguished self, he is established through these various divisions.
Therefore, the Kṣetrapāla, who is superior in every respect, must be worshipped.
If anyone performs any ritual action anywhere without having first worshipped the Kṣetrapāla, the Kṣetrapāla destroys the fruit of that action; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the account of the forty-nine Kṣetrapālas;
[the author] now begins to describe the creation of Vaikharī speech.
In the second chapter of the Śāradā [Tantra].
Next, I shall explain the manifestation of the letters in the mouths of men:
impelled by the vital air and constantly emerging from the cavity of the *suṣumnā*,
those letters appear in succession through the organs of articulation, such as the throat and so forth.
The syntactical connection is as follows: "I shall explain the manifestation of color in the mouths of men and the cause for the illumination of color.
Now, [one might object]:
"In a cage, there are parrots, pigeons, and other birds born of the avian species."

"Through association with the virtuous, they take up my auspicious and great name"—since this statement from the first chapter of the *Rudrayāmala-uttarakhaṇḍa* shows that even birds are seen to utter syllables, and because it is clearly understood from the *Mahābhārata* and other texts through such accounts as the dialogue between the swan and the crow (*haṃsakākīya-upākhyāna*). (p. 85)

If it is asked, "Since the recitation by birds is established through direct perception, why was it said 'of men' (*nṛṇām*)?", the answer is: True; however, it was said "of men" either because this is the general rule (*prāyikatvena*) or because it is obtained through the force of the context (*prakaraṇabalāt*), and not for the purpose of excluding birds and the like.
Alternatively, since the plural designation "of men" (*nṛṇām*) indicates a group of beings capable of articulating phonemes (*varṇa*), there is no fault whatsoever.
He states the manner in which the manifestation of color occurs, beginning with the words "impelled" (prerita), and so forth.
Impelled by the *maruts*, they reach the station of *paśyantī* and are made ready for emergence;
having exited through the aperture of the *suṣumnā*, they gradually manifest through the organs of speech, such as the throat—this is the connection.

Because there is no simultaneous utterance, it is said "gradually" (*kramāt*), as stated by Bhartṛhari: [The relevant verse from Bhartṛhari's *Vākyapadīya*: "First, the word-sound, being unmanifest, exists in the heart; then it becomes manifest in the throat, and finally it reaches the lips. (VP 1.78)
The self, having ascertained the objects through the intellect, joins them with the mind through the desire to speak;
the mind strikes the fire of the body, which impels the vital air;
the vital air, moving within the chest, produces the deep-toned sound.
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "throat etcetera," the palate and so forth are intended.
And so it is stated in the Śikṣāsūtra:
The eight places of articulation for the phonemes are the chest,
the throat, the head, as well as the root of the tongue, the teeth, the nose, the lips, and the palate.
According to the statement that will be cited later— "One should practice the pronunciation of the fifty mātṛkā-phonemes under a teacher"— this applies to human beings.
Even in the pronunciation of phonemes, association with a guru and virtuous persons must be understood as the causal factor, just as it is for birds.
Previously, the nature of the phonemes as being composed of the moon, sun, and fire was stated in general;
now, that is specified in the *Śāradā*.
Among these, the vowels are remembered as lunar (saumya), the consonants (sparśa) as solar (saura) and auspicious in their arising;
all the semi-vowels (vyāpaka) are fiery (āgneya), being the very forms of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire.
In these castes.
The vowels are renowned as sixteen, and the consonants (sparśas) are twenty-five;
the consonants are considered to be the essence of the principles (tattvas), because the letter *ma* is the Puruṣa.
Since the letter *ma* is the Puruṣa, the Supreme Self, whose nature is the Sun, therefore [it is so].
The meaning is that [the letters] beginning with *ka* and ending with *bha* have the nature of the *tattvas*, consisting of the twenty-four *tattvas* starting from *prakṛti*.
For this very reason, since the letter *a* is associated with Viṣṇu in all seed-syllables (*bījas*), it should be understood that they possess identity with the *puruṣa*.
This is well-supported by what will be stated later: "Because the letter *ma* is of the nature of the *bindu*, the *bindu* is said to be the Sun among males."
Because they are touched by the letter *ma*, which is the nature of the solar drop (*bindu*), these letters beginning with *ka* are called "contact consonants" (*sparśa*).
These ten are all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*) and bestow desire, wealth, and merit. They are pervasive because they reside within the objects that are corrupted by defects.
In this regard, they may also be called "belonging to Agni" (āgneya) because the fires (agnis) also exist therein;
or alternatively, they should be understood as "belonging to Agni" because the fire known as Nṛsiṃha-kālāgni ends with the letter *kṣa*.
Those letters, in their respective order, are: the vowels (*svaras*), which bestow desires; the consonants (*sparśas*), which bestow wealth; and the semi-vowels (*vyāpakas*).
The meaning is "bestowers of Dharma.
The manner of the origin of the *haṃsa* from the *praṇava* has been shown; now, in the third chapter of the *Prapañcasāra*, he describes the manner of the origin of all syllables from the *haṃsa*.
I shall explain in truth, according to their actual nature, the manner in which these fifty syllables become various manifestations within another body,
as they are impelled by the vital breath and emerge through the aperture of the Suṣumnā.
Striking against the points of articulation such as the throat and others, they attain manifestation in the mouth;
the upward-moving breath produces the udātta accent.
When [the breath] moves downward, it is the *anudātta* (unaccented); when it moves obliquely, it is the *svarita* (circumflex);
the combination [of these two] is the *samāhāra-svarita*.
The phonemes (lipi) are designated respectively as having one, two, three, or four morae (mātrā);
they are known as having the names "consonant," "short," "long," and "protracted.
Through the combination of the letters *a* and *e*, the phoneme *ai* is recognized.
By the conjunction of the vowel *ā* with that very [consonant], there arises the syllable *ai*;
likewise, by the conjunction of the vowel *u* with that very same [consonant], there arises the vowel called *o*. [This applies] to that vowel *ā*.
Through the conjunction with that very *au* sound, there arises the vowel called *au*.
There are four diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*) which are mantras that accomplish all aims.
The manifestation of the phonemes *ḷ* and *ḹ* is indeed not clearly demonstrated.
One should speak of *ajāpā* as the manifestation of the *bindu* (the point) and *sarga* (emission), and of the mind (*manas*).
Emission (*sarga*) issues forth from the throat; it is generally of the nature of the self (*ātman*), while that which follows it is perishable.
That emission alone is indeed *ucchvāsa* (exhalation), whereas *haḥ* is the *prāṇaka* (the vital breath).
Creation (*sarga*) is indeed emission (*visarga*), which is perishable and modified.
The connection is as follows: *ucchvāsa* is the air characterized by inward movement; thus it takes the form of the letter *u*.
Similarly, *praṇaka* (the vital breath) is the air characterized by outward movement, which would be the letter *ha*; that very [outward breath] is *ucchvāsa*, and thus *socchvāsa*.
