However, it is not called "visargagīti" because of the explicit negation by the word *nañ*. Alternatively, it is "sa-ucchāsa," meaning "with exhalation. Or, it is "prāṇaka," meaning "the vital breath which is the wind (*kāya-vāyu*)."
That creation is conjoined with the throat; one should impel the letters beginning with *ka* by means of the vital air (*vāyu*).
By the mere touch of the *varga* (consonant groups), *ka* arises; by the touch of the vowels (*svara*), however, *kha* arises.
From a slight and deep contact, *pa*, *gha*, and *ṅa* emerge externally.

The visarga, the palatals (śa-varga), and likewise the letter *ya* are produced at the palate (*tāluga*). The retroflexes (*ṛ*, *ṭu*-varga), the letter *ra*, and the letter *ṣa* are produced at the head (*mūrddhaga*). Likewise, the dentals (*la*-varga), the letter *la*, and the letter *sa* are produced at the teeth (*dantaga*). Those designated as *anuṣvadha* and *anusvāra* are produced at the lips (*oṣṭhya*).
With the teeth and lips, one should utter those respective syllables located in their corresponding positions.
Therefore, it is said in the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*:
The vowels, the *avarga* consonants (*ka*–*ca*), and the visarga are gutturals.
The vowels *i*, *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, *ḹ*, the *ca*-group consonants (*ca*, *cha*, *ja*, *jha*, *ña*), and *ya* and *śa* are palatals (*tālavya*).
The letters ṛ, ṭ, ṭh, ṛ, and ṣ are retroflex (mūrdhanya).
The phonemes *ḷ*, the *tavarga* (the dental stops), and *la-sa* are dentals.
The labials are the letter *u*, the labio-dental group (*pavarga*), and the *upadhmānīya*.
The [consonant] *v* is dental-labial.
Now, the gutturals and palatals.

In the tenth chapter of the Varadā-tantra.
The illustrious Śiva said:
O Śivā! O Maheśānī! Out of affection for you, I shall today declare that secret method for the pronunciation of syllables which is found in all tantras:
one should practice the pronunciation of the fifty mātṛkā letters under a guru.
The eight classes [of consonants] are proclaimed as *a*, *ku*, *cu*, *ṭu*, *tu*, *pu*, *yu*, and *śu*.
The vowel *u* is for the purpose of distinguishing the five groups of five letters each.
It should be known that *a*, *ka*, and *ha* originate from the throat (*kaṇṭha*), while *ca*, *ya*, and *śa* are remembered as originating from the palate (*tālu*).
The letters ṛ, ṛ, u, and ū are considered cerebrals (mūrdhanya); the letters ḷ, t, l, and s are considered dentals (dantya).
The places of articulation for the labials have been described to you.
Today I shall explain the specific details: the vowels are pronounced from the throat;
the two *ṛ*s are produced by the tongue and the palate; the two *ḷ*s are produced by the tongue and the teeth.
The consonants (hal) are to be spoken from the position of the mouth; the letter *kṣa* is produced by the impact of the throat.
When there is a conjunction of two consonants, the preceding vowel becomes long (*guru*).
In the junctions of the first letters at the end of a quarter-verse (*pāda*), there is the perception of both [sounds].
In a conjunction with the beginning of a word-final *apada*, the same is desired for *y* and *v* elsewhere;
however, the sound of *y* and *v* disappears and, like a vowel, attains the state of being heard.
O Parameśvarī! In the seed-syllable *triyā*, there is the sound of *ch* for the letter *ś*.
And when Jupiter and Venus are situated in the first house, there is likewise the attainment of learning.
In "sahasra" and so forth, as well as in "namas tasmai" and "āsthā" and so forth.
The status of being directly denotable (*samavācyatā*) belongs to the syllable *ha* when preceded by *ra* or followed by *ta*,
as in examples such as *varhah* and *nada*;
however, this is not clearly its denotability here, as it relies on a distinct class (*vaijātya*).
O Supreme Goddess! when [the letter] *va* is situated in the first position, one attains the fourth sound (*turyadhvani*). In the passage beginning with "external" (*bāhya*) and so forth:
"When *va* is situated in the first position, one especially attains the fourth sound."
In examples such as *āhvānam* (invocation),
even when [the suffix] begins with *l*, or when it begins with *n*, there is a difference in kind (*vaijātya*) and a very small denotation (*svalpavācyatā*),
as in *prahlādaḥ* and *ahnāya*.
In the case of *mā*, *di*, *sthe*, *me*, and *ca*, as well as for *ma* itself, the root of the nose is designated.
The letters *ṅa*, *ña*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *ma* are traditionally held to be born from the nasal root. The letter *ya* always assumes the third position of the *c*-group at the beginning of a word.
The same applies to armlets and other ornaments; elsewhere, however, it extends only to the neck.
In the groups ending with *ra* and *ya*, there is the substitution of *cha* for *śa* and *ṣa* when they reside in a *nāḍī*;
this occurs in [words such as] *praśna* and *snāna*. Among the subsequent letters, *ḍa* and *ḍha* are denoted by the "crooked tongue" (*vakra-jihvā*) and so forth.
Even though there is a difference in the types [of mantras] therein, one should practice that which belongs to the Guru alone.
The initial *repha* (the letter *r*) is declared to be other than the root *dṛś* (to see); those who are truthful should know this.
Having understood this, O Maheśānī! one should recite the hymn and mutter the mantra.

And the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), O Maheśānī! otherwise one shall not obtain the fruit. Wherever, O Parameśānī! one recites this hymn or the compendium (*saṃhitā*), there the wise man should proclaim the supreme mantra at its conclusion.
Thus ends the explanation of the manner of pronouncing the phonemes.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].

Among the vowels, those previously mentioned are short, while the subsequent ones are long; these two groups, in their respective order, consist of Śiva and Śakti, ending with the Bindu and the Sarga (Visarga).
The Bindu is declared to be the Sun, the Puruṣa, and the Sarga is the Moon, the Śakti.
Although the *ekāra* and *okāra* are long vowels, they possess technical shortness (*hrasvatva*) in this context.
These short and long vowels are, respectively, composed of Śiva and Śakti; the short vowels *a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ, e, o, aṃ* are composed of Śiva and are of masculine form—this is the meaning.
Ā, ī, ū, ṝ, ḹ, ai, au, and aḥ—these are the long vowels; they consist of Śakti and have feminine forms.

The *bindu* and *visarga* are of the nature of Puruṣa and Prakṛti respectively; with the intention of expressing that these two are distinct, the grammatical connection is that "they [the vowels] should end with the *bindu* and *sarga*."

The short vowels are joined with the *bindu* at the end, and the long vowels are joined with the *visarga* at the end; the meaning is that among the short vowels, the *bindu* is the eighth, and among the long vowels, the *visarga* is the eighth.
Since the *visarga* is said to be the "moon" (*niśākara*), the other vowels consist of its digits (*kalā*) and are of the nature of the lunar days (*tithi*).
For this very reason, it is said that the vowels are gentle (*saumya*).
That quartet which stands in the midst of the vowels is neuter;
for without the vowels, the manifestation of the others does not occur directly.
Therefore, the wise declare that the phonemes consist of Śiva and Śakti.

This is the intended meaning: it was previously stated that the vowels consist of Śakti because it is impossible to pronounce consonants without a vowel; thus, when they are pronounced together with a vowel, they consist of both Śiva and Śakti.
In the *Śāradā*:
"Since the Mātṛkā has arisen from the cause of the five elements,
therefore the phonemes consist of the elements, divided into groups of five."

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: since the *mātṛkās* have arisen from the cause that is the *bindu*, which itself arises from the union of Śiva and Śakti, for that reason the phonemes (*varṇas*), through their division into five groups of five, are to be known as being composed of the five elements.
The term *mātṛkā* is the designation for the collection of phonemes beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*.
He clarifies what was indicated:
"The letters of the fifty [phonemes] correspond respectively to air, fire, earth, water, and space.
Five are short, five are long, ending with the bindu, and they arise from the junctions."
The consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *la-sa-ha* are declared to consist of five parts each.
The mention of them in reverse order— beginning with wind (*vāyu*) and ending with space (*ākāśa*)— is intended to highlight the primacy of the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*).
Everything else is easy to understand.

If it is asked, "Why is the *visarga* not counted here?", it is said in reply: because, impelled by the vital breath (*prāṇapavana*) produced from the desire to speak arising at the *mūlādhāra*, it issues forth from the throat itself without reaching another location.
In this context, the creation consisting of primordial nature (prakṛti) among the elements is not counted.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sequence of the Origin of the Letters," in the first section of the *Śrīprāṇatoṣiṇī*.
Thus, when the castes (varṇas) had appeared—consisting of sounds—confusion could sometimes arise among men; therefore, their form was fashioned by the Lord as inscribed upon leaves.
This was stated by Bṛhaspati in the Jyotiṣatattva:
"Since even after six months a confusion arises [regarding the meaning],
because the letters were created by the Creator and placed upon leaves in the past"— thus,
the method of writing them is described in the first chapter of the *Varṇoddhāra-tantra*, following the question of the Goddess, by Śiva.
He said:
"In the tantra known as the *Varṇoddhāra*, however, I shall speak; listen to me:
'The fifty Mātṛkās are eternal, the direct embodiment of Brahman.
Having begun thus, he himself demonstrated the method for writing all the letters, which method will be shown hereafter."

In the Kāmadhenu Tantra.
O lady of tremulous glances! The letter *ṭha* is Kuṇḍalinī, whose form is liberation;

it has the appearance of a streak of yellow lightning, is always endowed with the three qualities (*triguṇa*), consists of the essence of the five deities, and is eternally accompanied by the three powers (*triśakti*).
In the Varṇoddhāra Tantra.

O Dear One! The deities presiding over the lines, which have the shape of a *vārttāku* flower or a circle, remain eternally in succession as the Moon, Sun, and Fire. O Supreme Goddess! The letter *Ṭha*, which has an upward-pointing crest and is devoid of a vowel-mora (*mātrā*), is [the form]. *Ṭha*.
In the Varṇodhāra Tantra.
The lines proceed from top to bottom, while the middle one is likewise curved;
Lakṣmī, Vāṇī, and Bhavānī are situated there in succession.
Thus, the measure (mātrā) whose form is Brahman is proclaimed as the Great Power (Mahāśakti). (Ḍa)
In the channel that extracts the [bodily] constituents.
A line proceeds from top to bottom, moving from left to right. (p.
96) Then that [line], in the form of Kuṇḍalinī, possessing the nature of Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Brahmā, consists of the Great Power (*mahāśakti*); its meditation shall now be described. (Ḍha)
In the Kāmadhenu Tantra.
O Supreme Goddess! The letter *ṇa* is herself Parakuṇḍalī;

she always has the form of a yellow streak of lightning, consists of the five deities, consists of the five vital breaths (*prāṇas*), O Goddess, and is eternally joined with the three qualities (*guṇas*).
In the *Varṇoddhāra-tantra*, it is said that [this] is conjoined with the principles beginning with the Self (*ātman*) and bestows great liberation.
The line that has entered the *kuṇḍalī* skin goes upward from the middle;
O Dear One! that very same line, having gone downward from the left, goes upward again.
She, in the form of Brahmā, Īśvara, and Viṣṇu, bestows the fruits of the four aims of life. (Ṇa)
In the fifth chapter of the Kāmadhenu Tantra.
Mahādeva said:

O lady of tremulous glances! The letter *ta* is itself the supreme *kuṇḍalinī*; it is a syllable consisting of the five deities, likewise composed of the five vital breaths (*prāṇas*), endowed with the three powers (*śaktis*), and joined with the principles beginning with the Self (*ātman*).
The syllable, accompanied by three dots, has a radiance equal to yellow lightning.
In the Varṇoddhāra Tantra.
At first she is the Bindu, then in the middle she attains the state of Kuṇḍalinī;
moving from the right to the left, she is the eternal one, possessing the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśvara. || Ta ||

In the *Kāmadhenu Tantra*: "O lady with tremulous eyes! The syllable *tha* is the form of liberation through Kuṇḍalinī; it is always accompanied by the three powers and endowed with the three points (*bindus*)."
In the Varṇoddhāra Tantra.
Having become coiled and looped from the left to the right,
and then having become coiled from the right to the left,
the line proceeds straight upward from below the right; these lines represent, in sequence, the gods and the Gaṅgā and other rivers.
Vāṇī, Bhavānī, and Lakṣmī—his meditation shall now be described. || Tha ||
In the Kāmadhenu Tantra.
Listen to the letter *da*, O lady of beautiful limbs! It bestows the fourfold aims of human life.
The phoneme is always composed of the five deities and consists of the five vital breaths. (Da)
In the Varṇoddhāra Tantra.
Within the line in the form of a triangle dwell three deities;
Viśveśvarī, the Mother of the Universe, is situated on the left shoulder. (Dha)
In the *Kāmadhenu Tantra*: "Listen to the letter *na*, O lady of beautiful limbs! It has the form of a streak of red lightning;
this phoneme consists of the five deities and is itself the supreme Kuṇḍalinī."
O Pārvatī, meditate upon the phoneme consisting of the five vital breaths within the heart;
[as stated] in the Varṇoddhāra-tantra.
To the left, there is a spiral line situated in an upward-and-downward sequence;
it consists of the forms of the moon, sun, and fire, and is proclaimed as the measure (mātrā) and the Goddess of Speech (Vāṇī). Na.
In the *Kāmadhenu-tantra*, page 97.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the imperishable syllable *Pa*,
that letter which bestows the four aims of life, whose luster is like the autumnal moon,
which consists of the five deities, and which is itself the supreme Kuṇḍalinī.

O Pārvatī, meditate within your heart upon that syllable which consists of the five vital breaths, which is always accompanied by the three powers, which is joined with the three qualities (guṇas), and which is conjoined with the principles beginning with the Self (ātman)— that syllable which bestows great liberation.
In the Varṇoddhāra Tantra.
From the corner of the left line, another curved line extends toward the right;
that too should be known as curved, and likewise the measure (mātrā) emerging from the left.
Śambhu, Brahmā, and the Blessed Lady reside in these [lines] respectively. ||pa||
In the Kāmadhenu Tantra.
Listen to the letter *pha*, O lady of beautiful limbs! It is like a streak of red lightning;
it is the syllable that bestows the four goals of human life, and it is eternally composed of the five deities.
This syllable consists of the five vital breaths and is always endowed with the three qualities (*guṇas*).
Always joined with the reality of the self and so forth, and accompanied by the three drops,
according to the Varṇoddhāra-tantra.
The curved line, moving to the left, becomes joined below;
from there, having moved upward starting from the right, it is Kuṇḍalī.
Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu—Kuṇḍalī is the very form of Brahman.
The measure (mātrā) is said to be Śakti, proceeding sequentially from the left to the right. Pha.
In the Kāmadhenu Tantra: "Listen to the letter *ba*, O lady of beautiful limbs! It bestows the four aims of human existence;
it resembles the autumnal moon and is eternally composed of the five deities."
The phoneme consisting of the five vital breaths, always accompanied by the three points (bindus).
In the Varṇoddhāra Tantra.
The line in the form of a triangle has the nature of Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Brahmā; it should be known as the supreme power of the Mātrās. Now, its meditation will be described. (Verse 6)
In the Kāmadhenu Tantra.
Listen to the letter *bha*, O lady of beautiful limbs! It is itself the supreme Kuṇḍalinī;
it is the syllable that bestows great liberation, possessing the radiance of the rising sun.
This syllable is eternally composed of the five vital breaths (*prāṇas*) and consists of the five deities.
In the *Varṇoddhāra-tantra*.
The lines proceed from top to bottom; on the left, however, Kuṇḍalī is curved.
That very same [line] goes downward again, and then upward again.
Brahmā, Śambhu, and Viṣṇu reside within them respectively. (Bha)
In the Kāmadhenu Tantra.
Listen to the letter *ma*, O lady of beautiful limbs! It is itself the supreme Kuṇḍalinī;
it resembles the rising sun, bestows the four aims of life, consists eternally of the five deities, and is composed of the five vital breaths (*prāṇas*).
In the Varṇoddhāra-tantra.
A beautiful four-cornered diagram, consisting of lines arranged from top to bottom, exists;
within it, Nārāyaṇa, Īśa, and Vidhi reside eternally.
The *mātrā* should be known as Kuṇḍalinī; her meditation shall now be described. || Ma ||
In the Kāmadhenu Tantra.
Listen to the letter *ya*, O lady of beautiful limbs! It is eternally composed of the four aims of life (*caturvarga*).
Resembling the smoke of straw, it is itself the supreme *kuṇḍalinī*.
This phoneme consists of the five vital breaths (*pañcaprāṇa*) and is eternally composed of the five deities.
In the Varṇoddhāra Tantra.
The line extending from top to bottom is indeed that which descends into the triangle;
Brahmā, Īśa, and Keśava reside within them eternally.
That measure situated at the top is proclaimed to be Śakti.
The line situated in its center is indeed remembered as being the form of fire;
that color is eternally devoid of qualities and never becomes possessed of qualities. || Ya ||
In the sixth chapter of the Kāmadhenu Tantra.
O lady of tremulous glances! [Meditate upon] the letter *ra*, conjoined with two earrings (*kuṇḍalinī*),
having the form of a red flash of lightning, eternally consisting of the five deities,
composed of the five vital breaths (*prāṇas*), and always accompanied by three dots (*bindus*).
In the Varṇoddhāra Tantra.
From the right side, there is a spiraling line that goes from left to right and downward;
then, moving again toward the right in two ways, it descends and ascends once more.
Bhavānī, Śaṅkara, and Agni reside eternally within them.
The half-mora, whose form is Brahman, is proclaimed as the Great Power (Mahāśakti). Ra.
In the Kāmadhenu Tantra.
O lady of tremulous glances! The letter *la* is joined with the three coils (*kuṇḍalī*), has the form of a yellow flash of lightning, and is radiant with all jewels;
it is a syllable consisting of the five deities and eternally composed of the five vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
O Pārvatī! Always meditate within your heart upon the syllable accompanied by the three powers (Śaktis) and the three points (Bindus), together with the principles beginning with Ātman;
thus it is stated in the *Varṇoddhāra-tantra*.

Joined with three coils, the line goes from the left to the right below, and then proceeds upward again; within those [lines] reside Nārāyaṇa, Śiva, and Brahma-Śakti. His meditation shall now be described. || La ||
In the Kāmadhenu Tantra.
O lady of tremulous glances! The syllable *va* is the unchanging liberation,
the coiled one (*kuṇḍalinī*), consisting of the five vital breaths, always joined with the three powers,
endowed with the three points (*bindus*), and united with the principles beginning with the Self (*ātman*).
The syllable consists of the five deities and is composed of yellow lightning;
it bestows the four aims of human life and grants all spiritual accomplishments.
O Goddess! It is always accompanied by the three powers and endowed with the three points.
In the Varṇoddhāra Tantra.
The line endowed with three corners consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
it is the supreme, eternal power of Māyā. Now, its meditation shall be described. (Ba)
O Supreme Goddess! O lady of pure smiles! Listen to the letter Śa.
It has the luster and form of the color red; it is itself the supreme Kuṇḍalinī.
O Goddess! The letter Śa is the embodiment of Brahman and bestows the four aims of human life.
O Dear One! This syllable consists of the five deities and has the nature of the five vital breaths;
it is always joined with the five jewels and endowed with the three dots (bindus);
it is accompanied by the three powers (śaktis) and united with the principles beginning with the Self (ātman).
In the extraction of the phonemes.
The line consisting of four corners proceeds sequentially from left to right;
within those [corners] reside Agni, Indra, Viṣṇu, and Īśa respectively at all times.
The vertical measure above is remembered as being of the nature of Śakti, equal to Mahālakṣmī.
The measure situated in the middle is the goddess of speech; she is remembered as the supreme (parā). Śa.
In the Kāmadhenu Tantra.

Listen to the letter *ṣa*, O lady of beautiful limbs! It is eternally composed of eight corners, resembling a red moon; it is itself the supreme Kuṇḍalinī, a syllable consisting of the four aims of life, with a form fashioned from nectar.
The phoneme consists eternally of the five deities and the five vital breaths;
it is always endowed with rajas, sattva, and tamas, and is accompanied by the three powers.
This phoneme is joined with the three points (bindus) and united with the principles beginning with the Self (ātman).
O Pārvatī, contemplate within your heart this complexion consisting of all the gods!
In the Varṇoddhāra Tantra.
The left [hand] is contracted, while the right hand moves downward in the shape of a cow's ear;
then it moves upward again—within these [gestures] are Fire, Moon, and Sun.
Bhavānī is to be known as their measure; her meditation shall now be described. (6)
In the Kāmadhenu Tantra.
Listen to the letter *sa*, O lady of beautiful limbs! It is the seed-syllable of Śakti, higher than the highest;
it has the form of ten million streaks of lightning and is joined with the three Kuṇḍalinīs.
O Goddess, it always consists of the five deities and is the essence of the five vital breaths (*prāṇas*).
Always joined with rajas, sattva, and tamas, and accompanied by three dots: Saḥ.
In the Kāmadhenu Tantra.
Listen to the letter *ha*, O lady of beautiful limbs! It bestows the fourfold aims of human life;
it is joined with two *kuṇḍalīs*, resembling a flash of red lightning;
it is ever endowed with *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas*, and consists of the five deities.

O Pārvatī! Always contemplate within your heart the syllable consisting of the five vital breaths (prāṇas), accompanied by the three powers (śaktis) and the three points (bindus). — From the *Varṇoddhāra-tantra*.
Contracted at the top, it has entered the state of Kuṇḍalinī in the middle, and goes downward;
then that very same [channel] goes upward again. Within them, Brahmā and the others reside in sequence.
Mātrā should be known as Pārvatī; her meditation will now be described. Haḥ.
In the Kāmadhenu Tantra.
Listen to the letter *kṣa*, O lady of beautiful limbs! It is joined with the three *kuṇḍalīs*;
it is a syllable consisting of the four aims of life (*caturvarga*) and always embodies the five deities.
This syllable is the essence of the five vital breaths (*pañcaprāṇa*) and is ever accompanied by the three powers (*triśakti*).

O beautiful one, meditate in your heart upon the syllable *kṣa*, which is accompanied by three dots (*bindu*), conjoined with the principles beginning with the Self (*ātmatattva*), and resembling the autumnal moon. *Kṣa*.
In the third part of the Yoginītantra, in the seventh chapter:
"One should not draw the letters of the mantra on the ground, nor should one write them in a book.
The book should not be set down apart [from oneself], nor should one pick it up when it has been set aside."
O Goddess of gods! If during an earthquake or an eclipse, a syllable or a book remains on the ground, then in birth after birth one becomes a fool;
therefore, O Goddess of gods, one should avoid that [place].
Thus is the prohibition against writing letters and so forth upon the ground.
If one should write a letter with a bamboo needle, his loss will certainly occur;
but by means of a copper needle, there shall be prosperity, and no depletion shall take place.
By means of a gold needle, Mahālakṣmī shall be eternally attained; indeed,
by means of a needle of *vṛhannala*— which is well-known in Gauḍa as *vola*— an increase of intelligence is produced.
Likewise, O Goddess, through those made of fire— meaning those made of variegated wood— the acquisition of sons, grandsons, and wealth occurs.
Through bell-metal there is great prosperity; through bronze, death shall occur;
and likewise through brass.
O auspicious lady! whoever writes a book with a pen measuring eight fingers, or ten fingers, or even four fingers,
shall indeed pass away within as many days as there are syllables in that work.

Just as in the statement beginning with "yathā rautyena," there is both injunction and prohibition regarding the same single object, so too here there is an injunction and a prohibition concerning the four-finger width, while injunctions and prohibitions apply respectively to the eight-finger and ten-finger widths.
Thus, regarding the auspicious and inauspicious nature of making a pen, the measurement of the book is also found in that very same place.

O Goddess, listen as I describe the measurement of the book in brief. One should obtain the fruit through the correct measurement; without measurement, prosperity is destroyed. [The sizes are] one cubit, one fist, up to the forearm, or twelve finger-breadths.
It should be ten or eight finger-breadths; one should not make it less than that. Thus ends the measurement of the book.

O Maheśānī! There are two types of piercing (*vedha*): one with a fist-sized hand and one measuring only a forearm, which is the ancient method. Regarding the binding of form (*rūpabandhaka*), starting from the hand and so forth, one should avoid making a piercing in the middle after leaving a space of eight finger-breadths (*aṣṭāṅgula*).

A hole should be made at the beginning of the *prādeśa* section, or one should perform it at two finger-breadths [from the end]; one should likewise consider piercing with a tool at the beginning and end of the book. Otherwise, there will quickly be the loss of a wife or the depletion of wealth.
If the piercing occurs in a burnt cavity, there will be suffering; if it is circular, it will be auspicious. If it is in a quadrangle, there is ruin; if in a triangle, death occurs.
(p. 101) Thus ends the result of piercing a book.

O Goddess of gods! O Beloved! One should have the book made on birch bark, or on teja-patra, or on palm leaf, or on ṭāḍī leaves; or even with agallochum (agaru), O Śaṅkarī! It may also be made, if possible, on a golden vessel or a copper vessel.

O Goddess! O fair-faced one! whoever writes [the mantra] upon the bark of another tree, or on a ketaki leaf, or on a mārtaṇḍa leaf, or on silver, or on a banyan leaf, or on any other beautiful-petaled leaf, and practices it;
He falls into an evil state of existence, and the loss of wealth will certainly occur;
such are the results of making a manuscript or a written document.
"He who, having transcribed the Veda, should recite it would become a slayer of a Brahmin;
or, if the book were kept in the house, a thunderbolt-fall would certainly occur.
Thus is the prohibition against transcribing the Veda in a book.
In the Satya Yuga, Śambhu—the trident-bearing, three-eyed Lord—remains established in the imperishable syllable (akṣara).
In the Tretā and Dvāpara ages, he is Prajāpati and the Sun himself.
In the Kṛta Yuga, he is the wielder of the Pināka bow, and in the Kali age, he is Hari in the form of written letters.
At both the beginning and the conclusion, one should honor the scribe,
as well as Hari, with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and with most beautiful garments; O beautiful lady, for every number of syllables on each leaf.
For that many thousands of yugas, he shall dwell for a long time in the world of Brahmā.
Thus ends the fruit of the worship of the scribe.
But he who, having written a document, should receive a salary,
shall dwell in hell for as many years as there are syllables in that document.
Thus ends the fault of accepting wages for that which has been written.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, named "The Bud" (*koraka*), concerning the description of the methods for writing letters and so forth, within the first section on cosmogony (*prathamasargakāṇḍa*) of the *Śrīprāṇatoṣiṇī*.
Thus ends the third [chapter], consisting of the exposition of the section on Śiva, within the fifth section on devotion (*bhaktikāṇḍa*) of the *Śrīprāṇatoṣiṇī*.
Section: For the sake of understanding the conventions of the Tantras, I shall extract and present here a few names of the letters from the Tantric scriptures for the delight of the learned.
The syllable *oṃ* is circular, the *tāra* (the sacred *praṇava*), and the *vāma* is the cause of the *haṃsa*.
It is the beginning of mantras, the *praṇava*, the truth, the power of the *bindu*, and the three deities.
It is the progenitor of all living beings, the five gods, the eternal, and the triad.
He is Sāvitrī, the three-crested, Brahman, the triple-guṇa, and the life-sustainer of the guṇas;
he is the primordial seed, the essence of the Vedas, and beyond that, the seed of the Vedas. He is the five-rayed one, the three-peaked, and the destroyer of existence within the three worlds.
The Lord who gives birth to the mantras and vidyās is the fivefold essence of the Gāyatrī; he is the imperishable source of the Mātṛkā, beginningless, and the bestower of non-dual liberation. Om.
Aḥ is Śrīkaṇṭha and Sureśa; the single-mātrā forehead [is Amṛta];
Pūrṇodarī, Sṛṣṭi, Medhā, Sārasvata, Priyaṃvada, Mahābrāhmī, Vāsudeva, Dhaneśa, Keśava, and Amṛta.
Kīrti, Nivṛtti, Vāgīśa, Narakāri, Hara, Marut, Brahmā,
Vāmādi, Aja, Hrasva, Karasū, and Praṇavādya;
the meaning is that [these] are the components beginning with the Praṇava.
Brahmāṇī, Kāmarūpa, Kāmeśī, Vāśinī, Viyat, Viśveśa, Śrīviṣṇu, Kaṇṭha, Pratipat, Tithi, Aṃśinī, Arkamaṇḍala, Varṇa, Ādi, Brāhmaṇa, and Kāmakarṣiṇī— AḤ.
Ākāra, Vijaya, Ananta, Dīrghacchāya, Vināyaka, Kṣīrodadhi, Payoda, Pāśa, Dīrghāsya,
Vṛttaka, Pracaṇḍa, Ekaja, Rudra, Nārāyaṇa, and Īśvara.
Pratiṣṭhā, Mānadā, Kānta, Viśvāntaka, Gajāntaka, Pitāmaha, Dviṭhānta, Bhūḥ, Kriyā, Kānti, Sambhava,
Dvitīyā, Mānadā, Kāśī, Vighnarāja, Kuja, and Viyat.
Svarāntaka, Hṛdaya, Aṅguṣṭha, and Bhagamālinī—Ā.
Iḥ, Sūkṣmā, Śālmalī, Vidyā, Candra, Pūṣā, Suguhyaka,
Sumitra, Sundara, Vīra, Koṭara,
Kāṭara, Payas, Bhrūmadhya, Mādhava, Tuṣṭi, Dakṣanetra, and Nāsikā.
Śānta, Kānta, Kāminī, Kāma, Vighnavināyaka, Nepāla, Bharaṇī, Rudra, Nityā, Klinnā, and Pāvaka. Iḥ.
The female form is Mahāmāyā, Lolākṣī, Vamalocanā;
Govinda is Śekhara, Puṣṭi, Subhadrā, and Ratna;
Viṣṇu is Lakṣmī, Prahāsa, Vāyu, Viśuddha, and Parāpara.
Kalottarīya, Bheruṇḍā, and Rati are Pauṇḍravardhana;
Śivottama, Śivā, Tuṣṭi, and the fourth, Bindumālinī;
Vaiṣṇavī, Vaindavī, Jihvā, and Kāmakalasanādakā.
Pāvaka, Koṭara, Kīrti, Mohinī, Kālakārikā, the pair of breasts, Tarjanī, Śānti, and Tripurasundarī—[these are the letters]. || ī ||
Uḥ is Śaṅkara, Vartulākṣa, Bhūta, and the speaker of auspiciousness; Amareśa is the right ear, Ṣaḍvaktra, Mohana, and Śiva;
Ugraprabhu, Dhṛti, Viṣṇu, Viśvakarmā, and Maheśvara.
Śatrughna, the maidservant Puṣṭi, the fifth Vahnivāsinī;
Kāmaghna, Kāmanā, the Lord, Mohinī, Vighnahṛt, Mahī;
the progenitor of the letter Ḍa, Kuṭilā, the ear, Pāradvīpa, Vṛṣa, and Hara. ||u||
Ūḥ, Kaṇṭhaka, Rati, Śānti, Kṣodhana, Madhusūdana;
Kāmarāja, Kujeśa, Maheśa, and Vāmakarṇaka; Arghīśa, Bhairava, Sūkṣma, Dīrghaghoṇā, and Sarasvatī.
Vilāsinī, Vighnakartā, Lakṣmaṇa, Rūpakarṣiṇī,
Mahāvidyeśvarī, Ṣaṣṭhī, Ṣaṇḍa, Bhū, and Kānyakubjaka— Ū.
Ṛḥ is Puradīrghamukhī, Rudra, the Mother of the Gods, Trivikrama, Bhāvabhūti, Kriyā, Krūrā, Recikā, and she who is supported by the nose;
she is Ekapādaśiromālā, Maṇḍalā, Śāntinī, and Water.
Karṇa, Kāmalabhā, Medhā, Nivṛtti, Gaṇanāyaka, Rohiṇī, and Śivadūtī—Pūrṇagiri is the seventh. (Ṛ)
Ṛḥ is Krodha, Atithi, Vāṇī, Vāmana, Go, Śrī, Dhṛti, Ūrdhvamukhī, Niśānātha, Padmamālā, Vinaṣṭadhī, Śaśinī, Mocikā,
Śreṣṭhā, Daityamātā, and Pratiṣṭhitā.
Ekadanta, Mātā, Haritā, Mithuna, Dayā, Komala, Śyāmalā, Medhī, Pratiṣṭhā, Pati, Aṣṭamī,
Brahmaṇya, Kīlāla, Pāvaka, and Gandhakarṣiṇī. (Ṛ)
Ḷḥ is Sthāṇu, Śrīdhara, the Pure One, Medhadhūmra, Vaka, Viyat,
Devayoni, Dakṣagaṇḍa, Vaheśa, Kaunta, Rudraka, Viśveśvara, Dīrghajihvā, Mahendra, Lāṅgali, and Parā.
Candrikā, Pārthiva, Dhūmrā, Dvidanta, Kāmavardhana, Śucismitā, and the ninth, Kāntirāyātakeśvara; Cittākarṣiṇī, Kāśa, and Tṛtīyakulasundarī. *Ḷ*
The letter *ḷ* is Kamalā, Harṣā, Hṛṣīkeśa, and Madhuvrata; Sūkṣmā, Kānti, Vāmagaṇḍa, Rudra, Kāmodarī, and Surā;
Śāntikṛt, Svastikā, Śakra, Māyāvī, and Lolupa; and Viyat.
Kuśamī, the very firm one, the mother, the blue and yellow one, the elephant-faced one;
Kāminī, Viśvayā, Kāla, the eternally pure, the pure, the doer; Sūrya, Dhairya, Akarṣaṇī, the solitary one, the progenitor of the Danujas. (Ḷ)
The letter *E* is the reality, Śakti, Jhiṇṭīśa, the eighth [vowel], the womb, and Marut;
it is Sūkṣmā, Ardhakeśī, Jyotsnā, Śraddhā, and Pramardana;
it is fear, knowledge, compassion, the steadfast, the shank, and the source of all.

[I shall describe] the mantras for the four directions of Kailāsa and for the practitioner.
O Supreme Goddess! There exist everywhere Tantras of four kinds;
there are millions upon millions of mantras, yantras, and practitioners on the earth, in the worlds of the gods, among the Gandharvas, and in the netherworld (rasātala).

In the world of men, in the world of sages, and among the kuṣmāṇḍas and rākṣasas, there exist tantras of various forms and specialized [teachings]. Among all these tantras and mantras, that which pertains to humans is distinguished as superior. Likewise:
I salute the Lord who wears a crescent moon as his crown, whose brilliance is like ten million full moons, and who is adorned with five three-eyed faces colored like pearls,
yellow, clouds, coral, and hibiscus; he holds a trident, axe, sword, thunderbolt, fire, a serpent-king, bell, goad, noose, and the hand that dispels fear.
I worship Him whose limbs are radiant with dark-colored ornaments.
Having prostrated, I shall speak of that supreme benefit for all the world:
in whatever place such-and-such conduct exists, there the Dharma is likewise;
by means of that, one becomes fulfilled, endowed with heaven and liberation.
No error should be made in that regard; then success arises. Likewise, on page 112, he spoke all the mantras into the mouth of the deity:
[he spoke them] into the mouths of the yakṣas, gandharvas, and nāgas, as well as into the yellow mouth.
With a face like a cloud, possessing the luster of a *kuṣmāṇḍa* fruit and free from obstacles,
he who is described among men as having the hue of lapis lazuli and the *javā* flower—
the Lord of Heroes (*Śureśvara*)— caused the Great Vidyā to be bestowed upon his disciples.
The method for causing the disciples to receive [the initiation] is found in the tenth Brāhmaṇa chapter of the Gāyatrī-tantra.
Śiva said:
O Lambodara! O highly fortunate one! Listen to my supreme word;
this great and well-composed [work] has issued from my mouth. This Tantra, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain, has emerged from the mouth of Pārvatī.
Having written this with great effort, go to Siddhāśrama, my son! There dwell sages who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas;
may you quickly become endowed with the powers of aṇimā and the other supernatural qualities, my son!
Thus addressed by Śaṅkara, he then became eight-armed;
having drawn [the image] with four hands, he should offer it to Śiva.
Śiva said:
"Go, my son! O mighty-armed one! Taking the *tantra*, go quickly to the delightful Siddhāśrama forest, which is like Indra’s Nandana grove.
Having bowed down and taken that *tantra*, he departed swiftly for that forest.
Having begun thus...
Then, having heard the sage’s words, he gave that tantra to the sage;
in this manner, having transcribed all the tantras, one should present them.
Thus ends the manner of the descent of the tantra upon the earth.
In the Viśvasāra:
O Maheśvarī! That Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) has entered into the millions of living beings;
O Maheśānī! The Great Knowledge is proclaimed by means of the individual soul (jīva) alone.
Through the soul, the perfection of being a living being is attained for the sake of attaining the divinity of the God of gods.
All mantras were born from the various letters of the *mātṛkā*. "Were born" means they manifested or came into being.
O noble lady! The Great Vidyā, the Great Pūrva, and the Great Mantras are said to be the seed of all things, according to the opinion of Śaṅkara;
this is also held in the *Tāpanī*, which is the commentary on the *Kulamūlāvatāra-kalpasūtra*.

The venerable Lord Paramaśiva, having effortlessly composed all eighteen branches of learning and all philosophical systems while assuming their respective forms, was questioned by the Goddess— who is non-different from his own self— through her five faces, and he then composed the five Āmnāyas which constitute the nature of the ultimate reality.
Śaṅkarācārya explains these [terms];
it has been stated thus in the *Parimalollāsa*: "The Supreme Śiva."
The first vibration of the Great Lord of Light, whose nature is gracious, is called the Śiva-tattva by the Supreme Lord.
The Bhaṭṭāraka is the maker of all regulations;
[as stated] in the seventeenth chapter of the fifth section of the Kulārṇava.
He is remembered as Bhaṭṭāraka because he pacifies the sins of existence, because he is the crest-jewel of the moon on his head, or because he protects that which is desirable.
The eighteen branches of knowledge well-known from the Śruti are as follows:
the four Vedas, the four Upavedas, the six Aṅgas, and the Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and Dharmaśāstra— these constitute that number.
The phrase "well-known in the Śruti" indicates that they are authoritative in every respect.
The four Vedas are the Ṛg, Sāma, Atharva, and Yajus.
The Upavedas are the Āyurveda, Gāndharvaveda, Daṇḍanīti, and Dhanurveda.
It should be understood that these correspond respectively to those whose Vedas have already been mentioned.
Thus, in the *Caraṇavyūha* as spoken by Śaunaka, it is stated: "The Ayurveda is the Upaveda of the Ṛgveda; the Dhanurveda is the Upaveda of the Yajurveda;
the Gāndharvaveda is the Upaveda of the Sāmaveda; and the Arthaśāstras (treatises on statecraft) and Astraśāstras (treatises on weaponry) are the Upavedas of the Atharvaveda."
The southerners recite "they become" as the fourth quarter [of the verse].
However, in the thirteenth chapter of the third book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, it says:
"He [taught] Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, Gāndharvaveda, and the Veda of the Self."
It has been stated that he created the Sthāpatya Veda from his mouths in sequence, starting with the eastern one.
Svāmī [Ānandagiri] explains that Sthāpatya is the science of Viśvakarman;
it is the science concerning the construction of houses, sacred sites (vāstu), sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa), and so forth.
Śaṅkarācārya placed these at the beginning of all the scriptures in order to proclaim their authority over the Śruti, the Vedas, and the various other treatises.
However, Śrīdhara Svāmin, in his commentary on the Śrī Bhagavad Gītā, [placed them] after the Smṛti scriptures.
The weakness of the science of punishment (*daṇḍanīti*) has been stated.
If that were the case, however, there would be no prohibition against consuming those great medicines mentioned in the *Āyurveda* that are otherwise unfit to be eaten or drunk.
Yet, the followers of the *Śarala* school maintain that there must be an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for consuming such medicines. That is not correct.
"According to the Smṛti, these very things are not forbidden for a sick person during medical treatment, nor is there any fault in those of a similar nature.
The "six auxiliary sciences" (ṣaḍaṅgāni) are: phonetics (śikṣā), ritual (kalpa), grammar (vyākaraṇa), etymology (nirukta), prosody (chandas), and astronomy (jyotiḥ).
The Purāṇa is that which is composed by Vyāsa and characterized by five marks.
Nyāya refers to the Mīmāṃsā of ritual action; furthermore, it also includes Ānvīkṣikī (logic), as will be stated later in the words, "Nyāya was [taught] by Gautama."
Mīmāṃsā refers to Brahmamīmāṃsā, that is to say, Vedānta. The Dharmaśāstras are those composed by Manu and others.
(p. 114) The teachers explain that these constitute the eighteen branches of knowledge (*vidyā*), which are the philosophical systems (*darśana*).

The systems of philosophy (*darśana*) are, according to their respective views, those of the Buddhists, Śaivas, Brāhmaṇas, Sauras, Vaiṣṇavas, and Śāktas. However, at present, the wise consider the Vedānta, Sāṃkhya, Mīmāṃsā, and the specialized treatises on Logic (*tarka*) to be the philosophical systems.
"By play" (*līlayā*) means that *līlā* is a particular kind of desire (*icchā-viśeṣa*).
Otherwise, if the Lord were a creator of the world without such desire, there would be no need for him to depend upon any other cause.
"Assuming those respective states" means becoming embodied as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Vyāsa, Nārada, and so forth.
For this very reason, it is stated in the first chapter of the Gandharva Tantra:

First, indeed, I proclaimed the Śaiva teachings, such as the Pāśupata and others; thereafter, they were proclaimed by Brahmins who were possessed by my power. And the great Vaiśeṣika scripture was proclaimed by Kaṇāda.
Likewise, Gautama taught the Nyāya system, while Kapila taught the Sāṃkhya. Furthermore, Dhiṣaṇa proclaimed the highly censurable Cārvāka doctrine;
and Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a Buddha, [taught it] for the purpose of destroying the Daityas.
Likewise, the Buddhist scriptures, as well as the "Blue Cloth" (Nīlapaṭa) and other such works concerning the ascetic's tonsure,
are shown to be censured by the world through the words of the Vedas;
indeed, it is established here that the very nature of their ritual acts is to be abandoned.

That which has fallen away from all ritual actions is called "impurity" (kalmaṣa). Indeed, all those who are devoted to the meaning of the scriptures spoken by Gautama have entered the womb of a jackal and are rendered doubtful regarding all ritual actions.
Therefore, in the Mahābhārata, within the Mokṣadharma section, in the dialogue between Kāśyapa and Indra:

"I was once a self-styled scholar, a ritualist who reviled the Vedas; devoted to the useless science of logic and dialectics, I used to revile and speak excessively against the twice-born during the Vedic sacrifices."
"O twice-born one, this attainment of the fruit [of my actions] is my state as a jackal"—this is the speech of a jackal addressed to a brahmin.

Now, one might object: since the statement "Ānvīkṣikī, Daṇḍanīti, and Trayī are the three beauties of heaven" identifies Ānvīkṣikī as the very essence of the Kālī-kula, and because she is included among the Thousand Names [of the Goddess], if the study and worship of Ānvīkṣikī— who is the very nature of the illustrious Dakṣiṇakālikā— were to result in the state of a jackal, then from where could the fruit of the four aims of life (caturvarga) be obtained?
If it is true that we call it the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī) and the knowledge of the self (adhyātmavidyā),
then it was composed by Dattātreya and not spoken by Gautama;
for so it is stated in the first book of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa.
Having been chosen by Anusūyā, he attained the status of Atri’s offspring;
as it is said that he taught the science of logic (*ānvīkṣikī*) to Alarka, Prahlāda, and others. Thus, being chosen by Atri, he became his son.
To the question "How so?", he says: it means not perceiving any fault in her by thinking, "He has chosen me, Anasūyā, as his own offspring. The rest is easy to understand.
Śrīdhara Svāmin has explained *ānvīkṣikī* as the science of the self (*ātmavidyā*).
If it is argued that the science taught by Gautama is not that [Vedic science], because it is well-known as being called "Tarka" (Logic), we say: not so.

For if that were the case, the qualification "Tarka-vidyā" (Science of Logic) in the verse from the *Mokṣadharma*—"Ānvīkṣikī is the science of Tarka"—and Amarasimha’s statement—"Ānvīkṣikī, Daṇḍanīti, Tarka-vidyā, and Arthaśāstra"—would be inconsistent.
Therefore, the name *anvīkṣikī* belongs to those two alone.
If it is then argued that the aforementioned fault remains as it was, that is true; however, you raise this objection without considering the intended meaning of the *Gandharva-tantra*. For instance:

The essential meaning of the statement is as follows: because the term *niṣṭhā* denotes a past object, those who have "entered the womb of a jackal" (*śārgālīṃ yonim āpannāḥ*)—meaning they have attained the state of being born as jackals—are all those devoted to the teachings of the treatises proclaimed by Gautama; yet, while being experts in the science of mere logic (*kevalatarkaśāstra*), they become skeptical regarding all ritual actions (*sarvakarmasu*).
This is the distilled sense of the passage.
The distinction from other treatises, however, is indicated by the particle *tu*.

For this very reason, they recite: "He who engages in the investigation of logic (*nyāya*) without disputing the meaning of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) shall attain the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*); otherwise, he will enter the womb of a jackal."
Regarding the meaning of the verses on the dharma of liberation:

"I am devoted to the science of logic (*mānvīkṣikī*) and have been abusive and a harsh speaker toward the twice-born; for one who reviles and speaks excessively against a Brāhmaṇa, the resulting fruit is birth as a jackal—this is my lot."
And this is appropriate, because Manu has established that verbal sin is of such a nature.
And so says Manu:

Through the defects of actions born of the body, a man goes to the state of an immobile being; through those of speech, to the state of a bird; and through those of the mind, to the state of a low-born caste. It will be explained later that mental sin does not apply to householders, or that it refers to [sins committed] in eras other than the Kali Yuga.
And so it is said in the First Book of the Bhāgavata:
"The sovereign king does not resent the Kali age, like a bee that consumes only the essence;
for his auspicious deeds quickly reach fulfillment, whereas other actions do not."
The construction is as follows: like a bee that takes only the essence, the sovereign king does not harbor malice toward the Kali age.
Meritorious deeds (*kuśala*) bear fruit quickly through mere intention;
other [deeds], namely sins, do not bear fruit quickly, because they bear fruit only when they have been committed, and not otherwise.
The meaning is that they are merely products of volition (*saṅkalpa*).
Amara states: "Volition is mental action.
However, if by the study of the science of logic (*tarkavidyā*) one were said to attain the state of a jackal, then [the text] would refer to one who reviles the *Mokṣadharma*, and so forth.
The wise should consider that otherwise the verse would be rendered meaningless.
In the Gāndharva [marriage].
By the twice-born Jaimini, through a doctrine devoid of a Lord and asserting that all the Vedas are meaningless, a very great treatise was composed;
"savimati" means accompanied by discernment, which consists of the nature of inquiry.
"By the Blessed One" means by the Blessed Lady, whose characteristic is the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss.
"As non-different from her own self":
"He indeed did not find delight; therefore, being alone, he does not find delight. He desired a second."
As much as this non-separation is—as when a man and woman are closely embraced—so much does he divide himself into two;
thus they became husband and wife.
Therefore, it is said that "this [self] goes as a half. And because of that, O Yājñavalkya, this space is filled in three ways.
Thus he united with her, and from that humans were born; "Then Yami looked upon him"—so says the Śruti.
This has been stated in the Svacchandabhairava:
Abiding in the roles of teacher and disciple, the Lord Maheśvara himself brought down the tantras through sentences composed of preceding and succeeding words.
Also in the *Parāpañcāśikā*:
"The Supreme Lord is the essence of light; for the Great Lord who is light, the state of having reflective awareness as his sole nature is never obstructed anywhere."
"By means of five faces" refers to the forms of Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Vāmadeva, Aghora, and Sadyojāta.
"The five traditions" (pañcāmnāya) refers to the Pūrva, Paścima, Dakṣiṇa, Uttara, and Niruttara [traditions], which consist of the specific textual contexts for each of all the deities.
This has been stated in the Bhairavatantra:
"East, west, south, north, and the unsurpassed.
Elsewhere it is also said: "The Eastern Tradition faces east, the Western faces west;
likewise, the Southern faces south, and the Northern faces north as the supreme."

Likewise, the unsurpassed [knowledge] above, which consists of the Siddhānta and the Āgama, and the thorough comprehension of the Upper Tradition (Ūrdhvāmnāya), is not the fruit of meager austerity. Elsewhere it is said: "The Eastern Tradition is of the nature of sound; the Southern is of the nature of the ear."
The western [tradition] consists of questions, while the northern likewise consists of answers;
the upper tradition (ūrddhvāmnāya) is the awakening to reality, consisting of pure experience alone.
Also in the Kulārṇavatantra:
"From my five faces, the five Āmnāyas have emerged," and so forth;
"of the nature of ultimate reality" means that they are the essence of all the Śaiva and other Āmnāyas.
Also in the sixth chapter of the *Nirvāṇatantra*:
O lady of excellent complexion, having meditated upon the auspicious lotus of Śiva,
one should then contemplate Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora,
Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna; thus the five faces are proclaimed.
The *sayojāta* is indeed white, resembling pure crystal;
likewise, the gentle *vāmadeva* is yellow-hued and captivating;
and the *aghora* is black-hued, equal [in power], and increasing one's dread.

O Goddess! One should meditate upon that red Tatpuruṣa, whose divine form is enchanting; likewise, one should meditate upon the dark-blue Īśāna, who is the essence of all gods and Śiva—the first in the west and the second in the north.
One should meditate with devotion, intent on the deity Aghora in the south, Tatpuruṣa in the east, and likewise know that Īśāna is in the center.
However, in the second chapter of the *Samayācāra-tantra*, the six traditions (*ṣaḍāmnāya*) are taught as follows:
When the mantra is the Pūrvāmnāya, then it is situated in the eastern direction;
I am the Lord Sadāśiva, proclaimed as Ācāra.
Likewise, the Dakṣiṇāmnāya is indeed situated in the southern direction.

In this very way, the Uttaramnāya is situated in the northern direction. O Goddess! That which was spoken by me in your presence regarding the upward-turned face—the Ūrdhvāmnāya—is difficult to attain even for the gods.

O Goddess! O Girijā! O Beloved! That which was spoken [in the beginning] regarding the Ācāra-mukha is called the lower Āmnāya; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O fair-waisted one! And the six Āmnāyas have been declared by the name of the Order of Origination (Utpattikrama).
O fair-faced one, I shall indeed declare for the benefit of practitioners those deities who have been mentioned in each respective [chapter],
along with the various forms of Śrīvidyā, Tārā, and Tripurā.
Bhuvaneśī and Annapūrṇā are proclaimed in the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya); Vagalāmukhī, Vaśinī, Tvaritā, Dhanadā,
Mahiṣaghnī, and Mahālakṣmī are proclaimed in the Southern Tradition (Dakṣiṇāmnāya).
The meaning is that she is Bālabhairavī, the Mistress.
Mahāsarasvatī-vidyā, as well as the supreme Vāgvādinī,
Pratyaṅgirā, and Bhavānī— these are celebrated in the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya).
Kālikā, together with her divisions, and joined with the various forms of Tārā— Mātaṅgī, Bhairavī, Chinnā, and the supreme Dhūmāvatī—
as proclaimed in the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya), bestow swift results in the Kali age.
All these, together with their various divisions, are proclaimed as belonging to Kālikā. (p.
118) Among them, the twenty-two-syllable mantra is celebrated in the Dakṣiṇāmnāya;
it is the supreme Vidyā beyond that, not hidden within other Vidyās.
The mantra of Parāprāsāda is proclaimed in the Upper Tradition (Ūrdhvāmnāya),
while the deities beginning with Vāgīśvara are proclaimed in the Lower Tradition (Adhāmnāya).
Only the Upper and Lower Traditions together shall be the bestower of liberation.

O auspicious lady! Other traditions have been proclaimed for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; by performing them according to the prescribed injunctions, one shall obtain the fruit. O beautiful one! Listen to the procedure for all of these, beginning with the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya).
By performing which one quickly obtains the most supreme fruit;
the six Āmnāyas are proclaimed as the givers of the fruits of the six duties for men. O Mistress of the Goddess! among them, the Northern Āmnāya (Uttarāmnāya) is the swift bestower of results.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Pādukāpañcakastotra* that [the lineage] is "endowed with the fruits of the six traditions" (*ṣaḍāmnāyaphalopeta*).

Regarding this, it was previously stated that any contradictions concerning the phonemes of Ambā and the others found in various Tantras, as well as the contradiction regarding the five or six traditions, are to be resolved by means of the distinctions between the traditions and so forth.
Or [it may differ] by the distinction of the kalpas.
Regarding that, the difference in conduct according to the difference in tradition has been stated in the first chapter of the Niruttara Tantra.

O Dear One! The ritual of the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya) is said to be that of the bound soul (pāśava). That which is taught in the Southern Tradition (Dakṣiṇāmnāya) is likewise remembered as belonging to the bound soul.
The ritual born of the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya) is based upon both the bound soul and the hero (vīra).
O Dear One! The rite born of the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya) is based upon the divine hero (divyavīra).
Even a divine practitioner should accomplish it through the state of a hero in the cremation ground;
indeed, without the heroic posture (vīrāsana), the divine one should perform worship in the cremation ground.
O Dear One! The ritual action proclaimed in the Ūrdhvāmnāya is based upon a divine state.
By this, the status of being an *āmnāya* (scriptural tradition) is established for the Tantras and so forth.
However, in order to demonstrate that they possess equal authority, Amarasiṃha has accepted that *śruti*, *veda*, and *āmnāya* are synonymous terms.
Therefore, in the first chapter of the Merutantra:
"A mantra does not exist apart from the *praṇava* [Oṃ], and the Veda arises from mantras;
therefore, the mantra is supreme to the Veda, and the *āgama* is remembered as a limb (*aṅga*) of the Veda.
Thus, the status of the Tantras as limbs of the Veda is stated. "Supreme to the Veda" (*vedapara*) means that which is higher than the Veda, i.e., the most excellent.
He whose Vedas are the mantras and whose limbs are the [auxiliary sciences] is thus described even in the Niruttara Tantra.
The Āgama is the fifth Veda, and the Kaula is the fifth stage of life (āśrama). Thus,

as seen in the previously mentioned commentary on the Tāpanī by Śaṅkarācārya, through the provision of the qualification "only so many" and the qualification "the eighteen mentioned in the Tāpanī," there is no separate enumeration of other systems of philosophy either.
However, while they possess the nature of knowledge (*vidyātva*), they are generally nothing other than sciences (*śāstra*).

These include, for example, the examination of gems, the art of dancing and gestures, the training of horses, elephants, and falcons, the construction of weapons, architecture, the *Keralī* system of erotics, music, augury, statecraft, poetry, and poetics.

Therefore, regarding the sciences (*vidyā*), the treatises (*śāstra*), the arts (*śilpa*), and [the arts] such as dance and song— if it is argued that since the sciences and treatises are mentioned separately in the *Sarasvatī-stava*, the arts and so forth must also be considered "treatises" (*śāstra*), and thus why they are not specified separately therein— the answer is: it is not so.

By the term "arts" (*śilpa*) and so forth, the practice of arts and the like is intended in the Tantra; therefore, there is no fault. As for the proof that these constitute a scripture (*śāstra*), it is the statement beginning with, "Like beasts, those who do not know the science of love (*kāmaśāstra*) do not find delight," because it exists in its current form among the Purāṇic sciences included within the eighteen branches of knowledge, and because it is accompanied by a commentary.
And because its meaning is free from doubt, the definition of a *bhāgavata* alone is stated in the seventh chapter of the second *rātra* of the *Nāradapañcarātra*.

Having heard the Bhāgavata, which consists of eighteen thousand verses, is divided into twelve skandhas, and was proclaimed by Śuka, one shall attain liberation. Formerly, it was spoken by the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa to Brahmā, and [subsequently] to Śuka.
That which is the pure essence of the Purāṇas is known as the Bhāgavata.
In the second chapter of the Śāradā [Tantra].
All mantras were born from the various phonemes of the *mātṛkā*.
The classes of mantras are twofold, according to the division into *mantra* and *vidyā*.
Mantras are to be known as having male deities, while *vidyās* are traditionally remembered as having female deities.
Also in the *Prayogasāra*:

Those mantras are declared to be of two kinds, according to the division between those belonging to Soma and those belonging to Sūrya. The mantras belonging to Sūrya have male deities and are proclaimed as *mantras*;
likewise, those belonging to Soma have female deities and are renowned as *vidyās*. This is for the sake of achieving specific applications of the mantras.
The *Śāradā-tilaka* states that there is a threefold nature [of mantras]:
"All mantras are declared to consist of male, female, and neuter natures.
Male mantras end in *huṃ phaṭ*, while those ending in *svāhā* are considered female."
The neuter [mantras] end with "namaḥ"; thus the mantras are said to be of three kinds.

If it is asked, "How can there be a conceptualization of male, female, and so forth for the mantra, which denotes bliss consisting of partless consciousness?"—it is true that in reality such a thing does not exist at all; it is a mere conceptualization for the sake of practitioners, as they say:
"Of that which consists of consciousness, which is non-dual, partless, and bodiless..."
The conceptualization of the form of Brahmā is for the sake of the ritual requirements of the lay practitioners (*upāsakas*).
According to the tradition, [the mantras] end with *huṃ* and *phaṭ*, whether used individually or collectively;
"ending with *dviṭha*" means ending with *svāhā*.
By the word *ṭha*, because of its similarity in form to the letter *lipi* (the bindu), the *bindu* is expressed by implication;

for according to the lexicon, "ṭha is in the void (*śūnya*) and in great strength. Its very nature as the void constitutes its doubling, by which the *visarga* is meant, and since that is of the nature of *Śakti*, the word *dviṭha* denotes the fire-power (*agni-śakti*).

"Endings with *svāhā* are for females; however, in the *Prayogasāra*, it is stated that mantras ending in *vaṣaṭ* or *svāhā* belong to females, while those ending in *huṃ* or *namaḥ* belong to neuters; thus, mantras are remembered as being of three kinds."
The mantras are also inferred by means of the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*) at their beginning, end, and middle;
just as [sexes] are known through the proximity of their physical forms— namely male, female, and neuter—
they are likewise proclaimed to be characterized by the presence of the *bindu*, the *visarga*, and the crescent moon (*indu-khaṇḍa*) at their ends.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
These three kinds of mantras are prescribed for the rites of subjugation, pacification, and malevolent sorcery.
In the Nārāyaṇīya [section].

The remaining males are recommended specifically for subjugation (*vaśya*) and eradication (*uccāṭana*); women are [recommended] for minor rites and the destruction of obstacles, while neuter beings are [recommended] for other purposes. Thus it is stated in the *Śāradā*.
The mantras for both the cruel and the gentle are to be understood as consisting of Agni and Soma.
Since it was previously stated that the manifestation of Kuṇḍalī, who is the Mātṛkā, is of the nature of Agni and Soma, the essential point is that the mantras are likewise so.
In that very context, for the two karmas, those consisting primarily of fire, stars, the end of space, and the ether have been described.
The construction is "of the two types of actions, cruel and gentle.
*Vahni* is the letter *ra*.
*Tāra* is the syllable *oṃ*.
The letter *kṣa* is the end;
the letter *ha* is the void (*viyat*).
The word *prāyaḥ* expresses abundance.
The *manavas* belong to Agni; those consisting mostly of *indva* syllables and ending in *amṛta* belong to Soma.
The word "belonging to Agni" (*āgneyāḥ*) is connected with the preceding [statement].
The moon is the letter *sa*,
because in the ritual placement of the principles (*tattvanyāsa*), the lunar orb is placed beginning with the letter *sa*.
Nectar is the letter *va*.
In this context, the truth consists in the predominance of one [element];
and it has been stated in the Īśānasaṃhitā:
Syllables beginning with *tā*, *rā*, *kā*, *śā*, and ending with *vā* and *nta* are fiery (*āgneya*); those other than these are lunar (*saumya*).
A mantra that ends with *namaḥ* is lunar even if it is fiery, and a mantra that ends with *phaṭ* is fiery even if it is lunar.
A fiery mantra is well-known for the accomplishment of cruel rites.
One who is gentle should perform gentle actions in the prescribed manner.
Also in the Nārāyaṇīya [section].
A mantra that predominantly contains the syllables *tāra* (om), *agni* (ra), and *viyat* (ha) at its end is considered to belong to Agni;
the remaining two are praised as belonging to Soma for the performance of fierce and gentle rites, respectively.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
The fires of the southeast awaken when the vital breath moves through the right nostril.
When the vital breath (prāṇa) is situated in the portion located at the navel, the gentle [deities] attain awakening;
when the vital breath has moved into two channels, all attain awakening.
Once awakened, they always bestow auspiciousness upon the practitioners (mantriṇaḥ).
The practice should not be performed at the time of sleep;
and it has been stated in the Nārāyaṇīya:
A mantra does not grant accomplishment if it is either asleep or merely awakened;
during the time of sleep it flows through the left [channel], and during waking it flows through the right.
This is the reverse of the fire-related mantra that is mind-pleasing.
At the time of sleep, the breath flows through the right nostril, and at the time of waking, through the left; this is the reversal.
One should know that the time of awakening occurs when the breath flows through both nostrils simultaneously.
Thus ends the ninth chapter (the eighth by name) in the first section on Creation of the *Śrī-Prāṇatoṣiṇī*, titled "The Description of the Keśara-forms of the Different Vedic Traditions.
Although the characteristics of defective mantras, such as those that are "cut" (*chinna*) and so forth, have already been maintained by the author of the *Tantrasāra*, nevertheless, regarding them—
It is written here for the purpose of explanation and to demonstrate various methods of purification.
In the *Śāradā*:
"Mantras that are defective due to being 'cut' (chinnā) and so forth do not protect the practitioner.
They are described as being 'cut,' 'obstructed,' 'devoid of power,' or 'turned away.'"
Deaf, blind, pinned down,
paralyzed, burnt, collapsed, terrified, soiled, insulted,
pierced, fast asleep, intoxicated with pride, and fainted.
Furthermore, [the types of] the child are: one whose vigor is stolen, one who is deficient, and one who is ruined;

likewise the youth: the boy, the adolescent, the mature, the old, and the sword-like (nistrimśaka); and furthermore the dull-witted: the one devoid of vigor, the one lacking accomplishment, the slow, and the fraudulent.
One who is partless (niraṃśa) is devoid of essence; one with squinting eyes is seedless.

One who is embraced by smoke is deluded, and one afflicted by hunger is likewise deluded. One who is excessively arrogant is said to be deficient in limbs, while one who is excessively enraged is so described.
One who is excessively cruel, yet also modest and tranquil-minded;
one who has lost his position, deformed, and very old—these are proclaimed as the types of ativṛddha (the excessively aged).
I shall now describe the characteristics of those who are devoid of affection and those who are afflicted.

By the words "likewise again," he states that the peak itself is partless (*niraṃśaka*). Regarding "excessively increased" (*ativṛddha*), this is a qualification of "devoid of moisture" (*niḥsneha*). Therefore, Rāghavabhaṭṭa maintains that after "devoid of moisture," the term "excessively increased" has been stated.
That mantra in which the seed-syllable *ānala* (RA) is said to occur at the beginning, middle, and end—
whether conjoined or unjoined, and further divided threefold by being overlaid with vowels,
or even fourfold or fivefold— that mantra is designated as "severed" (*chinna*).
The term "in the beginning, middle, and end" indicates a collective [application].
Whether conjoined (*saṃyukta*)—meaning joined with another syllable—or disjoined (*viyukta*)—meaning alone—each of these is connected twice.
That which has a distinguished or impure seed-syllable (*bīja*) is designated as "severed" (*chinnasaṃjñaka*).
The seed-syllable is the *śakti*-seed, conjoined with the vowels; it is conjoined with the long vowels: *ā*, *ī*, *ū*, *ai*, *o*—thus say those who know the tradition (*sampradāya*).
If it is asked how the word "seed" refers to the *māyā*-seed, it is stated in the *Śaiva* [scriptures]: [text follows].
The names of the seed-syllable of Māyā are: Māninī, Śivavallavī, Vātāvarttī, Kalā, Vāṇī, Bīja, Śakti, and Kuṇḍalī.

A mantra that is marked by the pair of *bhū* seeds at its beginning, middle, and end is to be known as "obstructed" (*ruddha*); it is devoid of both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*).
The *bhū* seed is *la*.
The term "pair" (dvandva) is connected to each [element] individually. In the *Piṅgalāmata*:
"In the beginning there are two by two, in the middle likewise, and at the end there should be two."
This mantra, which is the seed-syllable of Indra, is called "obstructed" (ruddha).
A mantra that is devoid of Māyā, the three tattvas, the Śrī-bīja, and Vārāhī is said to be powerless, provided that Māyā and the Bhuva-jeśī-bīja do not exist within it.
(Māyā is the *hrīm* syllable; Bhuva-jeśī-bīja is the *klīm* syllable.)
The three principles (tritattva) are either the syllable *huṃ* or the *praṇava* (*oṃ*).
*Vāra* is the syllable *phreṃ*. The seed-syllable *cī* is the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī.
There is no combination of these.
As it has been said:
"Where the seed-syllable of Māyā does not exist, nor the three principles (tritattva), nor even the repetition (vāra)."

Or even if it is the *śrīgṛha*, this mantra is proclaimed to be devoid of power (*śaktihīna*). Also in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "If the seed-syllable of *māyā* or the three principles (*tritattva*)—that is, the *śrīgṛha*—are not present there..."
Known as "one devoid of power," he destroys the capability of his ministers.
The seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*) is at the mouth, *māyā* is at the head, or else the goad (*aṅkuśa*) is there;
this is declared to be the "one with the face turned away" (*parāṅmukha*), the letter *ha* marked with a dot (*bindu*).
Its connection is with the phrase "in the middle of which," from the preceding verse-quarter.
At the beginning, in the mouth;
at the end, on the head.
The goad is the syllable *kroṃ*.
The word "vā" (or) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). This is as stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*:

The seed-syllable of desire (KĀM) is placed in the middle; at the beginning and end of the Māyā (Hrīṃ), there is the goad (Aṅkuśa). This mantra is called "Parāṅmukha" (Facing Away); it is known as Parāṅmukha for the sake of accomplishment.
Also in the Yantramuktāvalī:
"That [mantra] in whose middle position the seed-syllable of Kāmakalā is not found,
and in which Māyā is at the beginning and the Aṅkuśa at the end, should be known as 'parāṅmukha' (turned away)."
If there is no *bindu* at the beginning, end, or middle, it is considered deaf (*vadhira*).
The phrase "the letter *ha* is marked with a *bindu*" connects with the final quarter of the preceding verse;
it also connects with the statement "Indu [the moon] is marked with a *bindu*."
The phrase "in the beginning, end, and middle" does not imply a conjunction;
as it has been said:
"The void, conjoined with the bindu, [is placed] at the beginning, the end, or in the middle."
"Or he for whom there is no seed of life (jīvabīja) is considered deaf.
Some explain that by the word "bindu" they mean the letter *ṭha*;
however, this is also refuted by the term "seed of life."

A mantra that consists of five syllables but is devoid of the letter *ra*, the sun (*arka*), and the moon (*indu*), should be known as "eyeless" (*netrahīna*); it bestows suffering, grief, and disease. (In this context, *arka* refers to the letter *ha*).
In the Vaiṣṇava-kṛta-tattva-nyāsa.
The Sun is so called because the reality of the solar orb (arkamaṇḍala-tattva) is deposited as the letter *ha* and onwards, or because the letter *ha* has a masculine form.
The Moon is the letter *sa*.
The results [of these] are, respectively: "bestowing suffering, grief, and disease."
Since fire, sun, and moon constitute the three eyes, their causality should also be understood as being diminished by one or two [respectively].
This has been stated in the Piṅgalāmata:
The five-syllable mantra that is devoid of fire, moon,
and sun should be known as "eyeless," which brings about suffering, grief, and fear.

If the *haṃsa*, *prāsāda*, and *vāgbhava* mantras are found at the beginning, middle, and end [of a mantra], that mantra becomes paralyzed and an obstacle to success. The *haṃsa* is the essential form, the *prasāda* is the syllable *hoṃ*.
The seed-syllable of Vāgbhava is Aiṃ.

If the mantra of which [the syllable] is joined with fire (vahni) and wind (vāyu) is seen seven times at its head, the knower of mantras should consider that thread to be burnt. "Fire" is the letter *ra*; "wind" is the letter *ya*. It is conjoined with these, either above or at the head—that is, at the beginning.
Thus it is stated in the Piṅgalāmata:

"When a mantra is illuminated by the seven seed-syllables situated at the beginning, which are the winds (vāyu) and the letter of fire (ra), the noble ones declare that mantra to be 'burnt' (dagdha)."
The *astra* [mantra] is seen with two, three, six, or eight syllables.
That [mantra] is called "slipped" (*srasta*) whose opening is known as the *praṇava*.
Or, that [mantra] whose *astra*, namely the *phaṭ*-kāra, is seen with two, three, six, or eight syllables.
In the Piṅgalāmata, this is stated under the name "frightened" (bhīta):
"If a mantra is unjoined at its beginning, middle, and end, that mantra is called 'frightened' by the learned; it is devoid of fruit."
It is proclaimed as either *śiva*, or *śakti*, or that which is called *bhīta*.
This connects with the fourth quarter of the verse beginning with "yasya mukhena" (in whose mouth...).
In whose mouth—that is, at the beginning—there is neither *śiva*, the syllable *haṃ*, nor *śakti*, the syllable *sa*.
However, it has been stated by means of another mantra in the *Piṅgalāmata*.
They say that a mantra which lacks Śiva, Śakti, and likewise the syllable Oṃ at its beginning is deficient in the Mātṛkā and bestows inferior power.
That mantra which possesses four *m*s at its beginning, middle, and end is impure; one who knows mantras should avoid it.

There is a conjunction with "and so forth" (ādītyādeḥ). There is also a conjunction in the phrase "the four *mā* sounds. Therefore, taken together across the three locations, the four *mā* sounds are required.
This has been stated in the Piṅgalāmata:
A mantra-knower should always recognize that mantra as "defiled" (malina) in which the letter *ma* is seen in four ways at its beginning, middle, end, and location.

That mantra in the middle of which there is either the syllable *da* or the seed-syllable *krodha* (*hūṃ*) at the head in two ways, with the weapon (*astra*) standing [at the end], is declared to be "obscured" (*tiraskṛta*).
The seed-syllable *krodha* is *hūṃ*.
"In the middle" refers to the option between the letter *da* and the wrathful deity (*krodha*).
"At the head" means at the end.
The connection is that the weapon (*astra*) is twofold, namely, the double-weapon (*dvidhāstra*).
As it has been said: "That mantra in the middle of which the syllable *da*— the seed-syllable of Krodha— is situated,
and in which two *phaṭ*s are present when [the mantra] is attained, that mantra is disregarded."
Oṃ at the beginning, *dvayaṃ* (the two) at the mouth, *vaṣaṭ* at the head, and the weapon-syllable (*astra*) in the middle:
that mantra which is thus divided should be abandoned by the wise for the sake of spiritual attainments (*siddhi*).
[The word] "at the head" [also applies] to the end.
Vaṣaṭ! The weapon! Phaṭ!
In the *Mantramuktāvalī*:
"That mantra in which there are two *astra* syllables (*phaṭ*) in the middle and likewise at the end of *vaṣaṭ* is to be known as distinct [and] devoid of success."
Also in the Piṅgalāmata:
The two syllables of the weapon-mantra (astra) with *vaṣaṭ* at the end are likewise declared [to be used] in the middle;
this mantra, when thus divided, is proclaimed as the inferior one.
That which possesses the three colors but is devoid of the *haṃsa* is declared to be deep sleep (*suṣupta*).
By the term "three colors," the state of possessing the three colors and being devoid of the *haṃsa* is stated to belong to one and the same [entity].
In the Piṅgalāmata.

Where the three phonemes (varṇatraya) are devoid of the Haṃsa, that is declared by Śambhu to be the state of deep sleep (suṣupta); this is the established doctrine (siddhānta), which bestows the fruit of supernatural powers (siddhi).
Also in the Mantramuktāvalī:
A mantra consisting of three phonemes that is devoid of the syllable *haṃsa* should be known as "asleep"; it takes away the fruit of all accomplishments. (From the Śāradā-tantra)
Whether it be a mantra or a vidyā consisting of seventeen syllables,
beginning with five *phaṭ* sounds, which is declared to be "Intoxicated with Pride" (*madonmatta*);
that is one in which there are eight or ten syllables plus seven [making seventeen].
He is one whose [mantra] begins with the five syllables "phaṭ".
As it has been stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"Whether it be a Vidyā or a Mantra consisting of eighteen syllables,
preceded by five *phaṭ*-kāras, it is called Madonmatta."
Also in the Piṅgalāmata:
Whether it be a Vidyā or a King of Mantras consisting of seventeen syllables,
if there are five *phaṭ* sounds at the beginning, it is proclaimed as the Unmatta.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
That mantra in whose middle that weapon-syllable is situated is "stupefied" (mūrcchita).
The meaning is that the mantra in whose middle that weapon-syllable— or five seed-syllables consisting of *phaṭ*— is situated, is stupefied.
He whose [weapon] reaches the point of cessation is said to be "one whose vigor has been taken away.
This means that his weapon reaches the point of cessation at the end.
However, in the Piṅgalāmata, it is stated:
That mantra which has the weapon-syllable (*astra*) at its beginning, middle, and end, as taught by Śambhu, is known as "stolen" (*hṛtavīrya*); it does not bestow success.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
A mantra that possesses a square [of syllables] at the beginning, middle,
and likewise at the end should be known as deficient if it consists of eighteen syllables.
The word "at the beginning" implies a conjunction [with the middle and the end].
The four *astra* [mantras] combined in three places;
however, in another tantra, this is called by the name "Bhīta. Thus:

Bhairava spoke that eighteen-syllable mantra, which is joined with a square at the beginning, the end, and likewise in the middle, as "the Afraid One" (bhītam). Elsewhere, this same mantra is called by the name "The Terrible One" (bhīma).
Just as [it is] in the beginning, so it is in the middle and likewise at the end; this mantra, which consists of eighteen syllables and is joined with the square, should be known as Bhīma.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
A mantra of nineteen syllables that is joined with the *tāra*,
and begins with the seeds of *hṛllekhā* and *aṅkuśa*, is declared to be "destroyed.
*Tāra* refers to the *praṇava*.
Hṛllekhā is "hrīṃ";
the goad is "kroṃ".
It consists of nineteen syllables or eighteen syllables.
And likewise is the statement cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"It shall consist of eighteen syllables,
and [the mantra] of nineteen syllables is endowed with Māyā (Hrīṃ), the syllable Oṃ, and Aṅkuśa (Kroṃ)."
"This mantra is proclaimed as 'pradhvasta' by Lord Śambhu."
The mantra consisting of seven syllables joined with the *dhruva* is called *nistriṃśa*.
*Dhruva* refers to the *praṇava*. The rest is easy to understand.
A mantra of seven syllables is known as a child; one of eight syllables is a youth;
one of sixteen syllables is a young adult; and a mantra of forty syllables is considered mature.
The script and the letters.
Also cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
A seven-syllabled mantra is a child; an eight-syllabled one is a youth;
a forty-syllabled one is mature; and a sixteen-syllabled one is a young man.
A mantra of thirty syllables, sixty-four syllables,
one hundred syllables, or even four hundred syllables is designated as "vṛddha" (the aged).
The nine-syllable mantra joined with the *dhruva* is called the "sword" (*nistriṃśa*).
Both the state of having nine syllables and the state of being joined with the *dhruva* belong to this very same [mantra].
In the Piṅgalāmata:
The nine-syllable [mantra] is the "sword" (nistriṃśa), and when joined with the *dhruva*, it is called "death" (mṛtyuda).
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
That mantra at the end of which there is no *hṛdaya* (heart) or *śiras* (head), nor in the middle the *śikhā* (crest) or *varma* (armor), or which lacks the syllables *vauṣaṭ* or *phaṭ*.
Or, if it is devoid of the syllables of Śiva and Śakti, it is known as "powerless" (nirvīrya).
The Heart is *namaḥ*;
the Head is *svāhā*.
The topknot is *vaṣaṭ*; the armor is *hūṃ*;
