the auspicious one is the letter *ha*.
Śakti is the letter *sa*;
this is recorded by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
At the beginning are the seed-syllables of the heart and the head; in the middle are likewise the armor and the crest-mantras.
That king of mantras in which the two syllables consisting of Śiva and Śakti do not exist is declared to be powerless and is censured in all ritual acts.
But in another tantra, however:
But that which is devoid of vigor is declared to be "devoid of the syllable Oṃ" at the beginning.

In these positions, if the syllable *phaṭ* is seen six times, that mantra will be devoid of success; a mantra of ten syllables is considered weak. Furthermore, if there is a combination of these [syllables] at the beginning, middle, and end, it is likewise ineffective.

"Sixfold" (ṣoḍhā) means combined across the three locations. "Manda" refers to a *paṅkti* meter consisting of ten syllables; since the *paṅkti* meter consists of ten syllables, the mantra shall consist of the aforementioned ten syllables.
The *kūṭa* is the single-syllable mantra; it alone is said to be partless.
One who has two colors will be devoid of strength, while one who has four colors will be squint-eyed.
The six-syllabled mantra is devoid of a seed-syllable (*bīja*), while the seven-and-a-half syllabled mantra is as follows:
here, the state of being "seven-and-a-half syllables" and "twelve-and-a-half letters" will be explained later;
it should be understood that this is because there is no vowel at the end.
Alternatively, that which consists of twelve and a half syllables is "smoky" (dhūmita) and is censured.
Likewise, that which consists of twenty-one syllables [is formed] with three and a half seed-syllables;
the meaning is that the three and a half seed-syllables are also [treated] as before, and likewise "smoky."
As it is stated in the Piṅgalāmata: "A mantra of six and a half syllables, or one of twelve and a half syllables,
or even one of three and a half syllables, is declared to be 'smoky' (dhūmita)."
That which consists of twenty or thirty syllables is called the "embraced" (āliṅgita).
The twenty-two-syllable mantra is proclaimed as the one that deludes.
That mantra which consists of thirty-two syllables,
as well as one of twenty-seven syllables and one of twenty-four syllables, should be known as being afflicted by hunger.
A mantra consisting of eleven syllables, or twenty-five in number,
or twenty-three letters, is declared to be "haughty" (dṛpta).

Since the "excessively arrogant" (atidṛpta) was mentioned during the occasion of the enumeration (uddeśa), why is the definition of the "arrogant" (dṛpta) provided during the occasion of the definition (lakṣaṇa)?
This is not to be questioned, because even though the general rule (utsarga) remains the same, there is a distinction [between the two].
This has been stated in the *Mantramuktāvalī* as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
One [prefix] subverts the meaning of the verbal root; another conforms to it;
yet another qualifies that very same meaning; and another is employed as being devoid of meaning.
A mantra of twenty-six syllables, or likewise one of twenty-six syllables,
or one of twenty-nine syllables, is said to be "devoid of limbs" (aṅgahīna).
That which consists of twenty-eight syllables, or even thirty-one,
is said to be excessively wrathful and is censured for all ritual acts.
A mantra consisting of thirty syllables, or even thirty-three, is declared to be excessively fierce; it is censured for all ritual actions.

Beginning from forty and extending up to sixty-three syllables, that many mantras are declared to be designated as "with shame" (savrīḍa). The meaning is that starting from forty syllables and increasing by one syllable at a time, there are twenty-four varieties; such is the "shameful" (vrīḍita) mantra.
Those mantras that consist of sixty-five syllables are said to be "peaceful-minded. Those mantras declared to have up to ninety-nine syllables are called "fallen from their place" by the wise.
This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound of the type where the qualities are not included in the designation (*ataṅguṇasaṃvijñāna*), meaning "that whose beginning consists of sixty-five syllables.
Otherwise, since it was previously stated that [the section] of sixty-five syllables is characterized by a tranquil mind, this name would also apply to that.
This has been clearly stated in the Mantramuktāvalī as follows:
From sixty-five up to ninety-nine;
thus, by increasing one syllable at a time, there are thirty-four varieties known as "those fallen from their position."
Those mantras that consist of thirteen syllables or fifteen syllables are called "deficient" (vikala). They may number one hundred, or one hundred and fifty,
or two hundred, or ninety-two, or even ninety-nine.
Or, those which are said to be three hundred in number are "without moisture" (niḥsneha);
this means ninety-two less one, or ninety plus one.
Starting from four hundred and extending up to a thousand syllables,
that which is excessively prolix in its applications should always be abandoned by the Buddhas.
Mantras exceeding one thousand syllables are called *daṇḍakas* and are designated as *pīḍitas*.
Mantras consisting of two thousand syllables have been divided into seven parts.

These mantras, existing in their original form, should be understood as being in the nature of hymns (stotra). Likewise, practitioners of mantra (mantrin) must understand the vidyās in all ritual actions.
The meaning is that they are likewise possessed of faults.
As recorded by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
"Just as with mantras, so too are the vidyās divided from one another;
they should be understood by the lord of teachers as having been spoken in various tantras.
The phrase "divided from one another" means they are distinct by way of their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), but not in terms of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

However, some, reading "in all rites" (*sarvakarmasu*) as "in optional rites" (*kāmyakarmasu*), claim that since these defects do not apply to the recitation for the sake of liberation, the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and so forth need not be performed.
That is not correct.
Even when reciting for the sake of liberation, the purification and other rites to be described must certainly be performed, as stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
In the second chapter of the Śāradātilaka.
"The wise person who practices mantras without understanding these defects will not attain success even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Thus, one who applies to oneself those mantras corrupted by such defects—
One should purify [the channels] by means of the upward-moving breath while employing the bound *yonimudrā*.

The grammatical connection is as follows: the practitioner, having performed *kumbhaka* (breath retention) with the upward-moving breath while employing the bound *yonimudrā*, should purify [the channels] while joining the mantras within himself.
The method of purification, however, is stated as follows, as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:

Having bound that *yonimudrā* and contracted the foundational lotus (*ādhārapaṅkaja*), one should meditate on the syllables of the mantra arising from it as moving back and forth up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). Then, having filled [the body] with air, one should perform breath-retention (*kumbhaka*).
One should recite the mantra one thousand times for the pacification of defects in the mantra.
Because it seals the place of the *yoni*, it is called *yonimudrā*.
By means of the *mahāmudrā*, one should thoroughly purify the *mūlabandha*.
But the Mahāmudrā is as held by Rāghavabhaṭṭa: |||1||"
Pressing the vulva with the left foot and extending the right leg,
one should fill the mouth with both hands;
placing the face against the throat, one should hold the breath upward.
As for the *mūlabandha*:
pressing with the heel, one should contract the perineum and the anus;
drawing the *apāna* upward, it is called the *mūlabandha*.
Now, the Yonimudrā is [described] in the sixth chapter of the Kubjikātantra.
Now I shall speak, O Maheśānī! O you whose face resembles the autumnal moon!
O Goddess, this is exceedingly supreme; it must never be revealed.
This must not be disclosed, O Goddess! It is like one's own womb, O Pārvatī!
At midnight, with hair loosened, naked, and endowed with power,
the wise practitioner should meditate upon his chosen goddess, who is the embodiment of yoga for yogins;
he should join the left ankle to the secret place.
p. 129) Having made the body steady, one should place the palate upon the tongue; O Maheśvarī! the tip of the nose should be joined with the eyes.
Likewise, having assumed the posture of the throat (kaṇṭhāsana), one should contemplate the upward-flowing [current].
One should meditate upon the Goddess in the form of a serpent, residing in the *mūlādhāra*;
in the morning, within the lotus of the *ādhāra* above the orb of fire,
one should contemplate the Great Goddess with four arms, nourished by supreme nectar.
The eternal Great Goddess is dark-complexioned and seated upon a great lotus throne; she always holds the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting in her right hands,
while in her left hands she bears a sword and a severed head.
With disheveled hair and a smiling face, she dwells in the abode of the cremation ground;
she is jagged-toothed, with her right side covered, her hair loose, and naked.
She wears a girdle fashioned from a multitude of corpses and possesses a laughing countenance.
Wearing a dangling garland of severed heads, she is ever-auspicious;
she rests her right foot upon the heart of a corpse,
being intensely and utterly devoted to the pleasure of dalliance with Mahākāla.
The Goddess, endowed with the three eyes whose forms are the moon, the sun, and fire; bearing the crescent moon; possessing full and elevated breasts;
and accompanied on the four sides by auspicious goddesses of terrible roar.

I bow to Dakṣiṇakālī, who is unfathomable even to the knowers of the four Vedas, who is adorned by all the Vedas, who grants desires and assumes any form at will, who provides protection to her devotees,
who bestows the four aims of human life, and who is formidable.
In the Svādhiṣṭhāna [cakra], one should contemplate the Great Goddess in the form of the moon;
having meditated there upon the Goddess, as well as the stainless one who possesses the form of the universe,
with hands granting fearlessness and boons, O beautiful lady of the gods!
The Great Goddess, bearing a bow and arrows, and again holding a noose and a goad;
joined with the Bāṇaliṅga, possessing the splendor of the face of a dark blue cloud;
with a quivering tongue, she is the eternal form of Viṣṇu.
Her ears were adorned with a pair of youthful [ornaments], and she was the slayer of wicked asuras.

One should meditate upon the eternal one, a mass of splendor, in Maṇipūra— she who is clothed in a tiger skin, who dwells in the *brahmarandhra*, whose face is exceedingly gracious, and whose lotus-face is smiling.
The great goddess is naked, with a formidable face, loose hair, and four arms; she is red in color, wears red garments,
sits in the lotus posture, and is adorned with all the serpent ornaments.
To the goddess who holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus; who is worshipped by the gods;
who bestows dharma and artha; who provides protection to her devotees;
who grants all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis); and who, moreover, deludes the worlds.
She is Mahāmāyā, the deluder, the virtuous one who bestows knowledge upon the wise;
she is Sundarī, Ramaṇī, and Rāmā, the granter of the fruits of the four aims of life;
she is Śāntā, beloved of the peaceful, and Ugrā, the destroyer of fierce Daityas.

One should meditate upon the eternal Mother of all, who is worshipped by the gods— the Great Goddess who dwells in Mahākāla, who is accessible through devotion, who delights Yaśodā, and who is fond of honey and meat.
O Great Goddess! In the Anāhata [cakra], one should meditate upon the Supreme Deity—
the Great Goddess who has eight arms, who is red in color, who possesses the three powers (triśakti),
and who, O Śivā, holds a bow, an arrow, a sword, and a discus.
The Goddess who holds a noose and a goad, saluted by Brahmā and the other gods;
the Goddess who bears the crescent moon, with full and elevated breasts;
the Great Māyā seated upon a lotus, established on a great lotus throne.
Thus one should contemplate the Goddess, who proceeds by way of Brahman;
one should contemplate the Supreme Goddess within the pure Great Wheel—
the eternal Great Goddess, ten-armed and yellow in color.
The goddess, standing upon Kāmarāja, holds in her right hands a skull-cup, a shield, a conch, a mirror, and a fly-whisk;
in her left hands she holds a sword, a great lotus, a flaying-knife, a noose, and a goad.
[He saw] the Great Goddess, seated upon a great lion-throne,
wearing divine garments, adorned with a crown of matted locks,
a beautiful goddess worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahādeva.
O Maheśānī! at the Ājñā-cakra, the wise one should meditate upon her who has two arms,
mounted upon the shoulders of a lion, beautiful with two arms,
bestowing the gestures of boon and fearlessness, and adorned with various jewels.
She is endowed with a crown of matted locks, adorned with a crescent moon,
equipped with a jeweled girdle, and decorated with a garland of gems;
she is clothed in red garments and served by the Lord of Kamalā.

One should meditate upon the Goddess in the form of a serpent, who pacifies the suffering of saṃsāra and carries one across the ocean of existence, by means of the path of the *suṣumṇā*. One should meditate upon the Supreme Sovereign through the yoga of piercing the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*).
One should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess on the thousand-petaled lotus;
one should contemplate Kāma, adorned with five arrows, wandering within its center,
as well as all the holy fords such as the Gaṅgā and nectar in every circle.

O Great Goddess! It is adorned with all the seasons beginning with spring. O Great Goddess! It is white in color, possesses an excellent thousand petals, is joined by all the gods, and is endowed with all powers.

O Goddess! One should meditate there upon the Lord, who consists of all mantras, adorned by the four Vedas, who embodies the eleven great gods and the essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, and whose pericarp is the color of gold.

O Goddess! [I bow to] Paraśiva, who consists of consciousness, who is attainable through meditation, eternal, the essence of essences, higher than the highest, beyond the reach of mind and speech, continuous with perpetual bliss, incomparable, and the supreme, boundless reality known by the Vedas.
O Goddess! He consists of Śiva and Śakti; he is both devoid of attributes and the very essence of attributes.
Having the form of a lamp’s flame, he is the embodiment of meditation for yogis.
He is the Lord whose nature is pure consciousness, nourished by the supreme nectar.
In the center of that, one should meditate upon the Goddess, eternal and composed of the three qualities (triguṇa),
with terrible fangs, a formidable mouth, and a lolling tongue, possessing four arms;
her upper left lotus-hand holds a sword with a head recently severed.
Her right hands display the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons;
she has the luster of a dark blue cloud, is slender yet of terrible form, and is naked.
She is smeared with blood dripping from a garland of severed heads hanging around her neck.
She who is terrifying with a pair of severed heads used as ear-ornaments,
endowed with three eyes shaped like the orb of the rising sun,
and whose face is made radiant by streams of blood trickling from her two corners of the mouth.
With disheveled hair and a smiling face, she dwells in the abode of the cremation ground;
she has fashioned a girdle from the heaps of hands of corpses, her countenance laughing as she stands upon the heart of Mahādeva in the form of a corpse.
She was seated for the sake of pleasure with Mahākāla, afflicted by passion,
surrounded on the four sides by jackals making terrible howls,
her face exceedingly serene, her lotus-like countenance smiling.
The Unstruck (anāhata) [sound], however, is right there, with a luster equal to ten million flashes of lightning.
Above that, O slender one, is the crest (śikhā), which is the supreme digit (kalā) whose nature is consciousness (cidrūpa).
One should meditate upon the Self as being thus endowed with that.
She proceeds by way of the path of Brahman, indeed through the sequence of piercing the *liṅga*.
Having the brilliance of ten million suns and the coolness of ten million moons,
that nectar indeed resides within the *saṃjñā* [cakra], characterized by supreme bliss.
Having gone to the divine world of *kulākula*, one should enter the *kula* once again;
for one who practices in this way with ultimate certainty in this world,
there is liberation from the bonds of existence and from the sufferings of old age, death, and the like.
That fourfold creation proceeds within that womb;
this is declared to be the *yonimudrā*, the bestower of all accomplishments.
Within the lotus of the *mūlādhāra*, there is a most beautiful triangle.
One should meditate on Kāma, resembling ten million rising suns, wandering within that [space];
above him is the Kuṇḍalinī Śakti, possessing a brilliance equal to ten million flashes of lightning,
shaped like a sleeping serpent, and endowed with three and a half coils.
One should meditate upon that goddess, beautiful as a celestial maiden, within the triangle of the *mūlādhāra*.

Having repeatedly placed the Śakti— who dwells in the lotus-born [Brahmā]— together with the Self in these locations upon lotus-seated thrones, one should contemplate her, with the heart fixed steadily, in due order.

One should meditate upon her whose nature is consciousness, who resides within the great lotus-cluster of the sky-lotus bud at the end of eternal bliss, who is like a fresh rain-cloud, and who is the sole path to the way of liberation.

Having directly drunk the divine flood of nectar from the swan situated upon the great lotus in the sky— which possesses the luster of lac-dye— he should enter once more into the center of the *kula*.
Then, in each and every wheel (*cakra*), he should in due order satisfy all those deities, beginning with the *ḍākinīs*, with the spreading essences of the nectar-fluid.
One should satisfy that Kuṇḍalinī who resides within all the petals;
above that, in the Bodhinī [lotus], is Indra, and likewise Nāda;
then, in the Śakti [lotus], one should contemplate the Vyāpikā portion, and in the Manu-gocara [lotus], the Manu.
One should contemplate the syllables of the mantra as being strung upon the power of consciousness (cicchakti).
That very [power], in the supreme void nourished by the supreme nectar,
should reveal its own self-nature even without ritual worship, fire-offerings, and the like.
In this way, that yogi should contemplate the mantra; of this there is no doubt.
Freed from all sins, one beholds the chosen deity;
within six months, all perfections shall be attained, and one beholds one's own true self.
"At the end of the year, the eighteen great siddhis shall be attained. Thus one should meditate upon the Goddess, whose nature is that of the Supreme Self.
He alone is Śaṅkara manifest, he alone is the imperishable Viṣṇu;
he alone is the supreme Brahman, he alone is the highest of deities.
"Thus, O Goddess, O Maheśvarī, the Yonimudrā has been described to you!
By practicing for one year, one attains perfection; furthermore, one whose desires are fulfilled shall obtain it again.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
In the Kali age, men of inferior intellect are incapable of the yonimudrā;
how then can those who are capable in their practice attain the supreme goal?
Sadāśiva said:
Well asked, O Great Goddess, you who act for the benefit of all beings! O Maheśānī, the Yonimudrā cannot be performed by means of Māyā, nor by Śrī, nor by Kāma, nor by the Praṇava.
One should recite the root mantra in the *sampuṭa* (enclosed) form eight thousand times;
by that alone, it shall be well-accomplished, and one should perform the practice for the realization of the mantra.
Listen further, for I shall explain another most wonderful method of accomplishment.
By the mere performance of which all accomplishments (*siddhi*) arise:
the five short vowels, the conjunct consonants, space, fire, water, and earth;
[and] the last, the first, the second, the fourth, and the middle, in sequence.

The five-colored syllables, together with the final ones and the white moons, constitute what is called the "Earth-script" (bhūtalipi), consisting of forty-two letters. These are the fifth letters of the groups beginning with 'a', 'ya', 'va', 'ra', and 'ma', joined with the sibilants (śānta).
"The groups beginning with 'va' are to be known; these nine groups are traditionally taught as 'amau'.
This statement is also found in the sixth chapter of the Śāradā-tantra.
The meaning of this is as follows:
The five short vowels—a, i, u, ṛ, and ḷ—constitute the first group. The conjunct vowels—e, ai, o, and au—constitute the second group.
The letter *ha* is space (*vyoma*).
The letter *i* is fire;
the letter *r* is fire;
the letter *va* is water.
"Dharā" is the letter *la*; this is the third group.
Regarding the sequence of the letters of the five groups, he says "the last":
the last is *ḍa*.
The first is *ka*;
the second is *kha*;
the fourth is *gha*.
The middle [consonant] is *ga*.
This sequence applies to the other four groups as well; thus is the eightfold group (*aṣṭavarga*).
The letter *śa* ends with *ra*.
The letter *ya* is white;
the letter *sa* is the moon.
This is the ninth group.
Regarding the statement "āy-ambār-ṛṇa" concerning the first letters of the ninth group:
*ambār-ṛṇa* refers to the letter *ha*.
In the compound *aś-ca-eś-ca-ambār-ṛṇaś-ca*, following the sandhi of *a-e* into *ai*, and with *ambara* (*ha*) following, the substitution of *āy* occurs.
"Āmbara" refers to the fifth letters of the classes: the phonemes ṅa, ña, ṇa, na, and ma.
Combined with the "śānta" [vowel] and ending with the letter śa, the syllables are thus: a, e, i, ṅa, ña, ṇa, na, ma, and śa; this is the ninth class.
Śāradā reveals that the letters of the classes consist of the five elements.
The sky, air, fire, water, and earth constitute the various letters of the groups.
In the second group, there is no earth; in the ninth, there is no water or earth.
This is because the fourth letter of the second group does not exist as an element, and likewise for the final group.
The meaning is that neither [of these two] exists because of their being composed of the three *varṇas*.
Viriñci, Viṣṇu, Rudra, the Aśvins, Prajāpati, and the Lords of the Directions,
accompanied by the powers of action (*kriyā*) and so forth, are the presiding deities (*vargadevatā*) in successive order.

The lords of the directions—Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Candra—are all endowed with the powers of action (kriyā-śakti), knowledge (jñāna-śakti), and will (icchā-śakti); such is the grammatical connection. They are possessed of these threefold functions of the powers of action, knowledge, and will.
However, some say there are nine deities: the lords of the directions, along with the three beginning with Ekakriyāśakti. (p.
134) Dakṣiṇāmūrti is said to be the seer; the Gāyatrī is declared to be the metre;
and the supreme Goddess, the Mistress of the Phonemes, is stated by the wise to be the deity herself.

One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the six groups of consonants (*hādi-ṣaḍvarga*) together with their respective seed-syllables (*jāti*). One should meditate upon the Goddess at the root of the Tree of Letters (*lipitaru*), within a lotus composed of that [Tree].
The wise declare the supreme Tree to consist of the eternal letters.
The great seed of supreme consciousness has the *bindu* and *nāda* as its mighty roots;
it expands in all directions with the syllables of the earth as its branches,
and with the syllables of water as its leaves, it completely covers the three worlds.
Blazing with sprouts the color of fire like a tree in autumn with its jewels,
illuminating the beauty of his body with flowers radiant as the color of the wind,
and bowed down by fruits the color of space— he is the supreme refuge for all beings.
Sprinkling the Supreme Goddess with the nectar, ambrosia, and honey of the Vedas and Āgamas;
fashioned by the Vedas, Āgamas, and other scriptures, lofty and captivating;
consisting of Śiva and Śakti, it is the very embodiment of the three worlds resting within its shadow.
Relying upon this, those of excellent policy shall attain all their desires.
This is its meaning:

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: one should meditate upon the Goddess at the root of the tree of letters, which is a lotus composed of those [letters], that is, a lotus consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*).
He will describe the meditation later.
He states [the nature of] the tree of letters with the words "they say."
The wise always speak of the tree as being composed of the letters (varṇamaya). Of what nature is it? Its seed is the supreme consciousness, Kuṇḍalinī, or the Supreme Brahman.
Thus, its root is the *śiphā* (fibrous root), which consists of *bindu* and *nāda*.
[Objection: But if that tree is eternal, then how can it be called the "great seed" (*mahāvīja*) of the consciousness of another? [Reply:
True; it is metaphorically designated as a "seed" by virtue of being a manifestor (*vyañjaka*).
The rest is easy to understand.
He speaks of meditative absorption (dhyāna).

With breasts full and high, her head marked by the crescent moon, her eyes rolling from the intoxication of wine, proud of her youth, she holds in her hands a boon, a rosary, a sacred lore, and a skull— she who resembles ten million moons rising from their crests.
I take refuge in Vāgīśvarī, whose body is smeared with [sandalwood paste].
The meditation as described in the Kubjikātantra is as follows:
"Bow down to the Mistress of the Letters (Varṇeśvarī), who holds in her hands a rosary, a yellow deer, and a lofty axe; who possesses three eyes;
who bears the crescent moon upon her crest; who is ruddy in hue and wears a garland of lotuses; and who is bent by the weight of her breasts."
Likewise:
having formed the enclosure of the noose and the goad, one should then [place] Māyā, Vāyu (Wind), Agni (Fire),
Pṛthivī (Earth), Āpaḥ (Water), and thereafter Māheśvara.
Having uttered the *prāsāda* mantra, one should then utter the *śakti* mantra conjoined with the Sun;
thereafter, one should say, "The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of this [person] whose name is written on the ground are here.
(p. 135) Then, having again uttered the mantras, one should subsequently utter the *pāśa* and the other [mantras].

The wise one should then utter "the individual soul (jīva) is stationed here," and furthermore, he should sequentially utter these: "all the sense organs" (sarvendriyāṇi), followed by "speech, mind, eye, skin, ear, nose, and breath; having come here," he should then say.
Having recited "Sukhaṃ ciraṃ samuccāryya tiṣṭhantu vahnivallabhāḥ" (May they remain for a long time in happiness, O beloveds of Fire),
one should thus establish the vital breaths and meditate upon her for the attainment of desired success.
Having spoken thus, meditation has been explained.
Thereafter, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Thus it has been stated in the Śāradā:

The best of teachers should duly place the nine vowels in the nine substrates: in the locus of support, the foundation, the navel, the heart, and again the feet; then in the *bindu*, the *nāda*, the *śakti*, and finally in Śiva.

The meaning is that one should assign the nine vowels to the nine locations: the *mūlādhāra*, the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, the navel, the heart, the throat, the space between the eyebrows, the head, the region above that, and the twelve-petaled lotus.
Then, the wise practitioner should assign the consonants beginning with *ha* to the face, starting from the head.
The best of teachers, being composed, [should place] the groups of Vedas and the phonemes upon the arms and feet in the directions of Up, Mahendra, Yama, and West;
and the phonemes [should be placed] according to the sequence of the base, the secondary base, the tip, and the middle.
In that regard, the fingertips are the "upper parts" (agramaṅguli); the roots are the shoulders and so forth; and near the roots are the elbows and knees.
"Upāgra" refers to the first joint of the fingers and toes; "maṇibandha" and "gulpha" refer to the wrists and ankles.

By the term "samāhita," it is meant that one should remain attentive, avoiding any inversion of the positions. This has also been stated in the *Śāradā-tantra* regarding even those [mudrās] corrupted by improper mental disposition (*bhāva*).
One should place the three letters beginning with Śā [Śa, Ṣa, Sa] in sequence in the secret place, the heart, and between the eyebrows.
In the process of emanation (sṛṣṭi), it ends with emission (sarga); in the process of maintenance (sthiti), fire and wind are dear;
one should place [the letters] in the sequence of ether and earth, ending with the bindu and emission.
In the process of withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*), one should arrange [the letters] in reverse order, adorned with the *bindu*.
In the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), the meaning is that one should arrange that same sequence ending with the *bhūtalipi* at the conclusion of emission;
in the process of maintenance (*sthiti*), the meaning is that one should arrange it in due order, ending with the *bindu* and the *sarga*.
In this regard, the sequence is as follows:
ūṃḥ iṃḥ ṛṃḥ aṃḥ ḷṃḥ oṃḥ auṃḥ aiṃḥ eṃḥ raṃḥ yaṃḥ vaṃḥ haṃḥ laṃḥ khaṃḥ kaṃḥ ghaṃḥ gaṃḥ ṅaṃḥ chaṃḥ caṃḥ jhaṃḥ jaṃḥ ñaṃḥ ṭhaṃḥ ṭaṃḥ ḍhaṃḥ ḍaṃḥ ṇaṃḥ thaṃḥ taṃḥ dhaṃḥ daṃḥ naṃḥ phaṃḥ paṃḥ bhaṃḥ baṃḥ.
*Maṃḥ*, *saṃḥ*, *ṣaṃḥ*, *śaṃḥ*. However,

someone has said that one should first place all the letters of the fire-group (*vahni-varga*), then the letters of the wind-group (*marut-varga*), then these ending with water (*jala*) along with the nasal bindu (*bindu*), and finally the letters of space (*viyat*) and earth (*bhūmi*) with the visarga (*visarga*).
In the *Śāradā*:
"The most excellent practitioner, initiated by the path taught in the *Āgamas*,
should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) one hundred thousand times, recite [the mantra] that many times, and likewise offer ten thousand sesame seeds as oblations."
"Up to that point" means one hundred thousand.
In this regard, the sequence should be understood as one placement (nyāsa) and one recitation (āvṛtti). As stated in the Śāradā:
The wise practitioner should worship the Goddess daily upon the pedestal (pīṭha) previously described.
By the phrase "previously described," it is indicated that one should also worship the pedestal-shaktis (pīṭha-śakti) belonging to the section on Sarasvatī here as well.
Therefore, having fashioned an eight-petaled, sixteen-petaled, thirty-two-petaled, sixty-four-petaled lotus, and a square (bhūpura), one should [proceed] there.
One should worship the power of the seat (pīṭhaśakti).
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
One should prepare a seat with a lotus of [the appropriate] color and fashion the form with the root mantra.
One should worship the Goddess upon this [seat], together with her limbs and the surrounding enclosures (āvaraṇas).
It is taught that first comes the enclosure of the limbs, and afterwards the enclosure consisting of Ambikā and the others.
The second was proclaimed by the Mothers, and the third indeed by the eight Śaktis.
The fourth is declared to be the fifth [layer] with thirty-two Śaktis;
the sixth is remembered as having sixty-four Śaktis along with the world-protectors (lokapālakas).
The seventh is the enclosure of these, and the eighth enclosure shall be within the mantra.
Having provided a seat upon the lotus of the [respective] color and having conceived the form there by means of the root mantra, one should worship the Goddess therein;
having worshipped the limbs (aṅgas) upon the filaments, one should worship the four Ambikās and others above that; then Brāhmī and the others upon the petals of the directions;

then Karālā and the others upon the sixteen petals; Vidyā and the others upon the thirty-two petals; and Piṅgalā and the others upon the sixty-four petals. One should perform the worship in this manner.
Above that, on the *bhūpura*, are the world-protectors (*lokapālas*) and their weapons. With the syllable *he sauḥ* upon a multi-colored lotus, there is the *bhūtalipi* (earth-writing) and Sarasvatī.
The ritual application is: "Obeisance to the Yoga-pīṭha."
Śāradā.
Thus should the venerable Śrībhūtalipidevatā, the sustainer of the world, be worshipped according to the rules in the aforementioned locations; her limbs should be worshipped as before.
As before, it is like the section on Sarasvatī.
Ambikā, Vāgbhavī, Durgā, and Śrīśakti are described by the aforementioned characteristics.
Brāhmī and the others are to be worshipped as before, along with Karālī, Vikarālī, Umā,
Sarasvatī, Śrī, Durgā, Gaurī, Lakṣmī, Śruti, Smṛti, and Dhṛti.
Śraddhā, Medhā, Mati, Kānti, and Āryā are the sixteen Śaktis.
Dark-complexioned and well-adorned, they should be worshipped as bearing swords and shields.
Furthermore, Vidyā, Śrī, Puṣṭi, Prajñā, Sinīvālī, and Kuhū.

Prabhā is the heroic power of Rudra; Nandā is auspicious and bestows prosperity upon those who grind [her mantra]. Kālarātri, Mahārātri, Bhadrakālī, Kapālinī, Prakṛti, Daṇḍinī, Muṇḍinī, Indukhaṇḍā, and Śikhaṇḍinī [are likewise].
The slayer of Niśumbha and Śumbha, the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura;
she who is Indrāṇī and Rudrāṇī, whose body is half that of Śaṅkara;
she who is Nārī and Nārāyaṇī, and who bears both the trident and the noose.
Ambikā and Hlādinī— these thirty-two auspicious Śaktis,
holding discs in their hands, with faces like Piśācas, and adorned with beautiful ornaments, are to be worshipped; as are Piṅgalāṅgī, Piśācākṣī, Samṛddhi, and Vṛddhi.
Śraddhā, Svāhā, Svadhā, Bhikṣā, Māyā, Saṃjñā, Vasuṃdharā;
Trilokarātri, Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Tridaśeśvarī; Svarūpā, Bahurūpā, Skandamātā, and Hutapriyā.
Vimalā, Āmalā, Aruṇī, and Pūrṇavāruṇī;
Prakṛti, Vikṛti, Sṛṣṭi, Sthiti, and Saṃhṛti;
Sandhyā, Māyā, Satī, Haṃsī, Mardikī, Raktikī, and Parā.
The divine mother is the blessed Devakī, whose seat is the lotus;
another is three-faced and seven-faced, the crusher of gods and demons;
she has hanging lips, upward-pointing hair, many heads, and a belly like that of a wolf.
After Ratharekhā, there was Śaśirekhā;
then Gaganavegā and Pavanavegā; after that, the one named Bhuvanapālā, and then Madanāturā.
Aṅganā, Anaṅgavadanā, likewise Anaṅgamekhalā,
Anaṅgakusumā, Viśvarūpā, Surabhayaṅkarī, Ākhyā,
Hvasatyavādinī, Vajrarūpā, and Śucivratā.
Varadā and Vāgīśī are proclaimed as the sixty-four [deities];
all of them bear bows and arrows, possess the splendor of a blazing ocean, and are endowed with great radiance;
they have fangs, their hair stands erect, and their minds are intent upon the commencement of battle.
Blazing with all ornaments, they are to be worshipped with great effort.
The Lords of the World (Lokeśas) are to be worshipped as before, and likewise the Vajra and other [deities].
The mantra-practitioner who worships the deities of the Śrī Bhūtalipi in this manner—
He shall become a vessel for the fortune of speech and will be honored even by the gods;
by offering ten thousand lotuses into the fire, one may bring a king under one's control;
likewise, for one who offers blue lotuses, great prosperity (Mahālakṣmī) arises.
By offering oblations of *palāśa* flowers for one year, one becomes a poet;
by an oblation of salt from a horse (*vājīlavaṇa*), one brings a woman under one's control.
The practitioner should also perform here the rites mentioned in the *Mātṛkā*.
The man who worships the mantra by encasing it with the *bhūtalipi* (earth-script) one hundred times,
both in direct and reverse order, for him the mantra becomes perfected;
thus it is stated in the *Kubjikātantra*.
Immediately after the meditative absorption.

Having meditated thus, O Maheśānī, one should recite that [mantra] with a tranquil mind. The preliminary rite (*puraskriyā*) consists of one hundred repetitions of the *bhūtalipi* (earth-script) in both direct and reverse order. Whatever mantra a person recites after encasing it within the *bhūtalipi*, [it becomes effective].

By means of a thousand repetitions, success will certainly be achieved through force. One should recite the mantra for one month enclosed by the *bhūtalipi* (earth-script) in both forward and reverse order, O lady of excellent hips; thereafter, unsurpassed success is attained.
For the purpose of pacifying defects in the mantra, the performance of the ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras) is also recorded in the Śāradā-tantra.
Therefore, this has been written by the venerable Bhaṭṭācārya Kṛṣṇānanda Āgamavāgīśa— the most eminent in the heart-felt assemblies of the very aged great-grandfathers— in his own *Tantrasāra*;
it should be consulted there by those who seek it.
Even regarding other defects, ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras) have been taught in the Samayācāra-tantra, as follows:
Having received the mantra from the guru and having recited it as a means to attain that goal,
O beautiful one, O lady of excellent countenance, if he should practice wicked conduct through negligence or even through laziness, that mantra will become devoid of power.
For the sake of destroying such defects as these, one should perform the ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras).
Thus concludes the procedure for pacifying defects in mantras.
Having extracted [the following] from the tantric scriptures for the purpose of awakening to the conventions of the seed-syllables (*bīja*),
I shall state some of the names of these seeds for the delight of the learned:
Māyā, Lajjā, Parā Saṃvit, Triguṇā, and Bhuvaneśvarī.

Hṛllekhā, Śambhuvanitā, Śakti, Devīśvarī, Śivā, Mahāmāyā, Pārvatī, she who assumes forms through her various manifestations, Parameśvarī, Bhuvanā, Dhātrī, and she who dwells within the life-force— strīṃ.
In the absence of fire (the letter *ra*), joined with the weapon (*ha*) and *māyā* (*ī*), it is proclaimed as the "stable *māyā*": *hrīṃ*.
The *Praṇava* of Lakṣmī is said to consist of *Śā*, *Agni* (Ra), *Śānti* (U), *Bindu*, and *Nāda*.
Śrī, Lakṣmī, Viṣṇu’s consort, Ramā, and she born from the Ocean of Milk—*Śrīṃ*.

The sixteenth consonant (ṣ), joined with the fire (r) and the left eye (ī) and the bindu (ṃ), mounted upon the seed-syllable of the moon (s)—this is known as the seed-syllable of the bride (badhū). *Badhū*, *vāmekṣaṇā*, *yoṣit*, *ekākṣī*, *strī*, and *kāminī* all refer to a woman. *Strīṃ*.
The twelfth deity, conjoined with *nāda* and *bindu*, is the *bhaga*;
the womb is Sarasvatī, the seed-syllable below is Vāgbhava, and it is Speech: *Aiṃ*.

The syllable *ha*, enriched by the left ear (*vāmakarṇa*) and adorned with the *nāda* and *bindu*, is called the *kūrca*, the wrathful, the fierce pride, and the long *hūṃ*. It is also known as Sound, the Long Armor, Tārā, and Procreation. *Hūṃ*.
The syllable of Kāma situated in fire (Ra), adorned with Rati and the Bindu—this is declared to be the seed-syllable of Kālī; indeed, that very same thing is the seed-syllable of Rati. *Krīṃ*.
The syllable of Kāmā, situated on the earth (Dha) and adorned with the drop of Rati (I), is this secret seed-syllable of Kālī; it is also known as the seed-syllable of Gopāla.
That is the seed-syllable of desire, the seed-syllable of Kāmeśī; she is the supreme Śakti. KLĪM.
The Śaiva temple is said to consist of six, two, four, zero, one, and nine [units]; *Hauṃ*.
The first [syllable] is Kalā, the seed-syllable Kledinī, and the syllable Kroṃ is named Aṅkuśa. Kroṃ.
The letter *Ā* with a *bindu* is declared to be the noose (*pāśa*) and the serpent Śeṣa.
*Sakalā* is Bhuvaneśānī; she is called the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Kāmeśī.
*Namaḥ* is the heart; *svāhā* is the pair of *dviṭha* (the two *ṭha*s), namely *ṭha-ṭhaḥ*.
Homage! Svāhā!
The pair of moons, Śiva, the Mother of the Vedas, she who is beautiful as fire—
Svāhā, the Supreme, the food of the gods, the two *ṭha*s, the pair of moons, the ladle, the oblation,
the Mother of the Vedas, the mouth of the gods, she who is beautiful as fire— Svāhā.
Śikhā is Vaṣaṭ, the center of the head, the mother of Śakra, and the beloved of Hara;
Śikhā is Vaṣaṭ.
Vaṣaṭ is the armor (kavaca), Krodha is the shield (varma), and also Hum.
I am the one called Wrath, and I am the attenuation [of the enemy] in weapons and the like; the enemy is designated as "Hūṃ. Hūṃ!
Vauṣaṭ to the pair of eyes consisting of weapons! Vaṣaṭ!
Phaṭ! Astra is the weapon, the armament. Phaṭ!
The third, however, is *hesauḥ*, the seed-syllable of the preta: *hesauḥ*.
The *haṃsa* is the *ajapā* mantra. *Haṃsaḥ*.
The syllable *ga* accompanied by the *bindu* is the seed-syllable of Vighna and the seed-syllable of Gaṇeśa.
The syllable *gaṃ* is the letter *ma*, with the vowel *i* and joined by the nasal drop (*bindu*).
The seed-syllable of the Earth is declared as *laṃ*.
The seed-syllable of the Bimba is the letter *ṭha* with a nasal bindu (*ṃ*), joined with the fire (*ra*), the eye (*i*), and the moon (*u*). It is: *ḍrīṃ*.
Now, the Kāmakalā consists of the left eye (I) joined with the Bindu (M), the Sun (R) with its measure (M), Kalā (L), Vāṇī (I), Nāda (H), Ardhendu (S), and Sadāśiva (AU).
This is the unutterable Turyā, the supreme Kalā who is the Mother of the Universe (Ń). [The mantra is: ŃĀDAḤ].
For the sake of awakening to the conventions of the Bhūtaḍāmara, the names of the seed-syllables (bīja) of the Bhūtaḍāmarīs are also written here.
The *praṇava* is the seed-syllable of poison; it is certainly known as *hālāhala*. It should be understood as the path of the ear of Time (*kāla*), multiform and stainless—the *praṇava*.
The seed-syllable residing in blood, having the sky as its mouth, adorned by Dhūmra-Bhairavī, and joined with Nāda and Bindu, is known as the essence of the vital breath (prāṇa). Hrīṃ.
One should know Krodhīśa as mounted upon Kṣata and adorned by Dhūmrabhairavī;
it is joined with the tongue (jihvā) and the bindu, and is remembered as Pitr-bhuvāsinī. KRĪṂ.

One should make the seed-syllable consisting of wrath and time (krodhakālātman) as derived from the elements (bhautika), known as Vāgbhava; joined with Nāda and Bindu, it is the fierce Bhairavī. This seed-syllable is said to be that which sets pure intelligence in motion. Aiṃ.
Krodhīśa with Balabhṛt and Dhūmrabhairavī, along with Nāda and Bindu;
Trimūrti and Manmatha, Kāmarāja and Trailokyamohana; seated upon Indra’s throne, the embodiment of Brahmā together with Manmatha: *klīṃ*.
Joined with Dhūmrabhairavī and situated upon the letter Ra, it is the consumer of offerings;
conjoined with Nāda and Bindu, it is the supreme seed-syllable of Kiṅkiṇī: Hrīṃ.
The great mantra known as Viśikha, joined with *nāda* and *bindu*, residing in the blood, consuming the sacrificial offering (*balibhojana*), and seated upon the throne of Kālarātri: HRĀM.
Vasiṣṭha, whose face is embraced by [the goddess] Vidārī and who is drenched in blood, joined with the *nāda* and *bindu*, is to be known as Piśitāśana. HŪM.

Beneath the smoke-bannered [letter *dhūmra*] is the Fire of Time (*kālāgni*), together with the upward-pointing hair (*ūrdhvakeśī*) and the lunar drop (*indubindu*). This seed-syllable that brings about the end of the age was revealed by Bhairava: *SPHEṂ*.
Having taken up Kapardin, whose body is smeared with blood, who is united with Dhūmrabhairavī, and who possesses the syllable *kṣauḥ* along with the *nāda* and *bindu*: *prīṃ*.
Taking up two skull-bowls adorned with Mahākāla, this is declared to be the "Equal Seat" (samāsana); one should employ it as being enriched by Caṇḍikā.
Ṭhaṃ ṭhaṃ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ.
Seated upon blood, with a face like the sky and adorned with a crescent moon, she is proclaimed as Khadyota; she is Grāsinī, joined with Kālarātri. Hraṃ hraṃ.
The sky sprinkled with blood, adorned with sound and the bindu,
further embellished by the vidārī [mudrā], and the seed-syllable of the son of Vivasvat— HRĀṂ.
And that which is called Kīrtti, with its mouth of Time, was accomplished by Mahākāla;
it is the primordial five-rayed rite that effects creation, preservation, and destruction. Om.
Situated in the sky, located in the *tālajaṅgha*, adorned with the *bindu* and *nāda*,
the *kūrca*, Kāla, Mahākāla, the seed-syllable of Wrath, the stainless *Hūṃ*.
Pṛthvīpāla, the lord of Navadvīpa, the high-minded Kṛṣṇacandra, that great soul who was honored for his learning and Brahmanical status,
begot this self-controlled Īśānacandra; from him was born he who, through the grace of his chosen deity, attained the station of a world-conqueror while still in the womb.
Therefore, let this wonderful section on creation, which yields the desired fruit for the learned, be commenced today.
The *haṃsa* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the moon is the mind (*manas*); Kṛṣṇa has entered the middle of these two.
At the rising of the Gauḍa [wine], the two suns and moons—the illustrious Prāṇa and Kṛṣṇacandra—appear together.
Because he caused the auspicious rite of the distribution of food (annadā-maṅgala) to be performed in the local dialect,
therefore, in a foreign land, [the fame] of King Kṛṣṇacandra shone like the new moon.

This pure, radiant light, arisen in the language of the Jinas, illuminating the universe and acting as the sun for the world, has emerged from the *Śrī-Prāṇatoṣiṇī*. On this earth, there was a glorious swan named Prāṇakṛṣṇa, who attained liberation and has not set.
"Endowed with eternal fame, he is forever possessed of constant rising.
Thus ends [this section] in the *Śrīprāṇatoṣiṇī*, composed by the scholar Śrī Rāmatoṣaṇa Vidyālaṅkāra, approved by the illustrious Prāṇakṛṣṇa Viśvāsa.
The Sarga-kāṇḍa, comprising the tenth chapter consisting of the description of the fruits [of actions], is completed.
End of the first Kāṇḍa; the Sarga-kāṇḍa is finished.
